Costa Rica has built a tourism economy on the promise that its wildlife stays where it is, and the law that protects it does not distinguish between deliberate trafficking and a souvenir picked up without a second thought. Enforcement at the airports has been running for years. What is new is the effort to explain it before anyone reaches the gate.

World.title: Costa Rica Pressed to Improve Conditions for Indigenous Coffee Workers
World.content:
More than 500 people and organizations, among them three former presidents of Costa Rica and Panama, have signed a public statement demanding that the Costa Rican state guarantee decent living, working and social protection conditions for the Ngäbe-Buglé workers who pick coffee each year.

The Kioscos Socioambientales program at the University of Costa Rica, which coordinated the effort, reported 512 signatures in all. They include roughly a hundred Indigenous, labor, community, feminist, coastal, environmental and social organizations from Costa Rica and Panama, along with academics, artists and professionals.

Former Costa Rican presidents Abel Pacheco de la Espriella and Laura Chinchilla Miranda signed, as did former Panamanian president Ricardo de la Espriella Toral, who governed from 1982 to 1984. Writer Ana Cristina Rossi Lara, musician Manuel Obregón López and the bands Malpaís, Sonámbulo Psicotropical and Un Rojo Reggae Band are also among the signatories.

The statement was presented publicly on July 21, roughly four months before the main harvest opens in November and while coffee regions prepare for seasonal labor arrives.

It responds to a February internal report written by Randy Ramírez Coto, acting chief of the Judicial Investigation Agency’s Los Santos Regional Unit, and addressed to the OIJ press office. Ramírez wrote that his purpose was to make visible what he described as the dehumanization of the Ngäbe-Buglé population in Los Santos, the coffee-growing region south of San José that supplies a substantial share of national production. The report linked the conditions he described to barriers in health care access, an absence of institutional follow-up and the deaths of children.

Between January 1, 2020 and February 11, 2026, the report recorded 19 deaths of Ngäbe-Buglé minors from Panama in the Los Santos area. Bronchopneumonia was the registered cause in 10 cases. The document also listed two suicides, one death during childbirth, one caused by parasitic infection and five cases awaiting forensic autopsy.

According to the report, the cases shared health-related circumstances that included births in inadequate settings, untreated respiratory illness and missing vaccinations. The document stated that all of the deaths could have been prevented, tying that assessment to the absence of timely preventive public health care, vaccination and epidemiological reporting. An initial review of child deaths across the region identified 17 cases; a subsequent review focused specifically on the Ngäbe-Buglé population raised the count to 19.

The Los Santos harvest generally runs from November through late February. The report noted that the work historically depended on Costa Rican and Nicaraguan labor, but in recent years has fallen mainly to Ngäbe-Buglé workers from Panama, many of them from Bocas del Toro, Chiriquí and Veraguas.

On housing, the report described workers being placed in temporary lodgings known locally as baches, with conditions that varied sharply. Some sit near canton centers with access to basic services. Others are in remote mountain areas among the coffee plantations, where residents depend on transport provided by farm owners. The report questioned whether those spaces are subject to regular oversight, stating that the regional unit’s inquiry found no evidence of follow-up visits during the period some of the lodgings were in operation.

The document also raised a registration gap. Costa Rica manages seasonal agricultural migration through the Migrant Labor Traceability System, known as SITLAM and administered by the Ministry of Labor and Social Security. In the deaths reviewed by the Los Santos unit, the report stated, SITLAM did not appear actively connected to the people involved, a difficulty the document placed in the context of irregular entry through mountainous sectors of the border with Panama.

The Ministry of Health has said it carries out physical and sanitary assessments of the lodgings used by coffee workers, both before and during the season, to verify sanitary requirements and habitability. On the deaths recorded by the OIJ, the ministry said the people involved had entered the country irregularly, which complicates the traceability and follow-up built into official registration and migration control mechanisms. The ministry added that irregular entry does not restrict access to health services, and that these workers retain the right to care under existing regulations and the country’s public health principles.

The Coffee Institute of Costa Rica, ICAFE, has said it takes part in working groups aimed at regularizing pickers’ migration status, promoting adequate hiring conditions and circulating information among producers and farm managers. The institute noted that enforcement of labor, migration, sanitary and housing rules falls to the competent authorities in each area, and said that everyone working in the coffee sector should do so in dignified and safe conditions consistent with Costa Rican law.

ICAFE reported that 39,608 pickers received temporary coverage through the Costa Rican Social Security Fund and a work-risk policy from the National Insurance Institute during the 2025–2026 harvest. Separately, ICAFE board president Fernando Naranjo Retana wrote in mid-July that 14,400 migrant pickers entered the country for that same season, and that the National Coffee Sustainability Fund invests between ₡600 million and ₡700 million a year — roughly $1.3 million to $1.5 million at the Central Bank reference rate — in primary health care for pickers and their families.

He also wrote that the Casas de la Alegría program, which provides childcare, meals and health monitoring for pickers’ children while their parents work, served more than 3,000 children across the country’s seven coffee regions last season. The statement asks authorities to investigate the circumstances surrounding the children’s deaths and determine institutional responsibility; to strengthen primary care, vaccination, epidemiological monitoring and maternal and child health services throughout the coffee season; and to carry out periodic, effective inspections of housing, transport, hiring and working conditions on all farms and in all lodgings used during the harvest.

It calls for full compliance with labor, sanitary, migration and social security law as it applies to migrant Indigenous workers, and for permanent coordination between public institutions, Ngäbe-Buglé organizations, host communities, coffee companies and human rights groups.

It further asks that information on health, work, housing and rights protection be published regularly, that coffee companies and every actor in the commercial chain assume responsibility for the rights of the workers who sustain the industry, and that the Labor Ministry build a permanent map of the coffee value chain — identifying principal companies, contractors and intermediaries, and geolocating their farms and lodgings — to monitor legal compliance and assign responsibility.

The organizers noted that in August 2020, more than a hundred social organizations issued a similar warning about conditions facing Ngäbe-Buglé workers during the harvest. Six years later, the statement argues, those concerns remain unresolved and their consequences have reached an unacceptable severity. Costa Rica’s General Protocol for the Attention of Labor Migration during harvest seasons was last updated in May 2024; the signatories contend that the gap lies between the rules on paper and their application on the ground.

The document was presented by Kioscos Socioambientales together with the Environmental Human Rights Clinic of the Institute of Latin American Studies at the National University, the Center for Research in Culture and Development at the State Distance University, and the Labor Relations Observatory at the University of Costa Rica’s law school. Speakers included Zeidy Brukwä Rodríguez, a Ngäbe-Buglé leader and member of the National Front of Indigenous Peoples; Rosibel Víquez Abarca of the State Distance University; Sharon López Céspedes of the National University; and Mauricio Álvarez Mora of the University of Costa Rica.

Days before the statement was released, the health ministries of Costa Rica and Panama signed a memorandum of understanding creating a Binational Health Card for Ngäbe-Buglé workers who move between the two countries for temporary agricultural work. Costa Rican Health Minister Alexander Sánchez Cabo and his Panamanian counterpart, Fernando Boyd Galindo, signed the agreement in San José in the presence of First Vice President Douglas Soto.

The physical card will be issued each July and remain valid for six months, a window that matches the period of heaviest cross-border movement. Panama’s health ministry designated the Bugaba intermediate care post in Chiriquí as the main issuing and renewal point. Boyd Galindo said the card would carry vaccination histories and other clinical information, and would help stop children from receiving repeat immunizations because their records were unavailable.

The Ministry of Labor and Social Security declined to say what action it had taken on the matter, indicating that it would not comment because the OIJ report is an internal document. The ministry has changed hands twice in recent weeks: Roy Thompson Chacón resigned on June 30, and President Laura Fernández Delgado named attorney Mercedes Flores Badilla as minister on July 20.

The harvest that prompted the statement begins in November. Whether the inspections, health coverage and registration the signatories are demanding will be in place by then is the question now sitting with the institutions named in the document.

World.title: Costa Rica Cuts 2026 Growth Forecast as El Niño Raises Cost Risks
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Central Bank has lowered its economic growth forecast for 2026 as weaker exports, slower household demand and the expected effects of El Niño increase pressure on agriculture, electricity generation and consumer prices. The bank now expects the Costa Rican economy to grow 3.4% this year, down from the 3.5% forecast issued in April and the 3.8% projected in January. Growth is expected to reach 3.5% in 2027, also one-tenth of a percentage point below the previous estimate.

The revision does not point to a recession, but it confirms that the economy is losing momentum after expanding 4.6% in 2025. Economic growth slowed from 4% during the first quarter of this year to 3.4% in the second quarter. Household spending and construction remain the main sources of support. Household consumption is forecast to grow 2.9% in 2026, while investment in buildings, equipment and other fixed assets is expected to rise 5.3%.

Construction grew 8.9% year over year during the second quarter. Financial and insurance services expanded 5.9%, while information and communications grew 4.4%. Exports present a more uneven picture. Total exports are expected to rise 2.4% this year, but that figure masks a projected 5.3% increase in goods exports and a 1.7% decline in services exports.



The slowdown reflects weaker international demand and reduced activity in business and manufacturing-related services. Costa Rica’s free trade zone economy is still expected to grow 4.6% during 2026, compared with 3.2% for businesses operating under the domestic tax system.

El Niño adds another layer of uncertainty. Current projections call for significantly below-average rainfall in the Pacific, Central Valley and parts of the Northern Zone, alongside higher temperatures across much of the country. Rainfall could fall as much as 60% below normal in the North Pacific and about 40% below normal in several other affected regions. The Caribbean and parts of the Northern Zone may experience the opposite pattern, with rainfall above historic averages.

Drier and hotter conditions could reduce yields for crops such as coffee and pineapple while limiting water and pasture available for cattle. Higher temperatures may also increase the spread of certain fungi and plant diseases. The outlook has already led to lower expectations for the agricultural sector. The Central Bank projects that agricultural production could contract in 2027 as weather damage combines with higher fertilizer and operating costs.

The risks extend beyond farms. Costa Rica depends heavily on hydroelectric plants, and lower water levels in reservoirs could force the Costa Rican Electricity Institute to generate more power using imported fuel. Thermal generation is substantially more expensive than hydropower. Greater reliance on fuel-powered plants could eventually raise electricity rates for homes and businesses, particularly if international oil prices remain elevated.

The Central Bank estimates that hydrocarbon prices will increase by an average of 28.2% during 2026. Fuel prices were already 15.5% higher in June than a year earlier. Those pressures are expected to gradually lift inflation after an extended period of unusually low or negative price growth. Average inflation should rise above 2%, though it is expected to remain below the bank’s 3% target.

Food and electricity represent the clearest risks for consumers. Lower agricultural production can push up grocery prices, while more expensive power generation can raise household bills and operating costs for hotels, restaurants, manufacturers and other businesses. The exchange rate continues to complicate the picture. The colón’s appreciation has helped limit the local cost of imported goods, but it has also placed pressure on tourism companies, exporters and other businesses that earn dollars while paying many expenses in colones.

The Central Bank reported purchasing $944.8 million in the foreign exchange market for stabilization purposes through July 30. International reserves stood at approximately $20.8 billion on July 28, equal to 18.1% of gross domestic product. The bank lowered its monetary policy rate to 3% in July, continuing a series of cuts that began in March 2023. Lower policy rates can eventually reduce borrowing costs, although the decline has only partially reached the interest rates offered by commercial banks.

Public finances remain another concern. Central government debt reached 61.1% of GDP in May, placing it above the 60% threshold that triggers stricter spending limits under Costa Rica’s fiscal rule. The government maintained a primary surplus, meaning revenue exceeded spending before interest payments, but the surplus fell from 0.7% of GDP in May 2025 to 0.6% a year later. The overall financial deficit increased from 1.1% to 1.3% during the same period.

Costa Rica’s economy is still growing faster than many developed countries, and strong construction, financial services and goods exports provide some protection against a sharper slowdown. However, the revised forecast shows that the country is entering the second half of 2026 with less room for error. A stronger-than-expected El Niño, further increases in fuel prices or weaker demand from major trading partners could place additional pressure on growth and household costs.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan Leads in Race to Head United Nations
World.content:
Costa Rican diplomat Rebeca Grynspan emerged as the early frontrunner to become the next leader of the United Nations after receiving the strongest support in the first informal vote by the U.N. Security Council today. Grynspan received 10 “encourage” votes, one “discourage” vote and four votes expressing no opinion from the council’s 15 members.

The secret, nonbinding vote was the opening round in what is expected to be a months-long process to choose a successor to Secretary-General António Guterres. Former Guyanese Foreign Minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett finished second with nine encouraging votes, while Rafael Grossi of Argentina, who heads the International Atomic Energy Agency, received seven.

The result places Grynspan in a strong early position, but it does not guarantee that she will advance to the final stage. The first rounds do not reveal whether opposition comes from China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom or the United States, the five permanent Security Council members with veto power.

A single veto from one of those countries could eventually block her candidacy. Later votes will use different-colored ballots to show whether discouraging votes come from permanent or elected members of the Security Council. Several rounds are expected before the council reaches an agreement, possibly in September or October.

The Security Council must ultimately recommend one candidate with at least nine votes in favor and no veto from a permanent member. The recommendation then goes to the 193-member U.N. General Assembly, which traditionally confirms the council’s choice. Other candidates include former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet, former Ecuadorian Foreign Minister María Fernanda Espinosa, former Senegalese President Macky Sall and Ugandan diplomat Olara Otunnu.

Bachelet and Sall each received six encouraging votes, while Espinosa received five and Otunnu received two. Diplomats familiar with the results said the first round showed no clear consensus despite Grynspan’s lead. The three candidates receiving the most support all come from Latin America and the Caribbean. The United Nations follows an informal system of regional rotation, and many diplomats expect the next secretary-general to come from the region.

There is also growing pressure for the United Nations to appoint a woman for the first time. Every secretary-general since the organization was founded in 1945 has been a man. Grynspan, 70, served as Costa Rica’s vice president from 1994 to 1998 during the administration of José María Figueres Olsen. She has also held senior positions with the United Nations Development Programme and the Ibero-American General Secretariat.

Since 2021, she has served as secretary-general of U.N. Trade and Development, known as UNCTAD. She took temporary unpaid leave from the position to concentrate on her campaign for the U.N.’s top job. Costa Rica officially submitted her candidacy on March 3, presenting her international experience, economic background and support for multilateral cooperation as central qualifications.

During her campaign, Grynspan has argued that the United Nations must become more effective, rebuild international trust and place greater emphasis on diplomacy and conflict mediation. She has also acknowledged that the organization faces severe financial pressure and will need to reduce duplication and set clearer priorities.

The next secretary-general will inherit an institution facing wars in several regions, growing tension among major powers and criticism over its ability to respond effectively to global crises. Funding shortages and unpaid contributions from member countries have also increased pressure for internal reform.



Guterres, a former Portuguese prime minister, will leave office on December 31 after serving two five-year terms. His successor is expected to begin a five-year term on January 1, 2027. Thursday’s result gives Grynspan important momentum and places a Costa Rican at the front of a major international contest. The more difficult test will come in later rounds, when the positions of the five veto-holding countries become clearer.

World.title: Costa Rica Investigates Jaguar Pelt Seized in Heredia Raid
World.content:
An apparent jaguar pelt found inside a home during raids against a violent criminal group has opened a separate wildlife investigation alongside an organized crime case involving drugs, weapons and homicide. The Judicial Investigation Organization (OIJ) carried out eight raids early this morning in Heredia, Aserrí and Desamparados. Ten suspects were detained, including alleged members of a group operating primarily from the La Gran Samaria neighborhood in Heredia.

Investigators believe the organization carried out tumbonazos, a term used in Costa Rica for armed robberies in which criminals steal drugs, money or other contraband from rival trafficking groups. Some groups pose as police officers to enter homes or intercept shipments.

Agents seized an apparent jaguar pelt inside one of the properties. Michael Soto, interim director of the Judicial Investigation Organization, said the discovery is now being examined as a possible violation of Costa Rica’s Wildlife Conservation Law. Authorities have not determined where the pelt originated, how it reached the house or whether the animal was killed in Costa Rica. It is also unclear whether the pelt was being kept as a trophy, offered for sale or moved as part of a wildlife-trafficking operation.

Investigators will also need to formally confirm that the skin came from a jaguar. The jaguar, known scientifically as Panthera onca, is classified as an endangered species under Costa Rican wildlife regulations. National law allows wildlife officials to confiscate animals, skins, body parts and other products linked to suspected illegal hunting, transport or trade.

The discovery could therefore produce an additional criminal case separate from the drug and homicide investigation. Any charges will depend on what authorities establish about the pelt’s authenticity, origin and chain of possession.

The criminal group targeted today is also suspected of involvement in the September 2025 killing of a man in Barreal de Heredia. Investigators believe the homicide followed a dispute involving drugs and that the group hired gunmen from southern San José neighborhoods to carry it out.

A pistol recovered during the raids could be connected to the killing and will undergo forensic testing. The suspects are also believed to have links to another organization dismantled during raids in Santa Bárbara de Heredia on July 9. Six people were detained in that operation, where authorities found counterfeit OIJ vests and high-caliber weapons allegedly used during armed home invasions.

The ten people detained today were transferred to prosecutors, who will determine what precautionary measures to request while the investigation continues. The jaguar pelt remains one of the operation’s most unusual pieces of evidence. What began as a raid focused on violent drug-related crime could now expand into an investigation involving the illegal possession, hunting or trafficking of one of Costa Rica’s most protected wild animals.

World.title: Krismar Espinosa found guilty of executing Wilbert Banks Jr. in jealousy-fuelled execution
World.content:
Krismar Espinosa found guilty of executing Wilbert Banks Jr. in jealousy-fuelled execution

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Thirty-six-year-old Krismar Espinosa was found guilty on Friday afternoon of the April 2024 murder of bicycle technician and cycling enthusiast Wilbert E. Banks Jr., who was shot seven times after being lured to the Lake Garden area of Ladyville by a woman at the center of the feud.

Justice Nigel Pilgrim delivered the verdict shortly after 1 p.m. in a courtroom filled with relatives of both men. The decision brought an emotional moment for Banks’ family, who had waited more than two years for the case to be concluded.

After reviewing the evidence, Justice Pilgrim said the court was satisfied that Espinosa shot and killed Banks without legal justification in what he described as an execution-style killing. The judge rejected Espinosa’s defence as untrue and found the prosecution’s main witness—Espinosa’s former girlfriend and Banks’ former partner—to be truthful, credible and reliable.

The woman testified by video link that Espinosa became jealous after finding a photograph of Banks and accused her of continuing a relationship with him. She said Espinosa threatened to kill her and her son unless she helped lure Banks to Lake Garden Road.

According to her testimony, Espinosa borrowed his employer’s vehicle and dropped her off in Belize City. Banks later encountered her and offered to drive her back to Ladyville. When they reached Lake Garden, she exited Banks’ vehicle and Espinosa emerged and opened fire from the passenger side.

Banks attempted to escape but was struck by additional gunfire, lost control of his vehicle and crashed. The witness said she ran from the scene, but Espinosa chased her, forced her into his vehicle and threatened her against speaking about the killing.

Police recovered her cellphone near the murder scene, leading investigators to the Lords Bank home where she and Espinosa were found. Officers had also recovered nine expended 9mm shells at the scene. Public reporting at the time stated that Banks was found mortally wounded inside his crashed vehicle shortly after 11:30 p.m. on April 5, 2024.

Justice Pilgrim acknowledged that the woman’s evidence had to be treated cautiously because she had participated in luring Banks to the location. However, he concluded that she acted under threats of violence and that her account was strongly supported by the gunshot damage to Banks’ vehicle, the medical evidence and the physical evidence recovered by police.

The court also questioned Espinosa’s credibility, particularly the conflicting explanations he gave for borrowing his employer’s vehicle. Espinosa claimed he had taken the vehicle to run an errand, later said he went to purchase food and also alleged that the vehicle ran out of fuel. The judge found that those explanations did not correspond with his employer’s testimony.

Espinosa had denied the allegations, claiming he was home between approximately 8:50 and 11 p.m. on the night of the murder and that the case against him had been fabricated.

Banks, 38, worked for several years at Ordonez Bike Shop and was well known within Belize’s cycling community. Friends and relatives publicly remembered him as a quiet, humble and helpful man who was passionate about bicycles and cycling.

Crown Counsels Maria Santana-Nembhard and Joseph Perez prosecuted the case, while Espinosa was represented by attorney Michael Peyrefitte.

Sentencing has been scheduled for September 7, 2026. Justice Pilgrim ordered the preparation of a Social Inquiry Report, a prison report and a Victim Impact Statement ahead of the sentencing hearing.

World.title: Belize Rural North Area Representative rejects voter transfer “incentives”, says resources should benefit community
World.content:
Belize Rural North Area Representative rejects voter transfer “incentives”, says resources should benefit community

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Today, Belize Rural North Area Representative Marconi Leal publicly rejected the practice of offering incentives to encourage voters to transfer into a constituency, saying he will not compromise his principles or divert resources away from community development to increase the voters list.

Leal described the voter transfer period as a “stressful season” for area representatives and said he has faced direct requests from individuals seeking payment in exchange for transferring and voting for him.

“As much as I want to increase my voters list, I will not do it at the expense of having to give ‘something’ before you have even had the opportunity to vote for me,” Leal wrote.

He questioned the commitment of individuals who transfer into the constituency for incentives and later move their registration elsewhere, describing them as “jumpers” who, in his view, have little interest in the long-term development of the communities he serves.

Leal said he has been receiving messages from people asking, “What are you willing to give me to transfer and vote for you!?” He criticized what he described as a transactional approach to voter transfers, arguing that some individuals are more concerned about what they can receive than the development of the constituency.

The area representative said he remains focused on serving the 24 villages in Belize Rural North and responding to their development priorities. “If I were to lose the next elections because of not doing so then so be it,” Leal said adding that he would rather use available resources to support residents and communities than pay individuals to transfer their votes.

Leal said he welcomes eligible voters who seek guidance on polling locations, electoral boundaries or limited transportation assistance, saying such requests demonstrate concern for their communities and country.

World.title: International News: Heat wave scorches U.S. as millions face alerts and temperatures near 120°F
World.content:
International News: Heat wave scorches U.S. as millions face alerts and temperatures near 120°F

By Zoila Palma: A dangerous heat wave is gripping large parts of the United States, with more than 39 million people under heat alerts as temperatures soar across the South and Southwest.

Temperatures have climbed above 100°F in several cities, while highs of 119°F were recorded Thursday near Topock, Arizona, and Tecopa, California, according to the National Weather Service.

The heat dome that previously brought extreme temperatures to central and eastern parts of the country has shifted west and is expected to intensify before spreading into the Intermountain West and northern High Plains.

Parts of the Southwest could see temperatures between 110°F and 120°F through early next week, with some areas potentially experiencing one of their 10 hottest days on record, Yahoo reports.

Extreme heat warnings are in effect across parts of Arizona, California, Nevada, Utah, Oklahoma and western Arkansas, including major population centers and popular national parks. Heat index values could reach 120°F in parts of southern Arizona and South Texas, while overnight temperatures are expected to remain dangerously high, offering little relief from the heat.

World.title: International News: Fast- fashion giant Shein reports $99 million quarterly loss as US tariffs weigh on sales
World.content:
International News: Fast- fashion giant Shein reports $99 million quarterly loss as US tariffs weigh on sales

By Zoila Palma: Fast-fashion giant Shein has reported a $99 million loss for the first three months of 2026, a sharp reversal from the $395 million net income recorded during the same period a year earlier.

The company attributed part of the decline to slower US sales following the removal of a tariff exemption on low-value packages, while ongoing uncertainty over US-China trade tensions has also affected its business.

Shein said the elimination of the US “de minimis” exemption, which previously allowed goods valued at $800 or less to enter the country without tariffs, has negatively affected sales and overall revenue growth.

In response to higher duties and taxes, the company said it is considering several measures, including raising prices in the US to offset some of the increased costs, BBC reports.

The company also reported that the conflict involving Iran had weakened demand, raised operating costs and caused delivery delays in some markets. However, the first-quarter loss included a $328 million paper loss linked to an accounting change involving special investor shares, meaning the underlying financial performance was affected by factors beyond direct operating results.

The latest financial disclosure comes as Shein prepares for a potential stock market debut in Hong Kong after receiving approval from China’s securities regulator.

World.title: Consumer confidence dips slightly in June as Belizeans remain cautious about major purchases
World.content:
Consumer confidence dips slightly in June as Belizeans remain cautious about major purchases

By Zoila Palma: Consumer confidence in Belize edged lower in June 2026, with the national Consumer Confidence Index (CCI) falling marginally by 0.4 percent to 41.1, down from 41.3 in May, according to the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB). The decline continues a downward trend seen in recent months, although at a slower pace than the sharper decreases recorded earlier in the year.

The SIB said the decline was mainly driven by weaker sentiment toward major household purchases and current economic conditions. The Durable Goods component fell by 8.5 percent, from 37.6 to 34.4, indicating increased pessimism about purchasing items such as homes, vehicles, furniture and appliances. The Present component also declined by 0.9 percent, from 37.9 to 37.6, as consumers became slightly more pessimistic about current economic conditions and their household finances.

However, consumers were more optimistic about the year ahead. The Expectations component rose by 6.4 percent, moving from a pessimistic 48.3 in May to an optimistic 51.4 in June, reflecting improved views of future economic conditions and household finances. By district, Orange Walk recorded the largest decline in confidence, falling 8.9 percent to 36.0, while Cayo saw the biggest improvement, with confidence rising 6.5 percent from 38.5 to 41.0.

The CCI, which ranges from zero to 100, measures consumer sentiment about the economy, household finances and major purchases, with a score above 50 generally indicating optimism. The index is considered an early indicator of future household spending, saving and investment, and therefore can provide insight into potential economic growth.

World.title: Ministry of Agriculture conclude Value-Added Beekeeping Products Training for Maya Mopan Bee Cooperative
World.content:
Ministry of Agriculture conclude Value-Added Beekeeping Products Training for Maya Mopan Bee Cooperative

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Stann Creek Department of Agriculture, through the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries (MAFSNGI), successfully conducted a Value-Added Beekeeping Products Training for members of the Maya Mopan Bee Cooperative.

The training was funded through the Climate Resilient and Sustainable Agriculture Project (CRESAP).

The training was designed to strengthen the capacity of beekeepers by introducing value-added processing techniques that enable participants to diversify their enterprises and maximize the economic potential of hive products.

CRESAP noted that by expanding beyond honey production, beekeepers can explore new market opportunities, increase the value of their products, and improve the sustainability of their operations.

World.title: UNICEF, Caribbean Climate Change Centre strengthen partnership on child-focused climate action
World.content:
UNICEF, Caribbean Climate Change Centre strengthen partnership on child-focused climate action

By Zoila Palma: UNICEF and the Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (CCCCC) have signed a five-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) aimed at strengthening efforts to protect children’s rights and well-being from the growing impacts of climate change across the Caribbean.

The partnership will promote child-sensitive climate policies, resilient social services, climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction, while giving young people greater opportunities to participate in climate action and decision-making.

Children across the region are increasingly exposed to hurricanes, flooding, droughts, extreme heat and environmental degradation, threatening access to education, healthcare, nutrition, clean water and sanitation.

UNICEF Representative Sajid Ali said climate change is not only an environmental issue but also a child rights challenge, noting that children are among those least responsible for the climate crisis while facing some of its greatest consequences.

CCCCC Executive Director Dr. Colin Young welcomed the agreement, saying children and youth have not traditionally been a central focus of climate resilience programming and that the partnership will help place them at the heart of regional climate action.

A key area of collaboration will focus on climate-resilient sanitation services, alongside efforts to strengthen education, health, nutrition, water and sanitation systems and disaster preparedness.

World.title: Wheatley granted injunction barring IC charges until judicial review
World.content:
Andrew Wheatley

The Supreme Court has granted an injunction preventing the Integrity Commission (IC) from charging Cabinet Minister Dr Andrew Wheatley until the hearing and determination of an application by his lawyers for judicial review.

Wheatley had applied for leave to pursue judicial review against the IC’s recommendation that he be charged with illicit enrichment.

Observer Online understands that the Supreme Court on Friday granted Wheatley’s application, recommending that the judicial review be heard by a panel of three judges.

Before granting the injunction, presiding Judge Justice David Batts had suggested that the IC consider an undertaking not to charge Dr Wheatley until the hearing and determination of the judicial review.

The commission said it could not give an undertaking at this time. The judge then granted the injunction.

It is understood that the IC’s application for leave to appeal the ruling was denied.

The Integrity Commission had alleged that there is a disproportionality in Wheatley’s assets when compared to his income to the tune of $164 million.

Wheatley rejected the allegation and accused the IC of failing to take into consideration $168 million in rental income accumulated over a decade.

He is being represented by a high powered legal team including King’s Counsel Ransford Braham, Abe Dabdoub and Neco Pagon.

The Integrity Commission is being represented by King’s Counsel Kevin Powell.

World.title: DROUGHT ALERT!
World.content:
Principal Director of the Meteorological Service of Jamaica, Evan Thompson gives the forecast for the island over the next few months during a press briefing Thursday afternoon.(Photo: Karl McLarty)

With projections from the Meteorological Service of Jamaica showing prolonged dry conditions stretching into October this year, Water, Environment and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda has put Jamaicans on alert for full prohibition orders for water usage, which he says will take effect on August 10 if the forecast remains unchanged or worsens.

The warning comes following a Thursday morning meeting of the Integrated Water Resources Management Council — a Cabinet subcommittee comprising all stakeholders in the water sector; academia; municipalities; and the ministries of agriculture, health and national security. That report was complemented by forecasts of the Met Service and assessments of the Water Resources Authority, according to Samuda.

Since earlier this year, nightly water restrictions and scheduled supply cuts have been implemented in vulnerable Corporate Area networks, such as Kingston 20, given the drought conditions.

Speaking during a media briefing at the Half-Way-Tree Road offices of his ministry to discuss the rainfall and drought conditions, Samuda said given the indications that there will be “a dry August, a dry September, and a dry October…it is clear and should be clear to all Jamaicans that conservation is indeed imperative at this stage”.

“We are first encouraging conservation, but being very clear that as at August 10th…if the situation has not changed — meaning if the Met Services evaluation of rainfall in July is as we suspect — that we will have continued declines in rainfall, and if the rolling three-month forecast has not changed, or has worsened, prohibition orders will come into effect,” Samuda said.

The water minister said those orders will be targeted at “irrigation and watering of gardens, lawns, grounds, and farms, filling or supplying of pools, and other things for domestic services”.

“Washing of cars, watering and washing of roadways, and any purpose that would require unusual or non-essential use of water would be prohibited,” Samuda added.

He emphasised that the announcement was not to be interpreted to mean “that the systems and the storage are at critical levels today, but the rainfall that would normally come at the end of August is not projected to be experienced”.

Pointing to the learning loss that has already resulted from the COVID-19 pandemic as well as weather events such as Hurricane Beryl, Tropical Storm Raphael, and Hurricane Melissa, the minister said every effort will be made to ensure that schools receive the support needed.

“We simply cannot afford water to contribute to learning loss in September. So we will take the measures that we absolutely need to ensure that we’re able to safeguard the opening of schools in September and not contribute to learning loss. So that needs to be understood. We do hope that the situation will change, but with the information that we have, this is the best decision that we can make at this stage,” Samuda stressed.

“We do hope that the situation will change, but with the information that we have, this is the best decision that we can make at this stage,” he added.

Speaking during the briefing, principal director of the Meteorological Service of Jamaica Evan Thompson said as at the end of June the parishes of St Elizabeth, St James, St Ann, and St Mary “were determined to be experiencing drought conditions”. He said the parishes of Manchester and St Catherine “were both basically on the borderline, in that they were just about moving toward drought conditions”.

“It’s most likely that having not experienced significant rainfall during the month of July, that situation would have been worsened. We should be seeing that drought conditions at least would have extended to these two parishes. That’s what we’re expecting to pick up after the month of July has ended, as we begin to gather and collate and compare our data,” Thompson told members of the media.

He noted that the projections did not mean there would be “no rainfall” at all for the island, but that “the number of incidents of rainfall will be fewer”, influenced by the El Nino phenomenon which has caused “lesser than normal amounts of rainfall and higher than normal temperatures” over the past few months.

“However, we could have a bulk of rainfall that is intense, and so we could have very small areas that experience maybe even flooding events in small areas as these systems develop and as they continue to affect us, but generally we will experience dry conditions,” Thompson explained further.

He cautioned that with the forecast for August showing “higher-than-normal temperatures right through the month” and “lower-than-normal rainfall”, Jamaicans should be on the lookout for “climate-induced bushfires”.
