World.title: More for MSMEs
World.content:
WILLIAMS... it is a catalyst for the next era of public procurement in Jamaica.

ONLY about one per cent of the Government’s annual procurement spending currently reaches micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), a disparity Finance Minister Fayval Williams says the upgraded Government of Jamaica Electronic Procurement portal (GOJEP 2.0) is intended to address. The platform will increase MSME access to public contracts.

Speaking during Thursday’s launch of the updated digital procurement portal, Williams said the modernised system eliminates outdated technical requirements, and creates more opportunities for local businesses to access a share of the Government’s roughly $470-billion annual procurement spend.

“Let me put the scale in perspective. Each year, the Government of Jamaica spends roughly US$3 billion — translated into Jamaican dollars, that’s about $470 billion, depending on the currency at any point in time – and this procures goods, services, and works from the private sector. This is close to, I think, about 13 per cent of our GDP (gross domestic product). And yet, of that enormous sum, only about one per cent reaches our micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises,” the minister pointed out.

“That imbalance is exactly what we are determined to correct so that more Jamaican businesses can share in the billions that Government spends each year, particularly as we rebuild in the wake of Hurricane Melissa. So every procurement decision carries real responsibility. It must inspire public confidence, deliver value for money, create economic opportunity, and make certain that every dollar entrusted to Government works harder for the people we serve,” she said during the event held at AC Hotel Kingston.

According to Williams, GOJEP 2.0 is an upgraded version of the Government’s online system for buying goods, works and services from the private sector. She explained that the remodelling of the digital portal will see the removal of outdated barriers, put in place stronger record keeping aimed at making the process faster and more transparent.

“It’s easier to use. You no longer need to install extra software just to submit a bid. You log in from any ordinary web browser on any device, including your phone. It’s better connected. The system now talks to other government systems, so the same information doesn’t have to be entered twice, it keeps a proper record digitally,” explained the minister.

“Every key decision made during evaluation is captured and tracked automatically instead of living in a paper file or in someone’s memory. It cuts duplicate paperwork for government staff, and it collects far better data on how long procurements take, how much competition is there, and how well our small business set-asides are working,” Williams added.

She also pointed out that bidders and buyers will now be able to follow opportunities that the government brings to market, and see who ultimately wins the work. Furthermore, she assured that GOJEP 2.0 was not the finished product, noting that upgrades will continue overtime.

“It is a catalyst for the next era of public procurement in Jamaica. And, over the next years, we will build a fully integrated end-to-end digital procurement system, one that connects planning, tendering, evaluation, contract management, supplier performance, and payment.

“Imagine in a year or two being able to open GOJEP and see the goods, works, and services that government intends to buy over the coming years. A business could then prepare, assess its capacity, build partnerships, secure certification, arrange financing, and position itself to compete. For our MSMEs especially, that advanced visibility can be the difference between watching from the sidelines and winning the work,” said the finance minister.

Meanwhile, Chief Public Procurement Policy Officer Jovell Barrett also highlighted the gap that exists for MSMEs, pointing out that of the 300,000 active businesses registered with the Companies Office of Jamaica, less than 10,000 unique people and entities are awarded government contracts each year.

“Government is one of the largest purchasers of goods, works and services. And so, the question that we have asked ourselves at the Office of Public Procurement Policy is how many Jamaican businesses see government as a potential customer? How many entrepreneurs look to the public procurement system as an opportunity? And perhaps most importantly, how many do not see public procurement as an opportunity — and if they don’t, why?” said Barrett.

He hailed Thursday’s launch of GOJEP 2.0 as an opportunity to ensure that every taxpaying Jamaican has a fair chance to participate in the public procurement process.

“That’s the vision that I have and that’s what I want to see as a Jamaican. Why? I want to see more Jamaicans participating in public procurement. When public procurement operates as I want to see it happen… small businesses, hundreds and thousands of them in each community, [will] become a mechanism through which public procurement will work best and will be able to develop our economy more. It becomes the instrument of change that Government really wants it to be. That is the power of public procurement,” he said.

World.title: Dexta Daps stays true
World.content:
Dexta Daps.

As thousands of patrons prepare to descend on Montego Bay for Dream Wknd, few performers arrive with the kind of anticipation that surrounds Dexta Daps.

Over the past decade the dancehall star has built one of the genre’s most devoted followings by staying true to the soulful, emotionally driven sound that first set him apart.

“Staying true to the vibe that started my career and keeping the music honest and relatable,” he says when asked about the secret to his longevity. “I evolve with the production sounds, but I don’t chase trends; solid melodies, real emotion, and a performance that connects with the audience is always the goal.”

In a genre that constantly reinvents itself, Dexta Daps has remained relevant by refining his craft rather than reinventing his identity. As production styles and audience tastes have evolved, he has focused on strengthening the qualities that first resonated with listeners.

His creative process, however, has never stood still.

“It’s ever-evolving,” he explains. “I’ve continued to sharpen my sense of arrangement and storytelling while balancing intimate, soulful moments with the dancehall energy.”

That balance has become one of his defining trademarks. Whether delivering emotionally charged ballads or high-energy dancehall records, he has demonstrated an ability to connect with audiences on multiple levels, creating music that feels both deeply personal and widely relatable.

As with any artiste whose career has spanned several years, thoughts inevitably turn to legacy. For Dexta Daps, the impact he leaves extends far beyond chart success or hit records.

“If fans only remembered one thing about my career years from now,” he says, “I’d want it to be that I gave people real, heartfelt music that resonated beyond the dance songs, music that felt honest and performances that stayed with them.”

That same commitment to delivering memorable performances is what fans can expect when he takes the stage at Dream Wknd, one of the Caribbean’s premier entertainment festivals, which runs from July 30-August 3 this year.

Sharing the stage with Dexta Daps at Dream’s Montego Bay debut are some of the biggest names in dancehall, including Alkaline, Tommy Lee, Govana, Shaneil Muir, Tifa, Elephant Man, General B, Jamal, Skeng, and Armanii, alongside a number of international acts.

“It’s always great to share the stage with so much talent,” he says. “It’s about representing the culture well and keeping the energy high for the crowd. I don’t take that for granted.”

While he remains tight-lipped about exactly what fans can expect, he hints that patrons should be prepared for something special.

“Always a few surprises,” he says with a laugh. “However, I can’t reveal them because then it wouldn’t be a surprise.”

Looking beyond the summer, Dexta Daps’s focus remains firmly on creating new music while continuing to expand his reach internationally.

“More music, working on an album,” he responds.

So, with new music, an album in the works, and another Dream Wknd appearance on the horizon, Dexta Daps is continuing to build a career rooted in authenticity, one heartfelt performance at a time.

World.title: DOLPHIN COVE’S US$2.5-M LIFT
World.content:
Visitors interact with dolphins at one of Dolphin Cove Limited’s Jamaican attractions. The company has added approximately US$2.53 million to its net book value following a revaluation of its Jamaican properties

DOLPHIN Cove Limited has added approximately US$2.533 million to its net book value after revaluing its Jamaican properties, an adjustment disclosed while its majority shareholder has agreed to sell its controlling stake and is seeking to add four directors.

Property Consultants Limited valued the group’s Jamaican land and buildings as at March 31, but its report reached Dolphin Cove’s board after the company had published its first-quarter financial statements.

The appraisal increases the carrying value of property, plant and equipment by approximately US$2.576 million. After adjustments to deferred taxation, the net increase in Dolphin Cove’s book value is approximately US$2.533 million.

Applied to the previously reported March figures, the adjustment would lift property, plant and equipment from approximately US$26.65 million to US$29.23 million and shareholders’ equity from US$27.39 million to approximately US$29.92 million, before any other second-quarter movements.

The increase is equivalent to approximately nine per cent of the equity Dolphin Cove reported at the end of March.

It is an accounting adjustment rather than new income or cash. Dolphin Cove said the revaluation has no effect on revenue, operating results or cash flow for the period.

The revised values will be reflected in the company’s financial statements for the six months ended June 30.

Dolphin Cove did not identify the individual Jamaican properties covered by the appraisal, disclose their separate values or say whether the updated figures were considered in the proposed sale of the company’s controlling stake.

The transaction under way is a sale of shares in Dolphin Cove rather than a direct sale of the properties.

World of Dolphins Inc agreed on July 9 to sell all 313,901,858 Dolphin Cove shares it owns to Global Attractions Limited, a Saint Lucia company incorporated in March. The shares represent 79.99 per cent of Dolphin Cove.

Neither the purchase price nor the expected completion date has been disclosed. Completion is subject to conditions, including arrangements for the refinancing and discharge of Dolphin Cove’s existing credit facility with Sagicor Bank Jamaica Limited. The beneficial owners of Global Attractions, its financing arrangements and its plans for Dolphin Cove also remain unknown.

The property adjustment has now been announced as World of Dolphins seeks to add four directors to the listed company’s board.

The majority shareholder has nominated Colin Kerr, Darys Estrella, Alberto Bergés González and Sylvain Dominici for election, according to a notice signed by World of Dolphins representative and Dolphin Cove director Steven Strom.

Dolphin Cove has not published biographies of the nominees, explained their connections to World of Dolphins or said whether any of them is associated with Global Attractions.

It also has not explained why the selling shareholder is seeking to expand the board before the ownership transaction is completed.

The nominations were scheduled for consideration at Dolphin Cove’s annual general meeting on Thursday, July 30, at The Courtleigh Hotel & Suites.

However, the chairman was expected to seek shareholders’ consent to adjourn the meeting to allow investors at least 14 days’ notice of the proposed appointments. The outcome was unavailable at press time.

If shareholders approve the adjournment, the resumed meeting would be held between August 13 and August 28. The exact date has not been announced.

Based on Dolphin Cove’s latest public disclosures, electing all four nominees would expand its five-member board to nine if the present directors remain in office.

World of Dolphins currently holds enough shares to determine the outcome of the elections if it votes its 79.99 per cent stake. That could change if the sale is completed or the voting rights are transferred before the adjourned meeting.

Once completed, the acquisition will trigger a mandatory offer allowing minority shareholders to sell their shares to the new controlling owner. The price and other terms have not been published.

Dolphin Cove said its properties in Saint Lucia and the Turks and Caicos Islands will also be revalued. It did not say when those appraisals would be completed or whether it expects them to increase or reduce the assets’ carrying values.

World.title: ‘He who has the gold’
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (centre) addresses a round table press briefing at the end of the FIFA Executive Summit at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James in January 2018. Also pictured are Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts (left) and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani.

Veteran administrator Tony James says FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s proposal to privatise world football is “underhanded”, but cautions that developing nations under severe financial stress will find the promised US$40-million payout nearly impossible to resist.

James, who led the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) from 1985 to 1992 and has spent over 50 years working in football, offered a sharp critique of Infantino’s proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE). Under the plan, FIFA aims to create a private commercial entity valued at US$20 billion (over $3 billion) to handle broadcasting, ticketing, sponsorship, and hospitality rights for competitions like the World Cup. Developed alongside JP Morgan, the strategy involves selling up to 21 per cent to private equity investors — led by Joshua Kushner’s firm, Thrive Eternal — to raise US$4.2 billion (roughly $665 billion) in upfront capital. Kushner is the brother of US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

To win over member nations, FIFA offered a substantial payout of increasing baseline development funding from US$10 million (over $1.5 billion) to US$20 million (over $3 billion) per nation for the 2027-2030 cycle. Associations could also access an additional US$20 million upfront through a new FIFA Fast Forward Programme for infrastructure, putting up to US$40 million on the table per country ahead of a September 19 deadline. Infantino, however, warned that member nations declining support would continue to receive the baseline.

While continental governing bodies have moved to block the move, James says that for smaller member associations, the financial reality takes precedence.

“It is underhanded, and the cynical view is being reinforced by the way it is being proposed now,” James told the Jamaica Observer on Thursday. “He who has the gold makes the rule. That’s how people perceive of it; that it’s the current way of the world. You’re trumping (pardon the pun) institutionalised good governance structures, integrity, etcetera. That’s what’s being put out in the public now.”

Despite the governance concerns, James says smaller associations operate in a vastly different financial reality than European giants.

“This US$40 million for each affiliate will have traction in all the poorer and developing countries,” he said. “The focus will be on CAF [Confederation of African Football], and Concacaf, which includes the Caribbean, but it’s also the poorer countries in Asia and UEFA.

“UEFA’s principled position is understandable, but it’s fortunate in having three financial platforms. One is the World Cup, like everybody else, and their teams are the top of the heap. Let us call them Category A teams because they’re the ones who are going to get most of the money. All of the rest of us are Category B and C teams that should get money, but not like the A teams.”

James’s comments come as global opposition to Infantino’s scheme reaches a boiling point. After an emergency meeting, Concacaf — the governing body for North America, Central America, and the Caribbean — unanimously voted down the proposed enterprise plan, joining European governing body UEFA in open revolt. Concacaf made its announcement moments after the Observer’s interview with James.

In its official statement, Concacaf mentioned severe procedural failures surrounding the proposal.

“During the meeting, the membership expressed deep concerns about the lack of due process surrounding the proposal, the artificially short deadline imposed, and the absence of any review or approval by the relevant FIFA governance bodies,” Concacaf said on its website. “In addition, the need for private equity investment to fund new and existing FIFA Forward programmes following the most profitable FIFA World Cup in history was questioned.”

Concacaf confirmed all 41 member associations rejected the deal after UEFA’s warning that it would pull its teams from FIFA competitions entirely.

“As a result of today’s discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership,” UEFA said on its website on Thursday.

Despite Concacaf’s joint rejection, local sentiments reflect exactly what James described.

JFF President Michael Ricketts rejected all of the Observer’s calls to him seeking a comment, and declined to respond to questions posed on WhatsApp.

However, while speaking to Nationwide Sports, he struck a far more open tone regarding the commercial structure.

“I have not discussed it with my directors, but my personal feeling is that, on the face of it, I really don’t think that anything is wrong with it,” Ricketts said. “It’s workable. But the big problem I’m having is the — for want of a better word — non-transparent way in which it was done. We would’ve spent so much time together with the leadership of FIFA before, during, and after the World Cup, and we were never apprised of these discussions, and this would bring to the fore some level of non-transparency.”

Ricketts’s pragmatic view is tied directly to local circumstances. He told the Observer in an interview on July 14 that the JFF is strapped for cash after a costly, unsuccessful World Cup qualifying campaign. He also said in that interview that he would fully support Infantino’s plan to expand the World Cup to 64 teams as early as the 2030 tournament as it would provide a greater chance of qualification for Jamaica.

A US$40-million windfall would completely alter local operations. Furthermore, with Jamaica actively bidding to co-host the 2031 Women’s World Cup with the US, Mexico, and Costa Rica, maintaining good relations with FIFA ahead of Infantino’s re-election bid in March remains a practical priority.

While acknowledging the lifelines that FIFA funds provide, James warned that dumping millions into unprepared administrative set-ups brings serious risks.

“Regrettably, I don’t think most developing countries have an administrative structure to deal with this kind of money. They don’t,” he said. “You also have to ask, given our system, how much of this US$40 million would actually reach football development, because human nature says when you have money, it’s about a source of power, greed, corruption, football politics, and that syphons off the money.”

And on whether Infantino’s tactics amount to using FIFA’s massive wealth to secure political survival ahead of the upcoming presidential vote, James gave a blunt assessment of how the global game operates.

“He has been a disgrace,” James said. “But in a new world where the golden rule applies, when he hits FIFA and hits the politics, what do you think they’re going to say to him? When he tells them how much he has earned off this World Cup, that the vision was his, the planning was his, what he has had to do, ‘Listen, we had problems here and there, but at the end of the day, look at what I have done for you. Look at what FIFA has done for you. Who are you going to vote for?’ What do you think is going to be the response? It’s all about performance. Let’s face it, he has performed.”

World.title: 2026 Isuzu D-MAX: Built to last
World.content:
The durability, reliability, and ability shown through the history of the Isuzu D-MAX pickup continues in 2026. (Photo: Rory Daley)

Isuzu has long been one of the darlings of the commercial vehicle sector, having built a reputation for durability, reliability, and longevity over its long history.

The D-MAX pickup is endowed with these characteristics, and for 2026 continues to be so.

EXTERIOR

The four-door cab pickup is based mostly on function rather than form. Redesigned from the ground up, Isuzu calls it their ‘Spirit of Truck’ DNA, giving the D-MAX a masculine and no-nonsense look from its wide stance and wedge-shaped body lines. However, function over form still rules, and the D-MAX uses aerodynamic integration of the lower body to boost fuel efficiency and reduce wind noise. For those wanting style, up to 18-inch wheels can be had.

INTERIOR

Inside the new spacious cabin it reflects the working nature of the D-MAX. There’s a quality impression and the presence of durability to the cabin. There’s a mixture of hard-wearing plastics, with soft-touch materials at the main points of user contact. Ergonomics is a key word, with simple large buttons for the main functions to be accessed with ease under all conditions, and feel like they’ll be working for years to come.

Storage is plentiful for those who have to work. The deep centre console will swallow important gear, as will the dual gloveboxes. Cup holders and door pockets that all can hold a 1.5-litre bottle further contribute to the ability to hold personal cargo. The D-MAX has redesigned seats with improved internal materials for higher comfort, and better lateral support to increase occupant, especially driver, comfort.

The infotainment is similarly focused, using USB-C for smartphone-run connectivity and services.

ON THE ROAD

Powered by a 3-litre turbodiesel, the D-MAX is not lacking in this area. With 190bhp and 332lb/ft of torque, it manages to be both frugal and powerful. This is because there is tons of low-end torque to effortlessly pull the D-MAX along in the situations it’s built to operate in.

Boost response is good, and it rarely has to be taken into the higher rpms for more power. On road, this keeps engine noise and vibration low so as not to upset passengers in the cabin, meaning a strong case for prolonged on-road use.

But the D-MAX didn’t get its reputation for its on-road manners. Off-road, it has the ability to match the class leaders, because it’s all under the skin with a chassis boasting greater torsional and longitudinal rigidity. The same suspension that smooths out rough roads and can deal with highway travel can easily handle tough terrain with or without payload.

Rookie or professional, the D-MAX gives confidence in challenging situations, delivering up to 800 millimetres of wading depth, 30 degrees of approach angle, 22.9 degrees of breakover, and 24.2 degrees of departure angle. Being equipped with 2WD, 4WD, and 4WD Low, plus a rear differential, few things can slow, even stop, the D-MAX on a trail.

VERDICT

The D-MAX retains the ethos of the Isuzu brand. There’s a reason the company is a commercial equipment manufacturing powerhouse, and that all is installed into their flagship pickup. The durability, reliability, and ability shown through the history of the D-MAX pickup continue without question. 2026 adds some key updates and refinements to keep it a top contender.

World.title: Almost all of Ceuta migrants have returned to Morocco, Spain says
World.content:
People gather on a hilltop near Bab Sebta on the Morocco-Spain border, near Ceuta and the Moroccan town of Fnideq on July 30, 2026. | Abdelmajid Bziouat/AFP via Getty Images

“Most of the people that came yesterday are now back in Morocco,” an official said.

BRUSSELS — More than 48,300 of the approximately 50,000 people who entered the Spanish exclave of Ceuta from Morocco have returned, a Spanish government official told POLITICO.

“Most of the people that came yesterday are now back in Morocco,” said the official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, adding that the situation was “on the path back to normality.”

The influx of migrants could be linked to a recent Spanish court ruling that limited the use of the country’s immediate-return procedure for migrants, the official added.

The European Commission said “there are no onward movements towards the European continent or other member states” by the migrants.

World.title: Trump administration slams Spain’s Sánchez for migrant ‘invasion’ of Ceuta
World.content:
“This unacceptable incident is the direct result of the Spanish Government’s deliberate efforts to enable and facilitate mass illegal migration into Europe. We are considering actions to defend Americans at home and abroad from this threat and stand ready to assist other European allies considering similar options,” wrote the department.

Sánchez will hardly be surprised by the scathing American reaction, having emerged as the fiercest Trump critic among EU leaders, slamming U.S. military action in the Middle East and barring U.S. military planes from using Spanish air bases.

“Thank God POTUS was elected and our country’s border no longer looks like this. These images out of Spain are an unfortunate reminder of the consequences of mass migration and the radical left-wing globalist policies that have enabled the Invasion of the West,” wrote U.S. Vice President JD Vance.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security made the same argument, saying: “If Spain had their own President Trump, this wouldn’t be an issue.”

The U.S. criticism came as the situation in Ceuta escalated into a Europe-wide political flashpoint in little more than a day. Neighboring governments moved to tighten their response on Friday, with France restoring border checks and Italy calling for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen area, exposing divisions over the bloc’s migration policy.

Former Trump adviser and world’s first trillionaire Elon Musk initially shared a video comparing footage from the Ceuta migrant crisis with scenes from the 2013 zombie film “World War Z.” “Wow, the situation in Spain looks crazy!” he posted.

Clarifying the comparison was a joke, he then shared footage from 2023, showing hundreds of Venezuelan migrants attempting to cross into the U.S., captioning it: “This is what America looked like under Biden.”

World.title: Northern Ireland misses a deadline to fix its budget crisis
World.content:
Bryant, a former Anglican priest who’s never held a Cabinet post before, held his first press conference as Northern Ireland secretary shortly before meeting delegations from the region’s two main government parties, Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionists.

Bryant emphasized that the U.K. government expects Stormont to get more bang for its buck by reforming the delivery of local services, most crucially hospital care, where Northern Ireland suffers the worst waiting lists in the entire National Health Service.

“Look, we need to get to a budget,” Bryant said. “And I understand the financial pressures. I know everybody expects me to come with a checkbook. I’m actually coming with a checklist of things that I want to get sorted.”

Sinn Féin, which holds the key finance and economy ministries, has shied from taking any significant decisions on raising local taxes—not that the DUP wouldn’t immediately veto such moves. Nothing much can happen in Northern Ireland’s system of cross-community government unless the largest parties on each side of the divide can agree.

The two parties blame each other for delivering so little and agree that it’s up to the U.K. Treasury to break the budgetary impasse by providing them much more annually to spend. An independent budgetary watchdog, the Northern Ireland Fiscal Council, recently concluded that the region wasn’t being subsidized by English taxpayers to the same levels as in Scotland and Wales — and if it was, Northern Ireland could gain an extra £1 billion to £3.5 billion annually.

While few expect the Burnham administration to come anywhere close to that, both sides in Belfast do expect Bryant to take charge of key budget decisions — which is what his predecessors did when the Northern Ireland Executive collapsed in 2017 from a Sinn Féin walkout, and again in 2022 from a Democratic Unionist walkout.

World.title: London mayor Sadiq Khan accuses Palantir of bypassing procurement rules
World.content:
Palantir claims that Khan’s office blocked the contract unlawfully and “irrationally,” citing comments attributed to the mayor’s spokesperson which referred to the company’s unspecified “values and ethics.”

Louis Mosley, Palantir’s U.K. CEO, has argued that Khan’s decision puts politics above Londoners’ safety, while Met Police Commissioner Mark Rowley has said that the force’s inability to access Palantir’s technology would worsen the impact of cuts to the force’s budget.

In a pre-trial defense statement filed last Thursday and seen by POLITICO, lawyers for MOPAC said Palantir’s claim is “without merit and should be dismissed,” stating that the Met Police “conducted an award process that was unlawful.”

It says the Met Police and Palantir designed a pilot of the technology in 2025 so that the value remained below a £500,000 threshold at which it would have required MOPAC approval. MOPAC, led by Khan’s deputy mayor for policing and crime, oversees the Met Police.

Prior to the conclusion of that pilot in April 2026, the Met Police and Palantir started discussions on directly awarding Palantir a much larger contract to extend the pilot, according to the statement.

The Met Police intended “at each stage” to award the larger contract to Palantir, the statement says, adding that the approach that was “supported/encouraged/assisted” by the company.

World.title: UK to hold budget on Oct. 28, chancellor announces
World.content:
“Fiscal credibility is the bedrock of economic stability and national security,” said the chancellor in the letter. “That is why we will abide by the fiscal rules, ensuring we retain a buffer to protect us against uncertainty and the impact of instability in the Middle East.”

Healey also pledged the budget will move “money and power out of Westminster, and into every postcode around Britain.”

Burnham announced today that local English mayors will be given powers to retain and spend business rate taxes to boost growth in their regions.

The prime minister said mayors will soon have power over income taxes, but Healey will unveil a whitepaper and a “roadmap” on the topic at the autumn budget.

World.title: Andy Burnham calls on FIFA’s Gianni Infantino to quit
World.content:
“The idea that it could even be brought forward, in my view, shows that the FIFA [president] is the wrong man to lead the organization.”

In response to being told FIFA is plowing ahead with its plan despite widespread opposition, including from European football body UEFA, the PM said: “Oh wow. Have they actually done that? Oh wow.”

Burnham, who’s long called for the community ownership of football clubs, tweeted earlier this week that “football does not belong to investors” but “the people who fill the stands and who stand on the touchline week in, week out, rain or shine.

“The World Cup is not a product. It is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone’s to sell. Dress the deal up however you like. Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out.”

Infantino is under mounting pressure after UEFA voted unanimously to boycott the World Cup if the plans went ahead. The FIFA president also lost his senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro Friday, who called the proposal a “bad deal for football.”

World.title: Ceuta crisis puts Spain’s Sánchez under fire over migration policies
World.content:
In a post on X, the People’s Party’s secretary general, Miguel Tellado, said “no one can be surprised that thousands of people want to enter a country that regularizes more than a million irregular immigrants overnight. Not only are we not stopping the avalanche, but we are sending the message that those who come soon will be able to become Spanish.”

Meanwhile, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, the party’s high-profile president of the Madrid region, accused Sánchez of “allowing the invasion of Spain via Ceuta to try to cover up all of his trials,” referring to the tangle of corruption cases ensnaring the Socialist party.

Spain’s government hits back

A spokesperson for the foreign ministry retorted that the crisis in Ceuta had nothing to do with the government’s migration policies and pointed out that none of the people who have illegally entered Ceuta will be eligible to benefit from its legal status scheme.

“This process is based on very specific conditions, such as proof of residency in Spain before January 1, 2026, and having resided in Spain for five consecutive months at the time of application,” said the spokesperson. Moreover, the deadline for filing applications for the scheme, which was launched in April, was in June.

The Sánchez government has defended the legalization scheme as a necessary measure to ensure the country’s long-term economic growth amid declining birth rates, and the move was backed by unlikely allies like Spain’s conservative employers’ association and the Catholic Church.

But the scheme is contentious domestically, with some polls showing over half of Spaniards believe the country already hosts too many foreigners. It has also drawn criticism from figures like Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who challenged Sánchez’s policies during a meeting of European leaders last month.

World.title: Pro-Kremlin TV star decries ‘censorship’ after France orders expulsion
World.content:
“The government of Emmanuel Macron decided that my public comments … represented an immediate danger to the Republic,” she wrote on social media. “My behavior … consists of living in France for nearly ten years in compliance with the law, paying my taxes, but also having an opinion and expressing it as part of my work as a journalist,” she added.

According to the expulsion order seen by daily Libération, Fedorova was accused of “destabilizing public order,” spreading “disinformation” and acting “as a conduit for disinformation campaigns led by the Russian authorities.”

Fedorova headed RT France before it was shut down due to EU sanctions in 2023. She has since become a fixture on right-wing outlets owned by conservative French billionaire Vincent Bolloré — a powerful figure who has been accused of leveraging his media empire to influence French politics.

According to a government decree seen by POLITICO, France froze Fedorova’s assets for a period of six months on Thursday — a decision the pundit said she will appeal.

Fedorova is currently under house arrest and banned from working on French soil, though weak diplomatic ties between Paris and Moscow could make it difficult to deport her.

World.title: Wildfires: Var department once again facing the flames
World.content:
The fire has flared up again to the south of the blaze, which had been brought under control at the start of the week after burning 4,500 hectares.

 

In just six hours, the new blaze destroyed 1,000 hectares.

Firefighters had anticipated the risk of the fire reigniting. The mistral wind and temperatures close to 40 degrees fanned the embers.

According to the prefect of the Var, Simon Barbre, "the Var is experiencing an appalling tragedy" this summer.

2,500 people have been evacuated near the Gros Bessillon massif, and the village of Correns, which has around a thousand inhabitants, is cut off from the world. The flames have made the access roads impassable and the population is confined.

Seven hundred firefighters have been deployed, backed up by six water-dropping helicopters, eight Canadair water bombers and two Dash aircraft.

This is the fourth major wildfire to hit the centre of the département since 19 July.

Saturday has been classed as a high-risk day because of the wind and heat. Météo-France has issued an orange heatwave alert for the département until midday.

World.title: Strongest earthquake in years strikes volcanic area near Naples, injuring four
World.content:
Water Matters

Europe's water is under increasing pressure. Pollution, droughts, floods are taking their toll on our drinking water, lakes, rivers and coastlines. Join us on a journey around Europe to see why protecting ecosystems matters, how our wastewater can be better managed, and to discover some of the best water solutions. Video reports, an animated explainer series and live debate - find out why Water Matters, from Euronews.

World.title: Inside Ceuta: Residents face fear and uncertainty as migrant numbers soar; bread is scarce, shops are closed
World.content:
The autonomous city of Ceuta has ground to a halt following the mass arrival of migrants from Morocco. Most shops remained closed on Friday, fresh bread was becoming difficult to find and the Ceuta government suspended this weekend's patron saint festivities as authorities struggled to regain control of the situation.

 

As AFP observed on the ground, the usual bustle of the central Calle Real has given way to groups of migrants gathered in the streets, while the shutters of many businesses remain down. In the city centre, home to around 84,000 people, only a handful of pharmacies and a restaurant belonging to a well-known chain were open.

The Ceuta Business Confederation has advised shops and other businesses not to reopen "until security can be guaranteed", amid continuing uncertainty and the deployment of additional security forces.

Health sector sources contacted by Euronews said medical services were under severe pressure despite reinforcements being called in. The most common cases being treated include hypothermia, anxiety attacks and fractures.

"We are running out of bread. There was no fresh bread today because the bakeries are closed," municipal street sweeper Miguel Ángel Campana told AFP. He said some residents feared migrants could try to enter homes "asking for water and other things" and urged neighbours to "keep an eye on their balconies". Across the city, migrants could be seen stopping passing vehicles to ask for food, money or to borrow mobile phones to contact their families.

Migrants rest outside the Temporary Immigrant Centre (CETI) after crossing from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on 31 July 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Local authorities estimate that around 60,000 people have crossed irregularly from Morocco into Ceuta since the early hours of Thursday, many swimming around the border breakwater. The Spanish government says more than 37,500 have already returned to Morocco.

Police have been directing large groups of migrants, many of them young people, towards the border crossing to facilitate their return. The crisis has also triggered an intense political and diplomatic response, with the army deployed in Ceuta and several European countries criticising the way the situation has been handled.

"It remains a heartbreaking situation from a humanitarian point of view, seeing so many people with nowhere to go, without food or water, because the few services available for them are completely overwhelmed," a Ceuta resident interviewed by Euronews said.

At the same time, concern among residents is growing.Mohammed, a taxi driver from Ceuta, believes many migrants have decided to return to Morocco after seeing the conditions awaiting them in the city."They thought they knew what they were going to find here and they have been confronted with reality," he told AFP. Some had told him they were returning "because they had no food".

"There is nothing here. Those of us who are from here are struggling to get by. We are having a hard time," he added.

Mohammed said he and other neighbours stayed awake until the early hours of the morning for fear of possible robberies. "I have nieces who are afraid," he said.

That sense of unease is shared by 56-year-old Yolanda Moreno, who said she had felt "afraid from the start" of the migration crisis. "It was like during the pandemic: the feeling that it was better to stay at home than to go out onto the streets," she told AFP.

Another resident interviewed by Euronews also expressed concern that tensions could escalate, saying people increasingly feared violence. "This morning I was shocked to see people from here, from the neighbourhood, with lots of knives, trying to take justice into their own hands," she said. "I just saw one boy with a katana running after a Moroccan boy, without really knowing what was going on."

The scale of the crisis has forced the Ceuta government to cancel the patron saint festivities that were due to begin on Saturday. At the fairground, rides remain covered with tarpaulins and motionless — a striking symbol of a city whose normal rhythm has been brought to a halt as it struggles to cope with one of the largest migrant arrivals in its history.

World.title: Wildfire breaks out near Athens, prompting evacuation alerts
World.content:
A wildfire has broken out in a forested area in Aspropyrgos, west of Athens, prompting evacuation alerts and a major firefighting response.

 

According to the fire service, the blaze broke out at around 15:29 in forest land on the slopes of Mount Poikilo, in the Aspropyrgos area, and is moving south.

Firefighting forces have been reinforced. A total of 108 firefighters are operating at the scene with six ground teams from the 1st EMODE special wildfire unit and 27 vehicles. Five aircraft and six helicopters have also been deployed for aerial firefighting, one of them for coordination.

Related Crete wildfire kills two firefighters as fierce flames spread in Greece

Water tankers from the municipalities of Aspropyrgos, Fyli, Petroupoli and Peristeri are also assisting. In total, two messages have been issued via the 112 emergency alert system: the first at 16:03 informing people in the wider area about the fire, and the second at 16:22 calling on those in Afaia Haidariou and Ano Dasos Haidariou to move towards Peristeri via Athinon Avenue.

An earlier alert issued via the 112 emergency alert system had called on people in the wider area to remain on standby.

The fire service said the area is classified as Category 4 today, indicating a very high risk of wildfires, while the Western Attica Arson Crimes Investigation Unit has been activated to investigate the cause of the blaze.

Throughout the operation, the Fire Service's Operations Coordination Centre (ESKEDIK) has been receiving continuous imagery from a drone equipped with thermal and optical cameras.

World.title: Liberia sacks officials after record cocaine seizures worth $336 million
World.content:
Liberian President Joseph Boakai has sacked a dozen government officials and referred several others for investigation after a series of major drug seizures prompted public calls for tougher action.

 

A statement released late on Thursday said the dismissals included airport operations staff and senior law enforcement supervisors.

Earlier this month, Liberian authorities seized nearly four tonnes of cocaine worth an estimated $317 million (€277 million) near Roberts International Airport.

It followed another major seizure in June, when about 238 kilograms of cocaine worth an estimated $19 million (€16.5 million) was found hidden among ordinary commercial cargo, including Maggi seasoning cubes, at the airport.

The President ordered "the immediate dismissal, suspension and investigation of several officials of government and law enforcement personnel following his review of the latest status report on ongoing investigations into major narcotics trafficking cases".

Those dismissed included the airport's deputy director for operations, the police commissioner for criminal investigation, intelligence and Interpol, and the deputy director for administration at the National Security Agency (NSA).

The statement added that Boakai had also dismissed "all government employees and law enforcement officers indicted" in connection with the two major drug seizures. Those individuals were the airport's director of security and the deputy commander of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency at the airport, it said.

He also dismissed four employees from the National Security Agency (NSA) and the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, referring their cases to the Ministry of Justice for prosecution.

Following the initial airport drug seizure in June, Boakai launched a coordinated investigation to ensure that "every individual found responsible is fully accountable under the law".

According to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, West Africa is a key transit hub for cocaine bound for Europe.

Several hundred protesters additionally took to the streets of Monrovia two weeks ago demanding quick action and rapid charges, in a protest organised by the civic group stand.

World.title: One dead, five missing after a building collapses in Italy
World.content:
One person has been found dead after a two-storey building collapsed in the Italian city of Messina on Thursday, while five others remain missing.

 

The body is believed to be that of businessman Carmelo Leone. It was recovered by firefighters and taken to the mortuary at Messina's university hospital.

The building housed several businesses, including a supermarket and a shop, on the ground and first floors, while the second floor contained four apartments.

Firefighters launched a search for people feared trapped beneath the rubble after relatives reported they had been unable to contact family members who had been inside the building.

The cause of the collapse remains under investigation. An initial theory that a gas explosion triggered the collapse was ruled out by Messina's mayor. Local media reported the building shook before it fell, suggesting a possible structural failure.

Five still missing, including presumed victim's relatives

According to the Italian news agency ANSA, the missing include the presumed victim's two sisters, Sara and Rosa Leone, his husband, Santino Magazzù, as well as a Sri Lankan national who was with them, Lhairu Warnakulasuriya. The fifth missing person is Alessandra Frazzica, a shop assistant who was on the first floor.

Rescuers are racing against time, as the first few hours are critical for finding survivors. Firefighters are also using mobile phone signals to try to locate those still missing.

Risk of explosions complicates rescue efforts

Rescue operations are being complicated by the risk of explosions from flammable gases that may have been trapped beneath the rubble. Authorities fear the gases could ignite if exposed to oxygen.

"Until the very last moment, I thought I was going to die. I was breathing in dust and tiny particles, not air," Davide Lambiate, one of the three people injured in the collapse, was quoted as saying by the Italian news agency ANSA.

World.title: Italy suspends Schengen with Spain over Ceuta migrant crisis, closes air and sea borders
World.content:
Italy's Interior Ministry has ordered the closure of the country's sea and air borders with Spain, temporarily suspending the Schengen free movement regime between the two countries.

 

The move was announced on Thursday evening by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Deputy Prime Ministers Antonio Tajani and Matteo Salvini following the arrival of thousands of migrants in the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta.

"The temporary suspension of Schengen with Spain is a necessary choice to safeguard the security of our citizens and defend the European borders. A measure provided for by the treaties and made unavoidable today," Tajani wrote on X.

"The migrant crisis in Ceuta reminds us that the management of the Union’s borders is a shared responsibility among our countries, one toward the other. We must work together to prevent uncontrolled migrant flows from entering EU territory, with all the consequent risks and the threat of terrorism, which must be countered without hesitation."

The decision was formally approved on Friday morning during a meeting at the Interior Ministry chaired by Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi, based on assessments by Italy's Committee for Migration Analysis and Border Security.

France has also decided to strengthen controls along its land border with Spain, President Emmanuel Macron announced, while offering support to the Spanish authorities to help manage the emergency in the North African enclave.

Spain and the EU react

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez hit back at Italy on X, arguing that "solidarity and empathy are optional. Respect for European treaties and the facts is not." He cited Frontex figures showing that Italy recorded more irregular entries than Spain between 2021 and 2026 and called for "a strong and united European Union."

On Thursday evening, Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares condemned his Italian counterpart Antonio Tajani's call to suspend the Schengen agreement and summoned Italy's ambassador to Madrid for explanations.

According to Italy's ANSA news agency, Spain's Foreign Ministry stressed that the migration crisis in Ceuta "has nothing to do with the regularisation of migrants approved by the Spanish government", but was instead triggered by an interpretation of the recent Supreme Court ruling on migrants who entered by swimming, which was "exploited by mafias and criminal organisations".

By Friday, however, several EU countries had moved closer to Italy's position, including Finland, the Netherlands, Denmark, the Czech Republic and Sweden.

"Spain has completely failed to protect the external border of the Schengen area from incursions. This cannot continue," Finnish Interior Minister Mari Rantanen wrote on X.

"The situation in Ceuta is unacceptable and I am in close contact with the Spanish authorities. I reiterate that there are no movements towards mainland Europe or other member states," European Commissioner for Home Affairs Magnus Brunner wrote on X.

"The Schengen Borders Code," Brunner added, "contains special provisions that apply to Ceuta and Melilla, and checks on people departing from Ceuta remain in force."

Against the backdrop of an election campaign ahead of next year's general election, the proposal to suspend Schengen has sparked intense political debate in Italy and drawn praise from several European far-right parties, including France's National Rally, Germany's Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the UK's Reform UK.

World.title: Five wildfires still burn in Turkey as risk extends into next week
World.content:
Five wildfires were still burning across Turkey's western and southern coasts on Friday afternoon, as the agriculture ministry warned of elevated fire risk extending into next week and residents in burned areas described losing their homes and livelihoods.

 

"Five forest fires are continuing," Agriculture and Forestry Minister İbrahim Yumaklı said. "The fire risk looks set to carry over into next week. Our intervention will continue until every problem has been resolved."

The communications directorate warned of particular danger in the provinces of Çanakkale, Balıkesir, Bursa, İzmir, Manisa, Aydın, Muğla, Antalya, Mersin and Adana, where high temperatures and strong winds were forecast to persist. Officials said the risk of fires reigniting was significant.

Of 206 fires recorded since Wednesday — when strong winds began fanning blazes across the country — 202 had been fully brought under control by Friday, 133 of them outside forest areas.

The General Directorate of Forestry deployed 28 aircraft, 119 helicopters, 14 drones, 1,953 fire trucks, 2,766 initial response vehicles and 878 pieces of heavy machinery, with teams working around the clock from more than 1,600 positions.

'We have turned to ashes'

In Bodrum's Cine district, a popular tourist area, firefighters worked through the night to evacuate animals from four zones. By morning, nine helicopters, three fixed-wing aircraft, 42 fire engines and nine water tenders had taken part.

The fires had by Friday evening damaged or destroyed 65 buildings, almost all in Antalya and Muğla provinces, according to Environment Minister Murat Kurum.

The European Forest Fire Information System put the total area burned in Turkey this year at 22,587 hectares.

For those who lost their homes, the damage is devastating. Arzu Celep, an elderly woman evacuated from one of the affected areas, said, "We have turned to ashes, we have nothing left."

"My dog is gone, he was more precious to me than my own life," Celep said. Other residents described fruit and olive groves reduced to ash.

Turkey has suffered increasingly severe wildfires in recent years, driven by drought.

Heavy winter rains had until recently protected vegetation cover in the affected regions, which had largely been spared from fires earlier in the season.

Authorities had banned entry into the highest-risk forests at the start of summer. Yumaklı said the government was working to reduce average emergency response time down to 10 minutes, although it was close to the end goal.

World.title: Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea
World.content:
Intensifying clashes between Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea are threatening a crucial trade artery responsible for nearly a third of the world's wheat supply, stoking fears of soaring prices and shortages.

Advertising

Earlier in July, a Russian cruise missile struck the grain carrier Golden Leo, claiming ten lives. This marked the deadliest blow yet in a mounting campaign by both Russian and Ukrainian forces targeting cargo ships in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

"This is a new development in recent months," claims shipping analyst Yoruk Isik, who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. Isik warns that cargo vessels are caught in a deadly tit-for-tat.

"Ukraine has been targeting Russian seaborne bulkers in particular, the ones transporting stolen grain from the occupied territories of Ukraine," explains Isik, "Russia retaliated and hit Ukraine's civilian port infrastructure in Odesa; a mid-sized vessel carrying corn out of Odesa was totally sunk, other vessels were damaged, and sailors died," he adds.

Turkey’s Shipowners’ Association, having logged 136 incidents involving commercial vessels in recent months, is now urging its members to avoid the Black Sea altogether.

Beyond its role as a key channel for Russian oil, the Black Sea is a lifeline for global grain exports, with Russia and Ukraine among the top suppliers.

"It is very important to note that most of Russia's agricultural commodities are exported through the Black Sea, and that almost all of Ukraine's agricultural commodities are shipped via Ukraine's ports," warns Isik.

Bad timing for harvest

Around a third of the world's wheat moves through these waters. The surge in attacks across the Black Sea and the neighbouring Sea of Azov has brought exports to a near standstill.

"No port is officially closed, but almost no shipowner wants to go there, so trade is close to zero," claims Istanbul-based international grain dealer Can Atbasoglu. "Sellers want buyers to handle the vessels, and buyers want sellers to handle the vessels, but shipowners don't want to risk it."

This deadlock arrives at the worst possible moment: harvest time. "Normally, Russian sellers would have sold all their August cargoes by now; I don't know if anybody has any sales on their books at present," says Atbasoglu.

Turkey agrees deal to clear Black Sea of mines that threaten Ukrainian exports

Wheat prices are already reacting. "The price in Romania is, say, 20-25 percent higher – that's the clearest effect we're seeing. But everybody is waiting for some kind of intervention, and soon," adds Atbasoglu.

Turkey now leads a NATO mission, along with Bulgaria and Romania, to safeguard navigation in the Black Sea. However, former Turkish ambassador and navigation rights expert Mithat Rende believes Ankara will be wary of any effort to enforce passage for commercial ships. "It's very important that the Ukrainian war should not be transformed into a regional war," cautions Rende.

"Where would it stop? Would you fire missiles and intercept Russian missiles in the Black Sea? They (Russia) already accuse all of us of fighting Russia as NATO. It's very important to avoid such operations," he adds.

Full impact yet to be felt

Rende argues Ankara’s priority is diplomacy, having played a pivotal role in brokering the 2022 United Nations-backed grain export deal after Russian forces blocked Ukrainian shipments. "Turkey maintained a dialogue with both the Russian and the Ukrainian sides at the same time," says Rende, "But is there political will for a ceasefire now? I don't see it at present."

Grain trader Atbasoglu warns the full impact of the disruption is not yet reflected in prices. "Buyers are still not fully reacting. It's seen more as an August, or at the latest a September issue, and the markets still want to believe both sides will get together and talk," he says.

However, Atbasoglu cautions that time may be running out. "In 2022, Ukraine was completely closed off, and there was a major panic. We saw the effect: wheat prices jumped 50 percent in 2022, and we could expect something similar if this continues," he concludes.

Africa and the Middle East, which are heavily reliant on Black Sea grain, are beginning to seek pricier alternatives. Europe, too, may soon feel the strain, as drought-hit wheat harvests threaten to push global food prices even higher.

World.title: DR Congo Ebola outbreak becomes world's second-largest ever
World.content:
DR Congo’s fast-spreading Ebola outbreak has exceeded 3,500 cases, overtaking the country’s deadliest epidemic and becoming the world’s second-largest ever. The Bundibugyo strain has no approved vaccine or treatment.

The Democratic Republic of Congo's (DRC) latest Ebola outbreak has surpassed the total number of cases recorded during the country's deadliest epidemic between 2018 and 2020.

That epidemic killed nearly 2,300 people among about 3,500 infections.

Congolese officials said on Friday that in this year's outbreak 3,532 Ebola cases, including 1,556 deaths, have now been confirmed across five provinces.

Second-Largest Ebola Outbreak on Record

The outbreak has grown into the world's second-largest Ebola epidemic.

"It's the fastest-spreading Ebola epidemic that we have ever seen," said Carl Skau, acting executive director of the UN World Food Programme told ​Reuters.

"The world needs to pay much more attention," he added.

The outbreak has proven unusually deadly, killing five times more people in its first three months than previous Ebola outbreaks had by the same stage, according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.

Only the 2014-16 West Africa outbreak was bigger, with 28,616 cases reported across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), Ebola is a severe and often fatal disease that spreads from infected animals and through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people.

Experimental vaccines raise hope

The outbreak is being caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which no approved vaccine or treatment currently exists.

However, vaccine research is gaining momentum — the WHO has described a vaccine being developed by Singapore-based Hilleman Laboratories as the most promising candidate against the outbreak.

A separate Bundibugyo vaccine is also under development by the University of Oxford. Last week, the first volunteer received a dose as part of an ongoing clinical trial.

In DRC, fighting Ebola means fighting misinformation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ebola Spreads Amid Conflict and Instability

The outbreak is centred in Ituri province in northeastern DR Congo, near the borders with South Sudan and Uganda.

Health officials say the true scale of the epidemic remains unclear.

Since the outbreak was declared, cases have risen rapidly. Confirmed infections increased from 2,000 on July 15 to more than 3,500 within weeks.

The virus has also spread to four other provinces. These include North Kivu and South Kivu, where large areas are controlled by the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group.

DR Congo is grappling with ongoing instability in its eastern regions, where conflict involving the M23 rebel group continues despite peace efforts.

World.title: UK court allows plans for Chinese 'super' embassy to advance
World.content:
A court dismissed a legal challenge against Beijing's new embassy in London, which could become the largest in the UK. The case, brought by a neighborhood association, argued the embassy poses a security threat.

A UK High Court on Friday threw out a challenge against UK authorities' decision to permit a new Chinese super embassy in central London.

The challenge was brought by a neighborhood group called the Royal Mint Court Residents' Association (RMCRA), which represents families and businesses in roughly 100 properties around the planned embassy site.

What was the court case about?

The RMCRA argued the presence of the embassy could increase the risk of terrorist attacks, lead to the targeting of dissidents and be used to enforce "draconian" Chinese laws in the UK.

The association also claimed that the embassy could pose a fire risk, arguing that Chinese authorities might ignore safety obligations that would be difficult to enforce because of diplomatic immunity on the embassy site.

On that basis, the group argued the development should not have been approved by the UK government as well as the London Borough of Tower Hamlets.

Yet in its ruling on Friday, the High Court said the "RMCRA ​did not produce reasonable ⁠and convincing evidence of the likelihood that a violation of human rights ⁠affecting them ​personally would occur."

In a move that was widely seen as a goodwill gesture toward Beijing, the embassy received approval from the UK government shortly before then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer visited China in January this year.

Plans for Beijing's super embassy have drawn opposition and protests from nearby residents and diaspora groups (file photo) Image: David Cliff/NurPhoto/picture alliance

What makes a 'super embassy'?

If completed, the new Chinese embassy would be the largest embassy in the UK.

Beijing plans to build the embassy on the site of the former Royal Mint, next to the Tower of London. The site covers around 20,000 square meters (235,000 square feet).

Beijing purchased the property in 2018 for a reported $327 million (€283.9 million), with the intent of relocating its embassy there from its current premises in Portland Place.

London's new China super embassy — a threat to HK activists? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

RMCRA vows to continue fight

In response to the verdict, the RMCRA said it would seek permission to appeal, hoping to take the case to the UK Supreme Court.

"Beijing thinks this judgment is the final word. It isn't. The appeal is already in the works," Luke Pollard, head of the RMCRA, said in a statement.

Opposition to the project extends far beyond local residents.

Activists from Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement living in exile have also been skeptical of the project, telling DW they fear the embassy could help Beijing suppress dissidents abroad.

The UK is home to the world's largest Hong Kong diaspora, with an estimated 285,000 people of Hong Kong origin living in the country.

World.title: Why Europe's wildfires are getting harder to stop
World.content:
Wildfires may start with a single spark, but experts say climate change, drought and decades of forest management decisions have created the conditions for Europe's biggest blazes.

Wildfires almost always need a spark to ignite, whether it's lightning, arson, or a car's hot exhaust pipe touching dry vegetation.

In France's historic summer wildfires, authorities blamed a brush-clearing machine being operated around a high-voltage power line. Spanish investigators concluded that sparks from heavy machinery were behind major blazes there.

But scientists say those findings only explain how Europe's historic wildfires began, not why they grew into the megafires that have devastated the continent this summer.

Across Europe, a combination of human-caused climate change, insufficient planning and forests planted in ways that allow flames to spread quickly are fueling fires, say experts.

"It's not that wildfires are magic and just start. You have to have the right climatic conditions," said Silvia Abruscato, coordinator of FoRISK, a pan-European forest risk management hub.

Has Europe lost control of its wildfires? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Climate change is loading forests with fuel

Scientists point to three ingredients that determine whether a wildfire will spread rapidly: the amount of vegetation available to burn, how dry that vegetation is, and the weather conditions around a fire.

"When all three of these conditions are very much fire-prone and they align, then you have this kind of fire event," said Francesca Di Giuseppe, a fire forecast project coordinator at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.

Climate change is making these conditions more common and intense. A rapid analysis from World Weather Attribution found global warming made the extreme weather behind Spain and France's summer wildfires much more likely.

Residents watch smoke rise near Lege-Cap-Ferret, one of many towns caught in a summer of 'hydroclimatic whiplash' Image: Julien De Rosa/AFP

One reason is a phenomenon called hydroclimatic whiplash, where ecosystems suddenly swing between wet and dry conditions.

Essentially, as the planet warms, the atmosphere holds more moisture, intensifying rainfall that fuels plant growth.

"This has created an abundance of biomass that then has rapidly dried during a sequence of heat waves," Di Giuseppe said.

In spring, a warmer atmosphere draws water from soil and plants. Drought worsens, vegetation dries out, and landscapes become far easier to ignite. In simple terms, wet winters grow fuel, and dry springs turn that fuel into perfect kindling.

This summer, that's meant fires breaking out almost simultaneously in France, Spain, Greece, and Turkey — all driven by the same broad pattern of heat and drought.

Making matters worse, the fires themselves add to the problem. This year's blazes have already emitted nearly 18 million tons of planet-warming CO2, according to EU figures.

Spain turns to grazing to curb wildfires To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Some forests are built to burn

Once a fire begins, it can take thousands of firefighters days or weeks of effort to contain the flames. That's partly due to the way forests have been managed over decades. Across parts of Europe, large areas have been planted as monocultures, dominated by a single species grown for quick timber.

"Some of the fires we've been seeing in France and Spain are in places where you have these very flammable trees which are quite fine and they often are growing close together so fire spreads really easily," Doug Kelley, a land surface modeler at the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology, told DW.

More than three-quarters of the Landes de Gascogne forest in southwestern France, which is currently ablaze, contains maritime pine. Created after Napoleon III ordered the region's marshes to be drained and planted with pine in 1857, it became Europe's largest man-made forest.

But the pine species sheds coarse needles that blanket the forest floor, providing bountiful fuel for fires. Because the trees are of similar age and height across vast areas, they are particularly vulnerable to fast-moving fire.

Another fast-growing timber tree is the eucalyptus. In Portugal the oily species — which represents more than a quarter of the country's forestland — burned far and wide in 2017's deadly wildfire season.

"In some regions of Europe, farmland and lower-biomass shrubland were replaced by fire-prone conifer or eucalyptus species of higher economic profitability, increasing the risk of fire," the European Commission wrote in a case study report on the 2017 Portuguese wildfires.

That includes Spain, where some 3 million hectares (7.4 million acres) of former farmland and pasture were planted with pine and eucalyptus during and after the Franco dictatorship, which lasted from 1939 to 1975.

Helicopters drop water over Spain's Avila province, where scientists say this year's extreme fire weather was made much more likely by climate change Image: Miguel Riopa/AFP

Preventing the next disaster

Firefighters will always play a crucial role in suppressing wildfires. But experts say reducing risk before fires start is just as important. That starts with tackling the greenhouse gas emissions driving climate change and intensifying weather extremes.

"Trying to prevent in the first place the landscape becoming so flammable is one of the most effective ways to try to avoid this kind of extreme fire behavior," said Di Giuseppe.

Replacing monocultures with mixed forests would also go a long way. Forests with a wider variety of species are generally better able to withstand drought, windstorms, insect outbreaks, and fires, because different trees respond differently to environmental stresses.

Germany offers an instructive case for forest management. Demand for timber after World War II led to spruce being planted across mountain ranges like the Harz in former East Germany. But these monocultures proved vulnerable to drought and bark beetle infestation. Foresters are now working to convert them into mixed forests to improve resilience.

Planting broadleaf, deciduous trees — such as oak, beech, or maple — can help, as they typically store more moisture than conifers. Trees with thick bark, fewer low-hanging branches, and a higher moisture content tend to be more fire-resistant.

A post-event simulation study of Portugal's 2017 blazes found fires that overwhelmed firefighters in pine and eucalyptus stands, with flames over four meters tall, could be contained in broadleaf forest, where flame heights dropped to under a meter and a half.

Forestry experts also recommend creating breaks between rows of trees to slow fire spread as well as pruning lower branches so flames can't jump quickly to the canopy. Clearing the forest floor of incendiary leaf litter and dead wood, and using controlled burns to reduce underbrush prior to wildfire season helps too.

"We need to manage our forest well in order to avoid such big disasters from happening. So prevention, prevention, prevention," Abruscato said.

World.title: Sudan civil war: When drones strike the classroom
World.content:
Children in Sudan's besieged city of el-Obeid are afraid to go to school as drone attacks hit civilian infrastructure. Aid groups warn of a worsening humanitarian crisis.

Flattened houses and rubble where a school once stood: These are the scenes that have appeared in footage of the Sudanese city of el-Obeid published by Ayin Network, a nonpartisan Sudanese media outlet.

Drone attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have caused enormous damage to civilian infrastructure, including power grids, transformers, water treatment plants, schools, universities and hospitals in the capital of North Kordofan.

The local population is struggling to survive, according to Ahmed Awad, a native of el-Obeid and a project manager for children's rights organization Plan International there. The city — whose population previously numbered half a million but has now become home to several hundred thousand people who are displaced — is under siege, he added.

There is a shortage of medical supplies as well as food and safe, clean water, and Awad said he saw long lines of people at just one water pump: "Sometimes you can spend all day to get one liter of water for two or three days." Most of the time, children and teenagers are the ones sent to fetch water.

Millions across Sudan are going hungry, including over 825,000 children under 5 suffering from severe acute malnutrition Image: AFP

He added that a drone had hit a primary school and killed three children, which had caused trauma among other children, many of whom no longer dared go to school.

"One of the mothers said three of her children cannot sleep because they are always in fear of something happening again," he said.

Even when they're sitting in their classrooms, they live with the constant fear that a drone could strike at any moment. Awad and his colleagues at Plan International are working to provide psychological support to the affected children.

Sudan's strategic crossroads

El-Obeid is a strategically important location. The city is a trading hub in the middle of the desert on the only major route between Sudan's capital, Khartoum — which is controlled by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) — and the western Darfur region, large parts of which are under the control of the RSF.

El-Obeid is currently controlled by the army, which has some 13,000 soldiers stationed there, and has been on the front line since fighting shifted from Darfur to Kordofan at the beginning of the year. The RSF has deployed troops to about 30 kilometers (18.6 miles) beyond the city limits, and has been using drones to bomb civilian infrastructure.

Warnings of mass atrocities

Analysts, aid organizations and the United Nations have warned that the RSF could soon capture el-Obeid. They fear a similar scenario to that which unfolded in the city of el-Fasher in the neighboring state of North Darfur in October 2025, when the RSF began by bombing infrastructure before storming the city after an 18-month siege.

Earlier this year, a UN Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan presented to the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva detailed atrocities in the capture of el-Fasher and identified "hallmarks of genocide."

“We warn that an escalation of the situation could lead to a repeat of the horrific human rights violations and abuses against civilians that we documented in Al-Fashir,” numerous human rights organizations said in a joint appeal.

"We are alarmed by the ongoing hostilities around the city, including frequent drone strikes," said Pekka Haavisto, the UN chief's personal envoy for Sudan, in June. "These are already affecting the civilians and disrupting humanitarian aid to the city. Any further escalation of the situation would place thousands of people at risk."

Growing up under drones

The situation is particularly dire for the children trapped in el-Obeid, says Francesco Lanino, deputy country director of the children's charity Save the Children in Sudan. Drone attacks on schools and displacement camps have caused severe trauma.

Lanino recently visited the Tawila displacement camp near el-Fashir in Darfur, which was taken over by the RSF in October. There, he encountered children struggling to process what had happened to them.

"We met several children who refused to speak afterwards," Lanino said. Many found it difficult to understand why they had experienced such violence.

Lanino is concerned about the long-term impact of the conflict. "If these traumas are not addressed, they could seek revenge, because all this stress, all this trauma, could erupt in a new wave of violence."

Sudan's army has launched a new offensive in Kordofan from the capital, Khartoum, and says it has taken control of the 360-kilometer-long highway linking Omdurman, Khartoum's twin city, with el-Obeid.

SAF Chief of Staff Abdel-Fattah al-Burhan recently inspected the newly captured areas in North Kordofan by helicopter and congratulated his troops. The advance has reopened supply routes to SAF units in El Obeid.

Residents of the previously besieged city celebrated the arrival of army forces, as the immediate threat appears to have receded for now.

As they retreated, RSF fighters looted markets and villages in North Kordofan and committed human rights violations against local residents, according to the Sudan Tribune media platform.

Last Monday, RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as "Hemeti," told commanders in the affected areas they no longer needed to wait for orders from the high command and could instead launch counteroffensives at their own discretion.

The move could lead to further attacks on civilians and additional looting.
