El presidente del Gobierno ha explicado precisamente que ya se está estudiando el despliegue de boyas en el espigón que separa Ceuta de la ciudad marroquí de Castillejos, “para dar cumplimiento a la sentencia del Supremo y, para que se vea desde el punto de vista administrativo que existe una barrera de contención, una barrera física en términos visuales, para que se pueda facilitar la repatriación en frontera”. Tampoco ha descartado “desde el punto vista legislativo modificar algunos aspectos de las leyes para facilitar la repatriación de la forma más efectiva posible”.

Las llegadas previas al jueves provocaron las primeras peticiones de ayuda de Juan Jesús Vivas, el alcalde-presidente ceutí desde 2001, que ya advirtió de la situación de “colapso” al tiempo que pedía la respuesta “contundente y sin dilación” del Ejecutivo. “Todos los que estamos aquí no pensábamos que volveríamos a ver algo como lo de 2021. Se ha puesto de manifiesto la extrema vulnerabilidad de nuestra ciudad, que requiere de medidas extructurales para que no se vuelva a producir”, ha aseverado Vivas, que ha criticado la respuesta “tardía e insuficiente” del Gobierno.

Vivas, en el cargo desde 2001 y que es el dirigente autonómico que más años lleva al frente de una institución, pidió el jueves la activación de la emergencia nacional debido a la dimensión de la crisis pero el Ministerio del Interior justifica que no es posible hacerlo por una crisis migratoria, ya que esa figura jurídica esta está contemplada únicamente para riesgos naturales y tecnológicos.

En la crisis de 2021 Sánchez se comprometió como ahora a restablecer el control en la frontera con la máxima celeridad. “Seremos firmes para garantizar la seguridad ante cualquier desafío, ante cualquier eventualidad y bajo cualquier circunstancia”, afirmó en una declaración institucional en La Moncloa.

“La integridad de Ceuta como parte de nuestra nación, su seguridad y la tranquilidad de nuestros compatriotas y residentes allí están garantizadas por la acción del Gobierno de España, cualesquiera que sean las condiciones necesarias para ello y con todos los medios disponibles para ello”, declaró entonces el jefe del Ejecutivo. Como ahora, Sánchez se refirió a Marruecos de forma amistosa como “un país socio y amigo de España y así debe seguir siéndolo”.

04:08 Cronología de una jornada de entrada masiva en Ceuta Flotadores y migrantes tras traspasar la frontera entre Ceuta y Marruecos, a 31 de julio de 2026. Foto: Marcos Moreno

El tratamiento hospitalario del líder del Polisario, Brahim Gali, que fue ingresado en abril de ese año en un centro de Logroño, desató el choque con Rabat, que se dejó de responsabilizar del control fronterizo. “El cuidado de nuestras relaciones ha formado parte desde siempre de la política exterior española y así debe seguir siendo. Mi deseo, como el de todos los españoles, es estrechar aún más nuestra relación y reforzar la amistad con nuestros vecinos marroquíes”, destacó Sánchez en el apogeo de la crisis.

Un año después, La Moncloa, en un giro inesperado, tomó partido por Marruecos en el conflicto del Sáhara. Sánchez calificó la propuesta de autonomía marroquí para la excolonia española como la “más seria, realista y creíble” para resolver el conflicto. Mohamed VI dio por cerrada la crisis diplomática, que se prolongó durante 10 meses, pero la reconciliación con Rabat desató una nueva crisis con Argelia, alineada con las reivindicaciones del Frente Polisario. Argel suspendió en junio de 2022 el tratado de amistad con España y congeló el comercio después de que Sánchez ratificara en el Congreso la nueva postura en el contencioso por el Sáhara Occidental. La relación no se ha terminado de reconducir hasta la semana pasada, cuando el presidente del Gobierno visitó el país magrebí, donde acordó con su homólogo argelino, Abdelmayid Tebún, “reactivar todos los mecanismos” de cooperación e incrementar el suministro de gas. Los Gobiernos de ambos países acordaron celebrar en octubre su primera reunión de alto nivel desde hace ocho años.

Unos días más tarde, la comisión de Justicia del Congreso aprobó la concesión de la nacionalidad española a los saharauis nacidos cuando el territorio era considerado una provincia española más y a sus descendientes, con el voto a favor del PSOE y sus socios, la abstención del PP y el rechazo de Vox. Una semana después, Ceuta es el epicentro de una crisis mayor que la de hace cinco años.

World.title: Datos | ¿Por dónde entran los migrantes a Ceuta? ¿Cuántos suelen cruzar?
World.content:
Las llegadas de los últimos dos días se suman a varias semanas con cifras muy por encima de lo habitual

Miles de personas han cruzado en las últimas 48 horas la frontera que separa la ciudad autónoma de Ceuta de Marruecos, por tierra y por mar. En este mapa se ve por dónde lo han hecho: rodeando a nado el espigón, cruzando la frontera a pie y, una vez en España, saltando por las verjas del polígono industrial pegado a la misma.

La enorme mayoría de ellos ya han vuelto a Marruecos, según el Ministerio del Interior. A continuación repasamos los datos clave para situar y poner en contexto las llegadas de este jueves y viernes, que apenas tienen comparación.

¿Cuánta gente cruza normalmente de forma irregular de Marruecos a Ceuta? Entre 2017 y mediados de 2026 han pasado a Ceuta de forma irregular 20.037 personas, según los datos quincenales del Ministerio de Interior. De media, unas 1.000 al año, aunque con enormes diferencias según cuando se mire la serie. Las cifras que se manejan para las últimas 48 horas (unas 40.000 personas) superarían con creces incluso las del total de detectados desde 2017 y multiplican ampliamente las del año más alto, 2025.

¿Cuántos han cruzado este año? Las cifras de legadas de este año ya estaban siendo extraordinarias: solo hasta el 15 de julio (últimos datos oficiales) duplicaban las de años anteriores.

La situación se descontroló entre jueves y viernes, con estimaciones de más de 40.000 llegadas. Todo ello en una ciudad, Ceuta, que tiene una población de 84.000 personas. Pero es pronto para dar las cifras por cerradas: el Ministerio del Interior ha asegurado que en la mañana de este viernes al menos 37.500 personas ya han regresado a Marruecos.

¿Cuánto suelen suponer del total de entradas irregulares en España? Con cifras hasta el 15 de julio, las llegadas a España por Ceuta ya representarían un 19% de todas las que se han producido. Es una proporción que, de mantenerse a lo largo del año, superaría la más alta de la serie registrada en 2016.

En lo que va de año, Ceuta ha sido la tercera via de entradas irregulares detectadas en España.

¿De dónde vienen y de qué nacionalidades son? No hay datos actualizados de las nacionalidades de quienes cruzan concretamente a Ceuta, aunque sí estimaciones: son mayoritariamente jóvenes marroquíes procedentes de la vecina Fnideq.

Esta predominancia de los marroquíes se ve incluso cuando se mira el total de las rutas que marca Frontex, la Agencia Europea de la Guardia de Fronteras y Costa. Y deja una diferencia clara con el perfil de quienes vienen por la ruta Canaria, la más transitada y oficialmente conocida como Ruta Oriental Africana. Allí las dos principales nacionalidades de quienes llegan son Senegal y Gambia. Aún así, hay marroquíes que intentan el viaje por esa ruta, como se ve en la siguiente tabla con las utilizadas para llegar a Europa alrededor del Mediterráneo.

¿Cuántos mueren intentando llegar cada año? En las últimas 48 horas, al menos 57 personas han muerto intentando cruzar la frontera con España. Según las primeras informaciones, la mayoría habría perdido la vida intentando llegar a nado.

Las rutas migratorias hacia Europa dejan miles de muertos cada año. Según la Organización Internacional de las Migraciones, al menos 35.153 migrantes han fallecidos intentando alcanzar el Viejo Continente desde 2014. La vía del Mediterráneo Central, normalmente la más transitada, es también la más mortífera.

World.title: Los migrantes que han vuelto a Marruecos tras abandonar Ceuta: “Nos dijeron que tendríamos un lugar de acogida en España y era mentira”
World.content:
Una marea de jóvenes desborda la localidad de Castillejos en busca de ayuda para regresar a sus hogares tras haber irrumpido en la ciudad autónoma

La ciudad de Fnideq (Castillejos, en su apelación colonial española) se ha visto desbordada este viernes por una marea de miles de jóvenes que abandonan ahora decepcionados Ceuta, tras haber irrumpido en la ciudad autónoma española sin que las autoridades de Marruecos se lo impidieran. “En España no nos ha ayudado nadie. Nos habían dicho que tendríamos un lugar de acogida y un visado para viajar a Algeciras, pero todo era mentira”, explica Mohamed, de 18 años, junto otros jóvenes exhaustos a la sombra de una cafetería cerrada.

Mohamed ni estudia ni trabaja. Había llegado la víspera desde Fez, 290 kilómetros al sur, para cruzar hasta Ceuta por el espigón fronterizo. Así lo hizo. Pero este viernes ha vuelto a territorio marroquí. En Castillejos, junto a otros compañeros, repone fuerzas antes de seguir buscando algún medio de transporte para poder regresar a su lugar de origen.

00:38 Imágenes de los retornados a Marruecos grabadas en Castillejos Varios migrantes caminan por la costa de Castillejos tras volver de Ceuta. Foto: Samir Gabli

El sueño de obtener papeles en regla para viajar hasta la Península y emigrar legalmente a Europa no se ha visto cumplido. Muchos migrantes han dormido al raso en jardines y solares. Han comido gracias a la ayuda de los vecinos. O a los envíos de dinero de familiares a través de cajeros automáticos. Abrasados por el sol, extenuados, se agolpaban al mediodía en todo tipo de vehículos para intentar regresar a sus hogares en el profundo interior de Marruecos, después de haber fracasado en el empeño de abrirse un futuro fuera de su país.

Este camino de vuelta marca un nuevo hito de frustración para una generación desencantada. Castillejos es una ciudad sin apenas locales de negocios abiertos por miedo a los saqueos. En los pocos que quedan abiertos, grupos de muchachos en calzones se agolpan para intentar compra algo de comida. Echan de menos los refrescos helados, saturados de azúcar al gusto magrebí. La policía patrulla las calles con indiferencia mientras la mayoría de los vecinos permanecen en sus casas, temerosos de eventuales actos de violencia de una masa juvenil hambrienta y desengañada.

Más información La crisis migratoria en Ceuta, en imágenes

Los choques de la madrugada entre policías y migrantes en la frontera con Ceuta ya han quedado atrás a primera hora de la tarde, después de que las fuerzas de seguridad dispararan gases lacrimógenos y cañones de agua a presión contra los jóvenes que ocupaban las colinas circundantes. Apenas unos pocos migrantes irregulares se cruzaban aún en dirección a Ceuta con la multitud de retornados desde la frontera española. Familias enteras, con hijos menores y bebés en sus brazos, habían llegado hasta Castillejos atraídos por mensajes infundados sobre una apertura sin trabas de la frontera para poder viajar hacia España e intentar abrirse camino en Europa.

Grupos de migrantes irregulares atraviesan desde Castillejos la frontera en dirección a Ceuta en la madrugada del viernes. SAMIR GABLI

Una nueva vida en España

Saina, de 35 años, es madre soltera, una condición que todavía estigmatiza socialmente a una mujer en el Marruecos contemporáneo. Había viajado desde Larache (en la costa atlántica del norte marroquí). Con su hijo Yussef, de poco más de un año, intentaba empezar una nueva vida en España sin agravios gracias a su fluido castellano. “Pronto estaremos allí”, aseguraba convencida a primera hora de la madrugada de este viernes. Al amanecer, las fuerzas de seguridad marroquíes habían despejado completamente la zona.

La Asociación Marroquí de Derechos Humanos dio cuenta este viernes de que cerca de la frontera de Nador (norte) con Melilla se produjeron violentos enfrentamientos entre las fuerzas de seguridad y cientos de jóvenes, según informa la agencia Efe. Imágenes difundidas por las redes sociales mostraban disparos de fuego real de agentes de la policía en medio de escenas de tensión.

World.title: Lo ocurrido en Ceuta no es inmigración, es un ataque híbrido
World.content:
Artículos estrictamente de opinión que responden al estilo propio del autor. Estos textos de opinión han de basarse en datos verificados y ser respetuosos con las personas aunque se critiquen sus actos. Todas las tribunas de opinión de personas ajenas a la Redacción de EL PAÍS llevarán, tras la última línea, un pie de autor —por conocido que éste sea— donde se indique el cargo, título, militancia política (en su caso) u ocupación principal, o la que esté o estuvo relacionada con el tema abordado

La legislación en materia de inmigración es clara en cómo proceder a la devolución de las personas que han entrado en nuestro país de manera irregular. Pero sería un error ver un fenómeno de inmigración irregular masiva en la llegada de personas a nado a las costas de Ceuta. La regulación en materia de migración en España y los tratados internacionales que hemos suscrito en materia de derechos humanos nos recuerdan que no caben las devoluciones colectivas. También es necesario contar con un acuerdo internacional de readmisión con el país de origen para poder tramitar el retorno de quien ha llegado a nuestro país por una vía irregular. En este sentido, España ha celebrado una pluralidad de acuerdos de readmisión de personas en situación irregular con terceros países, especialmente Estados europeos (Suiza, Polonia, Macedonia, Francia, Italia, Estonia, Lituania, Letonia, Eslovaquia, Bulgaria, Rumanía o Portugal) y africanos (Argelia, Mauritania, Guinea Bissau o Marruecos).

En el caso de Marruecos, el acuerdo fue firmado en Madrid el 13 de febrero de 1992 y se vio posteriormente completado con un convenio celebrado en Rabat, en 2007, sobre la cooperación en materia de prevención de la inmigración ilegal de menores no acompañados; una realidad ésta, la de los menores no acompañados, de mayor complejidad, si cabe. ¿Es este instrumental jurídico adecuado para abordar los hechos que afronta España estos días? Difícilmente las previsiones de nuestra legislación de extranjería pueden ayudarnos a resolver un acontecimiento extraordinario que no responde genuinamente al fenómeno migratorio. Las personas que por miles han llegado de manera irregular y no han retornado voluntariamente a su país son personas cuya situación está descrita en la legislación de extranjería y a las que hay que atender debidamente y ofrecer una respuesta humanitaria adecuada. Esto no es posible sin un refuerzo de las capacidades que ofrecen hoy dos ciudades autónomas desbordadas por los acontecimientos excepcionales y en riesgo de colapso.

Lo aquí expuesto someramente en términos del tratamiento jurídico que ofrece nuestra legislación para la devolución ordinaria de las personas en situación irregular se completa con un mecanismo excepcional conocido como el “rechazo en frontera”. Así, la ley permite que los extranjeros que sean detectados en la línea fronteriza de la demarcación territorial de Ceuta o Melilla mientras intentan superar los elementos de contención fronterizos para cruzar irregularmente la frontera, podrán ser rechazados a fin de impedir su entrada ilegal en España.

Como ha dejado claro la sentencia del Tribunal Supremo del pasado 16 de julio, esta cláusula solo resulta operativa para aquellos supuestos en los que la entrada a España se realice a través de las vallas (o elementos de contención fronteriza) ubicados en Ceuta y Melilla. Este rechazo en frontera debe cumplir, además, con la normativa internacional en materia de derechos humanos y de protección internacional de la que España es parte. Resulta pertinente señalar que tal regulación fue avalada por el Tribunal Europeo de Derechos Humanos mediante una sentencia de la Gran Sala adoptada por unanimidad el 13 de febrero de 2020, revocando así un pronunciamiento previo de 2017 y declarando tales expulsiones compatibles con el Convenio Europeo de Derechos Humanos. Por tanto, este tipo de expulsiones no es subsumible en la categoría legalmente rechazable de las llamadas devoluciones en caliente.

Pero, como hemos apuntado, no es la legislación sobre extranjería el instrumental que nos puede ser de utilidad para abordar la situación que se está viviendo en Ceuta desde hace unos días, aunque las personas que han llegado a nado a nuestras costas tengan la condición administrativa de irregulares. No es, sin embargo, desde esta aproximación como surgirán las soluciones jurídicas para dar debida respuesta a lo que esta realidad representa. España está asistiendo a las consecuencias de una acción que, sin apoyarse en instrumentos de agresión convencional, constituye una amenaza híbrida a la soberanía territorial de nuestro país. No es fácil identificar las múltiples causas que podrían explicar lo que ha acontecido y que difícilmente serán hechas públicas, como ocurrió en 2021. Tampoco es tarea sencilla atribuir la autoría de la acción que ha inspirado el movimiento descontrolado de personas desesperadas hacia el territorio de otro Estado, sin encontrar resistencia alguna en su frontera.

Nada de esto impide, sin embargo, rechazar la categoría de inmigración irregular masiva como fórmula para describir la realidad del momento. Con todo, el resultado de esta agresión sí deja problemas que hay que abordar desde el ámbito humanitario, político, jurídico y diplomático: ¿cómo atender adecuadamente a quienes han llegado a nuestras costas?; ¿cómo transmitir confianza a quienes habitan en las ciudadanes autónomas frente a episodios similares futuros?; ¿cómo reforzar la resiliencia institucional de nuestras ciudades autónomas?; ¿cómo responder a quienes utilizan personas para ejercer presión sobre la soberanía de un país vecino?; ¿cuánto de lo que ocurre está conectado (o no) con la complejidad geopolítica actual? Quizás no haya todavía respuestas para tantas preguntas, pero no debería ser tan difícil asumir como válido que la unidad es la respuesta válida ante lo único que parece cierto: el intento de violación de nuestra integridad nacional. Convendría que todo el mundo lo tuviera claro.

World.title: El asalto a Ceuta: la debilidad de España ante Marruecos
World.content:
Por mucho que digan algunos, la cooperación con Marruecos en materia migratoria es cualquier cosa menos ejemplar. Si lo fuera, no entrarían en Ceuta miles de marroquíes saltando verjas (10.000 en 2021) o nadando (50.000 estos mismos días) ante la mirada impotente de los pocos policías y guardias civiles allí desplegados. La pasividad de las fuerzas del orden marroquíes, atestiguada en numerosos vídeos, no deja dudas sobre su complicidad o indiferencia ante un asalto multitudinario (“ataque y violación de nuestra soberanía territorial”, ha dicho Pedro Sánchez al aterrizar en la ciudad) que ya ha dejado una cincuentena de jóvenes ahogados y que proyecta una pésima imagen de nuestro vecino como un país del que la gente quiere huir en masa y aprovecha cualquier oportunidad para hacerlo, incluso al precio de la propia vida.

¿Ustedes se imaginan lo que es recibir a 50.000 personas en una ciudad de 18,5 km² y 83.000 habitantes? Gente con hambre y sin un lugar para dormir porque las instalaciones de acogida han quedado desbordadas. No se puede dar un paso por la ciudad, la gente está aterrorizada, las tiendas cerradas y se han aplazado las fiestas. El presidente de Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, acusa al gobierno de reaccionar de forma “tardía e insuficiente”, mientras nuestros socios europeos se inquietan ante la porosidad de una frontera europea y exigen firmeza. Todo ello a escasos kilómetros de Tetuán, donde el monarca Mohamed VI celebraba el mismo 30 de julio la Fiesta del Trono, el 27 aniversario de su entronización, desde el mismo palacio que ocupó el Alto Comisario español durante los años del Protectorado, con un discurso sin la menor mención a la huida en masa de su país de miles de jóvenes que no ven futuro dentro de sus fronteras.

Sin duda debe haber motivos para esta fuga en masa y para el silencio y pasividad de los responsables marroquíes que debían evitarla en primer lugar. O al menos esforzarse para intentarlo. Están ciertamente las brutales diferencias de renta y de perspectivas vitales entre España y Marruecos, que recuerdan la imagen del Libro Rojo de Mao Zedong de enclaves ricos asediados por los pobres de la Tierra. Eso no tiene arreglo a corto plazo. Está también la reciente visita de Pedro Sánchez a Argel para afirmar el restablecimiento de una relación que se vio afectada cuando su gobierno se alineó sorpresivamente con Marruecos al considerar la oferta marroquí de autonomía como la fórmula “más seria, creíble y realista” para resolver el problema del Sáhara Occidental. Argelia, que había roto relaciones con Rabat cuando Marruecos se incorporó a los Acuerdos Abraham y estableció relaciones diplomáticas con Israel a cambio de que Donald Trump le diera el Sahara, reaccionó airadamente, retiró a su embajador de Madrid y redujo sus exportaciones de gas a España mientras dejaba en mínimos sus importaciones.

Ahora, cuatro años después, es normal que se pase página y que se escenifique con esta visita y con la próxima celebración de una cumbre bilateral. No me parece que sea esta la razón. Se traduce también que este asalto a Ceuta se debe a la sentencia del Tribunal Supremo del día 8 de julio, donde rechaza las devoluciones en caliente si la frontera se atraviesa a nado y no por vía terrestre. Me parece muy poco afortunada, habría que corregir la Ley de Extranjería y puede que, junto con la regularización masiva emprendida por el gobierno, haya animado a muchos a pensar que en España todo el monte es orégano.

Otra posible razón es la proposición de ley para conceder la nacionalidad española a los saharauis que ya la tuvieron por haber nacido antes de 1976, cuando el Sahara era una provincia española como hoy son Barcelona o Cuenca, independientemente de que hoy residan en los campamentos del exilio de Tinduf o en el Sahara ocupado por Marruecos. Eso puede haber molestado en Rabat, muy sensible a cuanto toca al Sáhara, sobre todo si Madrid no se lo había anunciado antes, cosa que ignoro, aunque nuestro gobierno no se caracterice por tener esos detalles. Hasta hay quien opina que esto es un aviso para que cedamos a Casablanca la final del Mundial de Fútbol de 2030 que organizaremos también con Portugal. ¡Por imaginación que no sea!

Todo eso puede haber influido, (?) pero mi opinión es otra: la raíz última de lo que ocurre es la debilidad que el gobierno de Pedro Sánchez muestra con Marruecos por razones difíciles de entender, salvo la de comprar tranquilidad a corto plazo ignorando que ceder una y otra vez ante Marruecos es garantía de problemas futuros. Estoy convencido. Rabat confunde cesión con debilidad y más cuando las cesiones son continuas: no protestamos cuando Marruecos cerró unilateralmente la aduana de Melilla en 2019; no protestamos tampoco, a diferencia de lo que hizo Francia, que abrió una crisis con Marruecos, cuando Pegasus infectó los teléfonos del presidente y de varios ministros en las mismas fechas de la crisis bilateral que estalló cuando recibimos por razones humanitarias a Brahim Ghali, líder del Frente Polisario, en un hospital de Logroño; tampoco hemos dicho nada cuando desde hace unos años Marruecos somete a asfixia económica a Ceuta y Melilla prohibiendo todo comercio con su entorno marroquí; o cuando instala pesquerías en las Islas Chafarinas...

Yo ignoro las razones de esta falta de firmeza, pero sé que Rabat no lo interpreta como gestos de amistad, sino como pruebas de debilidad de un gobierno sin presupuestos, sin mayoría parlamentaria para legislar, y -aparentemente- sin redaños para defender sin miedo sus intereses y posiciones ante su vecino del sur. A Marruecos hay que tratarlo siempre con el respeto y el afecto que merece como vecino. Pero también con firmeza. Y esa me temo que a este gobierno le falta. De esos polvos, estos lodos.

Jorge Dezcallar fue el embajador de España en Marruecos, además de director del CNI y embajador en Estados Unidos y la Santa Sede

World.title: Dutch unions call 24-hour public transport strike on September 9
World.content:
Public transport workers across the Netherlands are to stage a one-day strike on Wednesday, September 9, bringing buses, trains, trams and metro services almost to a standstill.

The FNV union has called the strike in the latest escalation of its campaign against the government’s social welfare reforms, which it says will lead to lower living standards for millions of working people.

The three major unions FNV, CNV and VCP have vowed to fight the cabinet’s social welfare reforms, which are designed to secure €6.5 billion in cost savings during the goverment’s four-year term.

Social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief scrapped a plan to increase the statutory retirement age faster by raising it in step with life expectancy, but the unions want the cabinet to go further by abandoning cuts to unemployment pay and long-term disability benefits.

Staff working for NS, ProRail, urban and regional transport sevices and DB cargo will down tools for 24 hours on September 9, making it impossible to run timetables.

Delays inevitable

“We are aware that a 24-hour strike will cause disruption,” said FNV official Edwim Kuiper. “We regret that deeply. But the consequences of the dismantling of our social security are much greater for everyone and will last much longer.”

National train operator NS said it could not say exactly what the impact of the stoppage would be because it had not been officially notified by the union.

Lobby organisation OV-NL, which represents nine smaller public transport companies such as Arriva, QBuzz and the major city network operators GVB, RET and HTM, said it “understood up to a point” the reason to call a strike.

But it said it was “very unfortunate that passengers are being disadvantaged by a social and political debate”.

Union leader Henri Janssen said that the strike was being called on behalf of commuters. “Every working person has to deal with sickness, work incapacity or involuntary unemployment. They should be able to count on a decent social safety net,“ he said.

World.title: Amsterdam steps up Pride security in wake of attack in Berlin
World.content:
Amsterdam has stepped up security around this weekend’s WorldPride street parties and the annual canal parade in the wake of last week’s attack in Berlin.

A total of 250 concrete blocks have been placed along the canals and nightclubs are carrying out extra bag searches during the two-week event, which runs until August 8.

Richard Keldoulis of Club Church, one of Amsterdam’s best known gay clubs, told NOS: “I’ve never known anything like this.”

Venue owners are in constant contact with the police and intelligence services about appropriate security measures, although they conceded that it is almost impossible to prevent a so-called “lone wolf” attack by one person using a knife or a vehicle.

Last Sunday a woman was killed and 29 people were injured when a man drove a car into a crowd near the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin, where the annual Christopher Street Day parade, Germany’s main Pride event, was taking place.

The suspect, Abdul B., was later shot dead by police, who have said they are treating the incident as an Islamist terrorist attack.

Lone wolf attacks

“I come from Berlin and I was at the scene of the attack last week. I left the party few minutes before it all went wrong, but my friends were still there,” Keldoulis said.

“It’s always nice to feel safe, but ultimately you can never rule it out altogether. There were barriers and security measures in Berlin as well, but it still went wrong.”

Michel Peters, chair of the gay police association Roze in Blauw (“pink in blue”), said police would maintain a high-visibility presence during the weekend.

“We are there mainly to maintain contact with the [LGBTQI+] community,” he said. “We want to do more to show that we are there in the coming dys, so that people know they can approach us when something is going on.”

On Tuesday evening thousands of people in Amsterdam gathered at the Homomonument, the national memorial to victims of homophobic persecution, to commemorate the victims of Berlin.

City mayor Femke Halsema addressed the crowd, calling for courage and resilience. “We will win if we keep spreading hope loud and clear,” she said.

World.title: Dutch inflation rises to 3.1% in July as fuel costs soar
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Inflation rose slightly to 3.1% in July, sustaining the above-target trend of the last two and a half years, according to statistics agency CBS’s latest flash forecast.

A 9.7% spike in energy prices, including motor fuels, was the main driver of the increase as overall inflation ticked up from 2.9% in June.

Services inflation was measured at 4.1%, the same level as in June, while purchases abroad were 4.8% more expensive, down from 5.7% a month ago.

The harmonised European rate, which does not include the costs associated with owning or renting a home, was measured at 2.9%, up from 2.5% in June.

Since January 2024 inflation in the Netherlands has been persistently above the European Central Bank’s target level of 2%, peaking at 4.1% in December 2024 and April 2025. Its highest level so far this year was 3.5% in May.

The Dutch government has so far resisted calls to cut prices at the pumps, even though the Netherlands has the most expensive fuel in Europe, at €2.35 for a litre of petrol and €2.39 for diesel.

The CBS will publish the confirmed results with a more detailed breakdown on August 11.

World.title: Woman finds dinner-plate sized tarantula in her garden
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

A woman in Twente was enjoying the sunshine in her garden on Wednesday when she came face to face with a tarantula the size of a dinner plate.

Dierenambulance Enschede posted photos of the poisonous spider on social media after they were called to the town of Oldenzaal to retrieve the arachnid.

The woman spotted the creature in her yard and informed the regional animal ambulance, who were able to capture it by placing a container over the creature and slowly sliding the lid underneath.

Tarantulas do not live in the wild in the Netherlands and it is suspected the spider escaped from a neighbour’s house.

According to the Dierenambulance Enschede, tarantulas are largely harmless. Their bites are akin to a wasp sting.

A number of people admitted they would not have had the woman’s composure. “If I had found the spider, this spider would now be the new owner of my former house,” one commenter wrote on the animal organisation Facebook post.

World.title: Arne Slot rules himself out as next Netherlands head coach
World.content:
Former Liverpool and Feyenoord coach Arne Slot has ruled himself out as the next manager of the Dutch men’s national team, saying he wants to keep working in club football.

The 47-year-old was one of the names put forward to succeed Ronald Koeman, who resigned after the Netherlands were knocked out of the World Cup by Morocco in the round of 32.

Slot has also been courted by AC Milan and English Premier League side Fulham since he was sacked by Liverpool at the end of May after two seasons in charge.

The Dutchman, who arrived after steering Feyenoord to only their second Eredivisie title since the turn of the century, won the Premier League in his first season but could only manage fifth place last term.

The Dutch football association KNVB wants to appoint a manager well ahead of the next UEFA Nations League match against Germany on September 24.

Two other potential successors have also dropped out of the running. PSV manager Peter Bosz has extended his contract at the Eindhoven club, while former Ajax head coach Erik ten Hag recently joined his home town club Twente Enschede as director of football and has said he wants to continue in that role.

World.title: “I will always want to have a home in Amsterdam”
World.content:
Originally from the Philippines, Deepa Paul moved to Amsterdam nearly 15 years ago after her husband took a job in the capital. Her book about opening up her marriage, Ask Me How It Works, was longlisted for the Women’s Prize for Non-Fiction. She loves how the Dutch do kids birthday parties, strongly advises tourists not to cycle and wishes she could have met Mata Hari.

How did you end up in the Netherlands?

I was born in the Philippines to a Bengali father and Filipina mother. I met my husband at university in Manila. I was studying communication but also had a crazy pipe dream of going to Europe to train as a classical singer. His first job ended up being in Singapore, so we had a long-distance relationship for four years while I lived in Manila. After we were married, I moved to Singapore to be with him and found work as a writer and producer in TV. But Singapore wasn’t really my bag.

I pitched my husband the idea of one last adventure before having a baby: a round-the-world trip, him on unpaid sabbatical, me writing freelance. He thought I was crazy and suggested finding a job abroad instead.

A friend working at a Dutch multinational offered to put him in touch with a VP at their Amsterdam HQ. I remember thinking that the cold email my husband wrote sounded way too direct and maybe a bit too much. Turns out the Dutch are a direct culture: it worked! One job offer and six months later, we were on a one-way flight to Amsterdam.

How do you describe yourself – an expat, lovepat, immigrant, international?

I am an immigrant.

How long do you plan to stay?

I don’t see an end date. I will always want to have a home in Amsterdam, although I often fantasise about living a parallel existence somewhere warm in the winter.

Do you speak Dutch and how did you learn?

There’s nothing glamorous about how I accumulated the Dutch I speak now, which I’d describe as pretty passable for daily social life. It was one awkward conversation with one school parent at a time, lots of listening to how people actually talk, and relying on context clues to fill in the 20-30% I might not be grasping accurately when people talk fast.

My husband had negotiated 30 hours of Dutch lessons for both of us, through his employer, when he started his job. I paused for a year or two after I gave birth to my daughter, then went back and took classes at the Volksuniversiteit.

I find that when Dutch people switch to English with me, I can push back. My go-to phrase is ‘ik ben grappiger in het Engels’ [I’m funnier in English]. Humour is disarming, it smooths over the switch in social situations..

My greatest achievement was being interviewed live on NPO Radio 1 about my book in Dutch. The segment was only supposed to last 8 minutes, but it was the longest 11 minutes of my life! Turns out talking about love, commitment, sex and open marriage is far more complicated than chatting about the weather.

What’s your favourite Dutch thing?

You’re asking a polyamorist to choose just one?! I love the mobility and freedom of cycling. Gezelligheid. The simplicity of young children’s birthday parties. The straightforward ease of voting — if you don’t come from a culture of systemically corrupt and murderous elections, as I do, you might not appreciate what a privilege and relief that is. The progression of flowers in the spring, from tulips to hyacinths to cherry blossoms to peonies to roses to dahlias: what a gift it is to have a reliable abundance of beauty.

How Dutch have you become?

Not much — I’m still too short (1.56m). I would argue that living in the Netherlands has given me the space and independence to become more myself, rather than more Dutch.

Having said that, I am a lot more direct now, and I not only can handle direct communication, I prefer it. It’s quite a relief actually, coming from a conflict-avoidant, high-context culture. I’ve been nearly cured of my lifelong affliction of Filipino time, which means I’m only mildly late most of the time, and actually punctual the rest of the time.

Which three Dutch people (dead or alive) would you most like to meet?

Anne Frank, who inspired me to start keeping a journal at the age of nine. She was the first person to show me that writing about my inner world and observing my own life, no matter how small and ordinary, is a worthy endeavour.

Rachel Ruysch, the most prolific and commercially successful female artist of the Dutch Golden Age, whose floral still life paintings sold for more than Rembrandt’s paintings in that time.

Mata Hari, born Margaretha Geertruida Zelle in Friesland, a bold free spirit who harnessed her eroticism, feminine power and artistic expression to live a courageous life and extraordinary life for a woman of her time. Later biographies exonerated her of espionage in World War I, but her image as a powerful and mysterious femme fatale endures to this day.

What’s your top tourist tip?

Please don’t cycle in Amsterdam, especially not with your selfie stick out. It’s not Disneyland with tulips and windmills along every cycle path. Some of us have things to do and places to get to.

On a less grumpy note, try to book a visit to the Six Collection in advance. It’s a private art collection that spans over three centuries and 10 generations of the wealthy and influential Six family, who have one of the most celebrated Rembrandt paintings you’ve never seen hanging right in their living room.

Tell us something surprising you’ve found out about the Netherlands.

When I gave birth in 2013, I was taken aback that official paternity leave was two days — one day for the actual birth and a second day for the father to register it. It ran completely counter to the image of the Netherlands in my mind as egalitarian, progressive and liberal. It turns out that it’s still deeply patriarchal in small, hidden and entrenched ways.

If you had just 24 hours left in the Netherlands, what would you do?

If I’m not panicking about making sure everything is packed and ready to go, cycle around my neighbourhood and have a coffee at my favourite spots. If the weather allows, go for a walk and read in the sunshine at Westerpark, then go for a dip in the IJ.

Throw a big party at home for all the friends I’ve made over the last 15 years, all the people who have become part of my story (except those I’ve revoked access to). My husband will cook enough Filipino food to feed everyone one last time. Eat, drink, laugh, cry, hug and dance, maybe stay up talking until the sun comes up.

If we make it out early enough, go dancing until my legs give out or the club kicks us out. Cycle home as the sun rises and enjoy one last sleep in my own bed—or not.

Deepa was speaking to Molly Quell.

Ask Me How It Works is available for sale at the American Book Center. You can follow Deepa on Substack and Instagram.

Dutch drug criminal Jos Leijdekkers, known as Bolle Jos, has been convicted by a Belgian judge and sentenced to 14 years in prison.

The 35-year old was not present at the court in Antwerp when the verdict was announced on Thursday, having been on the run since 2024.

Leijdekkers was sentenced for his part in the Costa drugs case, in which a total of 56 people were accused of smuggling 25 tonnes of cocaine through Antwerp and money laundering. The drugs had a street value of €3.5 billion.

An investigation by Follow The Money revealed that the Brabant drugs baron has been living in Sierre Leone and is in a relationship with the president’s daughter.

Two years ago, a Dutch judge sentenced him to 24 years in 2024 for cocaine trafficking through the ports of Antwerp and Rotterdam.

In total, he has been sentenced to 103 years in prison across 10 trials.

The Dutch have requested his extradition from Sierre Leone, but the government denies any knowledge of his presence in the country.

According to drugs experts, the West African country has become a major logistical hub for the smuggling of drugs from South America to Europe.

Earlier this year, Spanish authorities intercepted a ship that had departed from the country and discovered 30,215 kilograms of cocaine, the largest intercepted cocaine shipment ever.

World.title: More sluice gates close but no national drought measures yet
World.content:
No national drought restrictions will be imposed immediately despite coastal water boards taking steps to keep sea water out of river mouths and the Rhine dropping to its lowest ever level.

At a weekly meeting to discuss the ongoing water shortage, regional authorities agreed to work together to ensure the “most efficient distribution possible” of water and announced local measures to protect drinking water.

The flow of the Rhine at Lobith, the point where the river crosses the Dutch border, has dropped to less than 700 m3 per second, one-third of its normal level for July and an unprecedentedly low rate.

River cruise operators have had to cancel or shorten their excursions on the Rhine, while water authorities are considering introducing restrictions such as one-way traffic to prevent ships becoming stuck in the shallow water. Such measures would extend delivery times or force freight companies to transport cargo by road.

The Netherlands is currently at level two on a three-stage scale of water shortages, which authorises officials in the ministry to hold crisis talks. An actual crisis is level three.

The canal locks at Eefde, which gives access to the Twentekanaal, closed for the first time because of drought on Friday. Local businesses say the closure of the sluice gates, which carry 15,000 to 20,000 ships a year, will have an impact on the economy around Almelo, Enschede and Hengelo.

Harsh measures

“We understand this is necessary for security, but it’s a harsh measure,” said Frank van Zomeren. manager of the Port of Twente Bornebroek.

Deventer is closing its harbour to shipping this weekend for the first time in eight years because the IJssel has dropped below safe levels.

In the west, Delfland water authority has restricted the opening of the Parksluizen gates between the Nieuw Maas and the Schie to prevent sea water encroaching on the river mouth.

Sluice gates at Maassluis, Schiedam and Vlaardingen were closed last week. Other authorities are also imposing restrictions to prevent drinking water becoming contaminated.

Recreational swimmers have been warned to look out for blue-green algae, technically known as cyanobacteria, which grows faster in warm water and can cause skin irritation or sicknesses such as diarrhoea if swallowed.

A Canadian multinational operator of convenience stores, Alimentation Couche-Tard, has announced plans to acquire Poland’s Żabka Group, which runs Europe’s largest chain of convenience stores. The company has offered 32 zloty per share, valuing Żabka at 32.6 billion zloty (€7.56 billion). Żabka’s main shareholders have agreed to sell their stakes, with final approval still required from stock market investors. If the transaction is completed, Żabka is likely to be delisted from the Warsaw Stock Exchange just two years after its market debut. Właściciel Circle K chce przejąć 100% Żabki. Cena w wezwaniu ma wynieść 32 zł za akcję =>https://t.co/61XEGuQnnB via @PawelBiedrzycki https://t.co/61XEGuQnnB — Strefa Inwestorów (@strefainw) July 31, 2026 The acquisition will be carried out through Alimentation Couche-Tard’s Polish subsidiary, Circle K, which runs petrol stations, and will cover all of Żabka Group’s more than one million shares. Alimentation Couche-Tard has already secured commitments to acquire at least 57.2% of the company. Heket, an entity linked to CVC Capital Partners owning 37.6% of Żabka’s shares, and PG Investment Company, holding 10%, have agreed to sell their entire stakes. A group of major individual shareholders, together controlling 9.6% of Żabka’s shares, has also agreed to sell its holdings to the Canadian buyer. The investors include members of the company’s management and former executives. They have also agreed to reinvest part of the proceeds from the sale into Alimentation Couche-Tard shares. The tender offer for the remaining shares was announced on Friday by Ipopema Securities, which is acting as the intermediary in the transaction. Alimentation Couche-Tard and Żabka expect subscriptions for the offer to open around 26 August, following a review of the tender document by the Polish Financial Supervision Authority (KNF). The companies foresee the transaction closing by the end of the year. The Canadian company expects Żabka to continue operating independently, under the leadership of its current management team, and to retain its brand. Żabka shares jumped after the announcement, rising from 29.26 zloty to around 31.60 zloty on Friday afternoon, an increase of about 8%. Żabka, which runs Europe’s largest chain of convenience stores, has made its stock market debut in one of Europe’s biggest listings this year. Żabka made its debut on the Warsaw Stock Exchange in 2024 in one of Europe’s largest initial public offerings that year, with a valuation of around €5 billion. World.title: The split in Poland’s opposition could help them unseat Tusk’s government [Opinion]
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles If Mateusz Morawiecki cuts his final ties with PiS and forms a new party, it may help broaden the opposition’s appeal by offering voters a more moderate, centre-right option. While the strings have not yet been fully cut, Poland’s main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), is splitting in two. A group of 40 MPs led by former Prime Minister (and PiS deputy leader) Mateusz Morawiecki have now formed a separate parliamentary caucus of their own, after last week refusing to sign a pledge of loyalty and quit the association they had formed – as had been demanded by PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński. Former Polish PM @MorawieckiM says 41 lawmakers aligned with him will form their own parliamentary caucus, deepening a split in conservative opposition party @pisorgpl. The proposed group would become the third-largest bloc in Poland's Sejmhttps://t.co/coOdpS7pia — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 The move means that Morawiecki’s caucus, known as Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), is now the third largest in parliament, while PiS, which is down to 147 MPs, has lost its status as the biggest. For now, most of Morawiecki’s followers officially remain members of the PiS party, a situation that will only change if they either resign or are thrown out following a disciplinary process that could take weeks. But unless either or both sides make major concessions, it seems only a matter of time before Development Plus becomes a separate party. A lot of international reporting has suggested that these developments will harm Poland’s right-wing opposition and boost the re-election chances of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s more liberal coalition at next year’s parliamentary elections. In fact, PiS’s split could well help the opposition win a majority. Over the last year, PiS has found itself in an increasingly difficult position. Its support in the polls has fallen below 25%, the party’s lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, combined support for two far-right opposition groups – Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) – has risen to over 20%, threatening PiS’s longstanding dominance on the right. In response, Kaczyński has pushed his party in a more rightward direction, picking a hardline figure, Przemysław Czarnek, as PiS’s prime ministerial candidate in March. That signalled that PiS was aiming to compete head to head with the far right on many issues, taking tougher positions on Ukraine, the EU, migration and climate policy. In many cases, that meant disowning the legacy of the PiS government led by Morawiecki from 2017 to 2023. It also meant that the party was ceding the centre ground, something Morawiecki, who represents the more moderate, technocratic side of PiS, was particularly concerned about (alongside his own waning influence). When in power, PiS launched a revolution in Poland's energy transition. But now, in opposition, it has disowned those achievements and returned to an emphasis on coal. This could be a missed opportunity to win back centrist voters, writes @OrzelBartlomiej https://t.co/8cGvubn7N2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026 Should Morawiecki now, as expected, launch his own centre-right party, focused on economic development, it would appeal to moderate conservatives who are opposed to the Tusk government but put off by the far right and PiS’s own hardline turn. Inevitably, some of the support for Development Plus would come at the expense of PiS – but not all of it, and possibly not even most of it. An example of something similar happening can be seen elsewhere among the opposition. Until last year, KKP was part of Confederation. However, its leader, Grzegorz Braun, was expelled after announcing a run for the presidency against Confederation’s official candidate, Sławomir Mentzen. In June 2025, KKP formed its own parliamentary caucus. Since then, support for Confederation has remained stable at around 13-14%, while KKP has risen to over 9% in the polls. So, by splitting, the two groups actually increased the size of their potential electorate, with KKP successfully appealing to an even more radical pool of voters than Confederation. It is possible that Morawiecki could do the same in the opposite direction – his new party winning over moderate conservatives while PiS continues to appeal to its most loyal supporters as well as competing with the far right. There certainly seems to be fertile ground for such a party. Regular polling by the state research agency CBOS shows that the proportion of Poles with a negative view of Tusk’s government rose to its joint-highest level this month, at 48%, while only 29% have a positive view. The last time that positive views outnumbered negative ones was in February 2024, the second full month of the current ruling coalition’s time in power. Among those who voted for Tusk and his allies in 2023, dissatisfaction is strongest among moderate conservatives. Both Tusk’s centrist KO and one of his coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), are polling only slightly below the proportion of votes they received in that year (30.7% and 8.6%, respectively). However, the most conservative part of the coalition, the centre-right Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance, has fallen from 14.4% of the vote in 2023 to only around 4-5% today for the two parties that constituted it, Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) and the Polish People’s Party (PSL) (which last year decided to go their separate ways). An IBRiS poll for Polsat News in April this year found that, whereas 84% of KO voters and 57.1% of Left voters have a positive view of Tusk’s government, that figure falls to 42.5% for Third Way voters, a majority of whom (51.6%) have a negative opinion. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 Moderate conservatives’ disillusionment with the government, combined with PiS’s shift away from the centre ground, gives a clear opportunity for Morawiecki. And Tusk’s coalition itself showed in 2023 the advantages for the opposition in offering a broader set of options. While some – in KO in particular – had pushed for centrist and left-wing parties to stand jointly on a single list at that year’s elections, instead they campaigned as three main blocs. That gave voters opposed to the PiS government a genuine choice, and likely played a big part in the record turnout that helped bring Tusk’s coalition to power. It is similarly possible now that a four-branched opposition, ranging from Morawiecki on the centre right, through PiS and Confederation, to Braun on the radical right, could together win a parliamentary majority. Polls currently show those four groups with combined support of around 50% (though polling regarding support for Morawiecki’s prospective party should for now be treated with caution). Jestem dumny z tego, co wspólnie zrobiliśmy dla Polski. I wiem jedno – nasza misja wciąż trwa💪🇵🇱#RozwojPlus pic.twitter.com/xOnxKDoroS — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 31, 2026 However, even if they do win a majority, it is far from certain what would happen then. In 2023, the three opposition blocs were, although standing separately, clearly aligned with one another and focused on removing PiS from power. When they together won a parliamentary majority, it was absolutely clear they would form a coalition government. By contrast, today’s opposition is deeply divided. Confederation and KKP regularly attack PiS. It is not at all clear that Confederation would be willing to form a coalition government with PiS, while Kaczyński has explicitly ruled out working with the pro-Russian, anti-American Braun. Meanwhile, Morawiecki’s split has followed months of bitter infighting within PiS, which has often been carried out in public. The manner in which he and his allies are now departing the party means that relations with PiS are likely to remain difficult. The national-conservative opposition PiS party's newly named candidate for prime minister has made overtures to the far-right Confederation. But he also ruled out Grzegorz Braun, an even more radical far-right figure, serving in a PiS-led government https://t.co/i3zOZJWdUN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 9, 2026 It would therefore be hard for the opposition to form a government, even if they do win a majority. In this situation, the role of President Karol Nawrocki may be vital. Though elected with the support of PiS last year, he was technically an independent and maintained good relations with Confederation and even, to some extent, Braun (who endorsed Nawrocki after being eliminated in the first round). When Morawiecki this week announced the “ten pillars” of Development Plus’s programme, he made clear his loyalty to Nawrocki: the second of those pillars is “respect for the president”. Nie ma silnej Polski bez wielkich ambicji. Nie ma wielkich ambicji bez ludzi, którzy je zdefiniują i będą gotowi wziąć odpowiedzialność za ich realizację. Bezpieczeństwo. Rozwój. Suwerenność. Ambicja. Tożsamość. Patriotyzm. To nie hasła wyborcze, ale fundamenty państwa, które… pic.twitter.com/G0YBbfhLye — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 28, 2026 Many on the right hope that Nawrocki can play a role next year in helping the opposition present a more united front during the election campaign. It is also the president who decides who gets the opportunity to try to form a government after the elections. That role would be of particular significance if, as is very possible, Tusk’s KO emerges as the biggest individual party but the opposition together may be able to form a parliamentary majority. Given that we are still over 14 months away from the elections, and Morawiecki has not even yet officially split from PiS, it is still far too early to make confident predictions. However, while Morawiecki’s likely departure is clearly a personal blow to Kaczyński – and a sign of the 77-year-old’s waning influence over not only the Polish right but even his own party – it may conversely provide a boost to the opposition as a whole. Poland has banned children from using smartphones and other electronic devices in primary schools and kindergartens in a bid to improve their wellbeing and safety. The new legislation, signed into law by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki on Thursday, will take effect at the start of the school year on 1 September, but schools will have until the end of 2026 to adjust. Prezydent podpisał nowelizację, która zakazuje korzystania z telefonów komórkowych w przedszkolach i szkołach. (PAP)#PAPInformacje pic.twitter.com/CK7YFU7sru — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) July 30, 2026 Under the new rules, pupils in primary schools and kindergartens will be prohibited from using smartphones and other electronic devices allowing communication or audio and video recording for the entire school day, including breaks and lessons held outside of school grounds. Schools will be allowed, but not required, to create designated places where pupils’ devices can be stored in a safe way and with respect for their privacy. The law, however, allows for some exceptions. When pupils need a device because of illness, disability or other special needs, school headteachers can permit their use. Phones could also be used in emergencies where there is a direct threat to life, health or property. Furthermore, pupils will be permitted to use mobile phones if a teacher deems them necessary for educational purposes and gives approval. The law also allows secondary schools to introduce bans on smartphone use if they choose, but does not make this compulsory, with such schools retaining autonomy to set their own rules through their statutes. The draft law banning phones from primary schools was first approved by the government in June. It then went to the Sejm, the lower and more powerful chamber of Poland’s parliament, which introduced amendments, including extending the measures to kindergartens. The Sejm then approved the bill in a rare near-unanimous vote, with only some MPs from the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) voting against it. Subsequently, the Senate passed the bill without amendments, sending it to Nawrocki, who could have signed it, vetoed it, or sent it to Poland’s constitutional court for review. Poland’s government has approved a ban on mobile phones in primary schools as well as tougher age-verification requirements for online pornography. Both measures still require parliamentary and presidential approval before becoming law https://t.co/y4Ycf46FQD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2026 The president ultimately decided to sign the law, with his office noting that the measures aim to “create safer learning conditions” and support the “healthy and responsible” use of digital technologies by pupils. Poland’s education minister Barbara Nowacka said last month that the law would “improve teachers’ power, autonomy and agency, as well as order and digital wellbeing in schools”. She added that, although many schools already have such bans in place, teachers had asked for legal backing to help enforce them. For more on the measures, see our earlier report from when the bill was approved almost unanimously by parliament, with only the far right voting against it https://t.co/9Mx0SfkE5V — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 According to a survey conducted in April by the Polish state research institute CBOS for the Polish Press Agency (PAP), 85% of Poles support a ban on the use of smartphones in primary schools. Poland has been recently stepping up efforts to protect young people from various digital threats. The topic has been a rare area of consensus between the government and Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record number of bills. Earlier this month, Nawrocki signed a law banning online content depicting illegal acts or other forms of abusive and degrading behaviour – known in Polish as “patostreaming”. Another measure approved by the government that is now being considered by parliament is the introduction of stricter age-verification requirements for accessing online pornography. In January, the digital affairs ministry also announced that it hoped to introduce measures blocking children from access to social media. Poland hopes this year to introduce measures preventing children from accessing social media, says the country's digital affairs ministry. It is working on tools that would require platforms to verify the age of users https://t.co/G7qeEl2q9x — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 5, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Polish authorities have confirmed that the object that violated Polish airspace and crashed in eastern Poland was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload. The missile entered Poland during a period of intensive overnight Russian attacks on Ukraine, travelling around 100 km over Polish territory before exploding in a field in the Lublin region on Thursday morning. Nie miejmy żadnych złudzeń. Tego typu sytuacje albo tego typu prowokacje będą się zdarzać – powiedział wiceminister obrony Cezary Tomczyk w @faktypofaktach, komentując wybuch rakiety na Lubelszczyźnie.https://t.co/IKxuGNwe05 — tvn24 (@tvn24) July 30, 2026 “We can confidently confirm that it was a Russian Kh-101 missile, a cruise missile capable of carrying even nuclear warheads, which exploded on impact,” deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk told broadcaster TVN24 late on Thursday. The object was “a potentially very dangerous missile,” Tomczyk added. Asked whether the incident could have been a deliberate move by Moscow, he said that no possibilities could be ruled out. “We don’t know, and if we do find out, it will mainly be through intelligence. I’m sure the coming weeks will provide us with more answers,” the deputy minister said. Tomczyk said Poland was working closely with Ukraine, adding that 20 of the roughly 70 missiles fired by Russia overnight from Wednesday to Thursday were at one point heading towards Poland. “It is also worth noting that the vast majority of these missiles were shot down by Ukraine over Ukrainian territory, which clearly bore the full brunt of the attack,” he said. He added that a Ukrainian pilot had tracked the missile that later fell on Polish territory but was unable to intercept it. “He turned back 20 seconds before reaching the border,” Tomczyk said, adding that the pilot “could not have flown into” Polish airspace. An object crashed into a field 100 km from Poland’s border with Ukraine overnight after a major Russian attack. Ukrainian officials said it was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, while Poland reported an "extremely difficult night for our air defence"https://t.co/QIpRQfej5S — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2026 Prosecutors who concluded their work at the site on Thursday said the missile contained a “significant amount of explosive material”. Investigators collected fragments and soil samples from the impact site, where the explosion left a crater around 10 metres wide and 5 metres deep. “The crater has been filled and the site handed back to its owner. The Territorial Defence Force combed through an area of approximately 3 km² and found numerous rocket debris, including propulsion components,” the Lublin prosecutor’s office said. Prokuratorzy właśnie zakończyli swoje czynności na miejscu zdarzenia. Lej został zasypany, a teren przekazany właścicielowi. Following the latest incident, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the government would, paradoxically, consider providing Ukraine with further military aid, including additional Patriot air-defence systems if necessary. “Our intention is to ensure that Ukraine does not lose this war,” Tusk said. The US ambassador to Poland, Thomas Rose, said that Washington was in close contact with Polish authorities and NATO allies following the incident. “Any breach of a NATO ally’s territory is a matter we take extremely seriously,” Rose wrote on X. “We are coordinating closely with Polish authorities as the investigation proceeds and remain committed to defending Allied territory and upholding NATO’s collective security.” We are in constant contact with the Government of Poland —including @KosiniakKamysz @sikorskiradek @marcin_przydacz @CTomczyk and @POTUS @usambnato Matt Whitaker following this morning’s violation of Polish airspace by a Russian fired projectile that impacted deep inside Polish… — Ambassador Tom Rose (@USAmbPoland) July 30, 2026 NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the incident “yet another reckless act by Russia and a dangerous consequence of its war against Ukraine”. Johann Wadephul, Germany’s foreign minister, said the violations of Polish and Romanian airspace showed that Russia remained “the greatest threat to our security”. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland will deport a Colombian citizen who performed a Nazi salute during his visit to the former German-Nazi death camp of Auschwitz-Birkenau. He is banned from re-entering Poland and the Schengen area for five years. The 34-year-old was charged with promoting Nazism, an offence carrying a maximum sentence of three years in prison, and desecration of a memorial site. “A place that symbolises one of the greatest tragedies in human history requires special respect, and insulting it does not go without consequences,” said the border guard. @PolskaPolicja zatrzymała ob. Kolumbii 🇨🇴, który na terenie Muzeum Auschwitz-Birkenau propagował nazizm i znieważył miejsce pamięci. Komendant #PlacówkaSGwKrakowie wydał wobec cudzoziemca decyzję o zobowiązaniu do powrotu oraz 5-letni zakaz wjazdu do 🇵🇱 i państw strefy Schengen. pic.twitter.com/kzfw1Kzw8w — Straż Graniczna (@Straz_Graniczna) July 30, 2026 Police in Oświęcim, the town where the museum is located, said in mid-July that they had detained a man after being notified by museum guards of a possible offence. A police probe found that the man, who had been living and working in the Wielkopolska province, had “posed for a photo making the Nazi salute” at the museum while visiting it. Prosecutors were informed of the case, police said, adding that the man was subsequently charged with two crimes: public promotion of Nazism and the desecration of a memorial site. He admitted to the offences and voluntarily submitted to his punishment, which consisted of a 2,000 zloty (€464) fine along with a decision for his verdict to be made public, they added. He was then handed over to Poland’s border guard, which decided to deport him and ban him from entering Poland and other Schengen countries for five years. The border guard said that the decision was “immediately enforceable”, and was based on “considerations of security and public order as well as the interests of the Republic of Poland.” It also noted that a court decided to place the man in a facility for foreigners in the city of Przemyśl, where he will await deportation. Polish prosecutors have indicted an Iranian-born German citizen for making statements denying the Holocaust during a tour of Auschwitz, which he then published in an online video Denying Nazi crimes carries a prison sentence of up to three years in Poland https://t.co/WCSm7O4gAx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 4, 2026 The Auschwitz Museum has in recent years dealt with various cases of visitors misbehaving, including in ways that are punishable by law. Earlier this month, prosecutors in Poland indicted an Iranian-born German citizen for making statements denying the Holocaust during a tour of Auschwitz. In 2025, an Israeli teenager who was seen doing a fascist salute at the former German-Nazi camp was fined for propagating Nazism. Auschwitz was first set up by Nazi Germany in occupied Poland in 1940 during World War Two as a camp to house Polish “political” prisoners, before later becoming primarily a site for the murder of Jews. At least 1.3 million victims were transported there, with at least 1.1 million of them killed at the camp. Around one million of those victims were Jews. The second largest group of victims – around 70,000 people – were ethnic Poles. Poland’s government has appointed a marketing and branding expert to develop a unified strategy for promoting the country abroad, saying the move will help boost tourism, support Polish products and attract foreign investment. Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, a professor at Wrocław University of Economics, noted that her appointment signals “a shift” from simple promotional activities to “managing the reputation of our great country”. The move comes as Poland seeks to capitalise on its economic success, including growth in tourism and continued investments. But the government says that current promotion efforts lack a single strategy and are fragmented. Czas na markę Polska! Witamy na pokładzie prof. Barbarę Mróz – Gorgoń 🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/PPX2eWTRSm — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 29, 2026 Last year, Poland’s sport and tourism ministry appointed Mróz-Gorgoń, who also advises companies and institutions on branding strategy and founded a think tank dedicated to promoting Poland, to an interministerial team tasked with developing a comprehensive new branding strategy for Poland. The government said, however, that efforts to promote Poland were so far fragmented and lacked a single strategy, which is why it created the post of commissioner for promotion of the Poland brand. As the first specialist to take the position, Mróz-Gorgoń will be tasked with preparing a strategy to build a national brand and help implement it, coordinate activities to help grow tourism, support investments, and improve Poland’s position on the world stage. “We will create one programme resulting in the joint promotion of our country’s brand,” said Tusk. According to the government, this will come at no further cost, but ensure that existing funds will be spent in a more “coherent and effective way”. Mróz-Gorgoń, meanwhile, noted that “the Poland brand is not the property of the government. It is created by entrepreneurs, artists, athletes, local governments and millions of Poles at home and abroad”. Developing this brand “means more investment, recognition of our brands and products abroad, and it also provides greater strength in international relations,” she continued. Last year, the sport and tourism ministry announced that it wants tourism to contribute 9% of GDP annually within a decade, from about 5% now, and for Poland to become a leader in the sector in central and eastern Europe. Foreign direct investment in Poland grew from just under 15.5 billion zloty in 2003, a year before the country joined the European Union, to around 61.3 billion zloty last year, according to figures from the National Bank of Poland (NBP). Various state and private companies – such as delivery giant InPost, insurer PZU, and train manufacturer Pesa – are establishing themselves abroad by buying some of their rivals. The international success of some Polish athletes – including football player Robert Lewandowski and tennis star Iga Świątek – has also helped improve Poland’s visibility. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday that Polish airspace had been violated during a massive missile attack by Russia on western Ukraine overnight, adding that there were no casualties or immediate threat to civilians. A suspected Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashed in eastern Poland, around 100 km from the Ukrainian border, prompting the deployment of police counter-terrorism officers and other security services to the site. The fall of the object, which is reported to have caused a powerful explosion, left a crater about 10 metres wide and scattered fragments in a field between Tarnawa-Kolonia and Tokary in Lublin province, about 2 km from the nearest buildings, according to local police. Ukraine has offered Poland assistance in investigating the scene, he added. Earlier in the morning, Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command (DORSZ) said that air defence radars had detected at least a dozen missiles over western Ukraine overnight whose trajectories could have posed a potential threat to Polish airspace. An unidentified object was detected in Polish airspace at 3:40 a.m. travelling westward, DORSZ said. An F-16 fighter jet was dispatched to identify and intercept it. At 3:46 a.m., before the object could be clearly identified, it disappeared from the radar. An Mi-24 helicopter was then sent to the area of the last radar detection to verify the indications. Its crew located what was believed to be the crash site. W trakcie rosyjskiego zmasowanego ataku rakietowego na zachodnią Ukrainę doszło do naruszenia polskiej przestrzeni powietrznej. The prime minister added that Polish forces had been prepared to shoot down the object had it continued flying in a way that posed a threat. World.title: Record number of Poles opposed to Ukraine’s EU membership
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Support for Ukraine joining the European Union has fallen sharply in Poland, with opposition reaching a record high of 40%, a survey carried out by the Polish state research agency CBOS shows. The figures show that 50% of Poles still support Ukraine’s EU membership, but that is a significant decline from 74% in October 2023, when the question was last asked, and from a record 90% in March 2022, shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The shift comes as public sentiment towards Ukrainians in general in Poland has deteriorated in recent years. The latest CBOS poll shows that, among those who support Ukraine’s EU accession, most favour a gradual process, with 41% of all respondents saying Ukraine should join the EU but “without undue haste”. “Only 9% of respondents currently support Ukraine’s earliest possible EU membership, which is the lowest figure in the history of these surveys,” CBOS reported. Meanwhile, opposition to Ukraine’s EU membership has increased by 23 percentage points since October 2023, reaching its highest level in the history of CBOS surveys. People with right-wing political beliefs are most likely to be opposed to Ukraine’s accession (53%), while the age group with the highest percentage of people opposed is those aged 18-24 (58%). The survey also found that a majority of Poles expect the war in Ukraine to end with territorial concessions from Kyiv – 55% of respondents said they believed Ukraine would lose some territory, a view that has remained dominant since December 2024. Compared with the previous survey, however, pessimism has eased. The proportion of respondents who expect Ukraine to lose part of its territory fell by 8 percentage points, while the number expecting Russia to take control of the entire country declined from 8% to 6%. On Western support for Ukraine, 39% of respondents said the military, financial and humanitarian assistance provided by countries in the West was sufficient. Meanwhile, 27% said aid was excessive, while 22% said it was insufficient. Russia has published purported archival documents relating to massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. Kyiv had warned that Russia was planning to release the files in order to stir tensions, while Polish media note that the material contains nothing new https://t.co/CI0cfAlDle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 6, 2026 Ukrainians are Poland’s largest foreign national group, with almost 1.6 million living in the country, but recent polls have shown growing hostility towards them, fuelled in part by anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from far-right parties and a tougher stance towards Kyiv from some opposition politicians. In its annual survey of attitudes towards national and ethnic groups, CBOS found earlier this year that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians increased by five percentage points this year, the largest rise recorded among all groups surveyed, reaching 43%. Tensions between the two countries have also been heightened by disputes over historical issues and a series of recent incidents targeting Ukrainians in Poland. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians rose by 30% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to newly reported police data. Last weekend, three men were filmed violently attacking a Ukrainian woman and her partner outside a shop in Wrocław, apparently because of her accent. Two of the assailants have since been detained by police, while their victims required treatment in hospital. In response, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for Poles to “wage war on violence”, saying that the perpetrators of such acts “have become emboldened precisely because they now have political role models, political patrons, and political support”. World.title: Budapest landmarks to go dark: Parliament, Buda Castle and Citadella lights switched off
World.content:
Several of Budapest’s best-known landmarks will temporarily go dark as Hungary introduces further energy-saving measures in response to the country’s critical electricity situation.

Officials announced on Friday that the decorative lighting of the Hungarian Parliament will be switched off, while the illumination of buildings in the Buda Castle District will be gradually turned off by Monday.

The measures come as the government prepares for the expected shutdown of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, which has been forced to reduce output because of historically low water levels in the Danube.

Parliament joins nationwide energy-saving effort

In a Facebook post, Deputy Speaker Anikó Hallerné Nagy, who is currently performing the duties of Speaker of Parliament, said the National Assembly would also contribute to national energy-saving efforts.

She said Parliament would place even greater emphasis on conscious and efficient energy use, with switching off the building’s decorative lighting forming part of those efforts.

Buda Castle, Carmelite Monastery and Citadella also affected

Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy announced that the decorative lighting of buildings managed by the Castle Administration would also be switched off gradually by Monday. According to the minister, the lights will remain off until operating them no longer places an unnecessary burden on Hungary’s electricity grid.

The measure will affect several prominent landmarks, including:

the Buda Castle complex,

the Carmelite Monastery,

the Ministry of Social Affairs and Family building,

and the Citadella.

Vitézy said reducing all non-essential electricity consumption is justified while the country’s power system faces exceptional pressure.
