World.title: Russian mass strike on Ukraine leaves several dead and dozens injured. Video from Lviv
World.content:
Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

Russia launched a mass overnight attack on Ukraine on 30 July, according to Ukrainian authorities, firing a total of 74 missiles and 284 attack drones. Ukraine said its air defences intercepted a significant number of the incoming targets, but some missiles and drones struck their intended targets.

Several regions across Ukraine came under attack, including Lviv, Kyiv and the Dnipropetrovsk region.

In Lviv, one resident was killed. In the village of Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, a ballistic missile struck the home of a large family. Six people were killed, including three children, while several others were injured.

Lviv Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said the city had suffered direct Russian missile strikes on residential buildings for the first time in a long period.

The heaviest damage was reported on Paton and Vyhovskoho streets, where more than 20 residential buildings, a school, two kindergartens and other civilian infrastructure were damaged.

Rescue workers recovered the body of a man from beneath the rubble.

According to the latest official figures, 34 people, including three children, were injured in the attack on Lviv. Nine people were rescued from damaged buildings. Emergency crews are continuing search and rescue operations and clearing the debris.

Lviv city authorities said some residents whose homes were damaged would be provided with temporary accommodation, while municipal services are assisting those left homeless.

Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

World.title: German broadcaster ARD investigates Georgia’s rise as a crypto hub
World.content:
Crypto mining in Georgia

“Crypto war: How Putin is using bitcoin to wage war against us” is the title of a 45-minute investigative documentary by German public broadcaster ARD, which portrays Georgia as a major cryptocurrency mining hub and an alleged transit route used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions.

The documentary focuses on bitcoin mining and crypto systems which, the journalists argue, have enabled Russia to adapt to international financial restrictions.

Georgia’s favourable conditions for crypto industry

The investigation’s authors say Georgia has developed a particularly favourable legal and tax environment for the cryptocurrency industry over many years. They argue that this was closely linked to political and economic decisions taken during the rule of the Georgian Dream party and its founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, turning the country into what they describe as one of the world’s cryptocurrency “grey zones”.

The documentary focuses in particular on the free industrial zones in Poti and Rustavi. According to the journalists, Russia can no longer sell natural gas to Europe at pre-sanctions levels, with some of that gas instead being used to generate low-cost electricity. The filmmakers argue that this electricity powers large-scale bitcoin mining infrastructure, the ultimate financial benefits of which serve Russia’s interests.

The German journalists say they travelled to Georgia and visited cryptocurrency mining facilities themselves, including infrastructure in the Rustavi Free Industrial Zone.

Russia said using cryptocurrency to circumvent sanctions

Nino Bakradze, founder of the investigative journalism organisation iFact, says in the documentary that Russia has not been completely cut off from the international financial system and is increasingly using cryptocurrency for cross-border transactions.

Nino Bakradze

She says iFact investigated exports of dual-use goods to Russia by conducting an undercover experiment. The organisation contacted a Russian trading company and asked whether it could ship around 30 drones to Russia. According to Bakradze, the company replied that such a shipment was possible and said it had carried out similar transactions before despite the risks posed by sanctions.

Bakradze says the investigation found that companies involved in such transactions use cryptocurrency to settle payments in order to circumvent sanctions, often without being detected by Western authorities.

‘Bitcoin mining in Georgia is profitable’

The documentary also features local bitcoin miner Nikoloz Museridze, who says the main advantage of mining bitcoin in Georgia is the country’s relatively low electricity prices.

Nikoloz Museridze

Museridze says his mining farm consumes about 2 megawatts of electricity. He estimates that, at this capacity, it takes about a year to mine one bitcoin, while the cost of producing a single bitcoin in Georgia is around $30,000-$40,000.

The miner describes bitcoin as “borderless money” that can be transferred anywhere in the world at any time and which, he claims, cannot be blocked or frozen.

World.title: Nauru withdraws recognition of occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The government of the Pacific island nation of Nauru says it has formally withdrawn its recognition of the self-proclaimed republics of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.

“The Government of the Republic of Nauru declares that it has withdrawn its recognition of the ‘Republic of South Ossetia’ and the ‘Republic of Abkhazia’ as independent states.

Accordingly, the Republic of Nauru has immediately terminated diplomatic relations with South Ossetia and Abkhazia,” the Nauru government said in a statement.

On 29 July, Nauru severed diplomatic relations with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation on the basis of shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

The self-proclaimed Abkhaz foreign ministry claimed that Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure” to end diplomatic relations with Abkhazia.

“The development of cooperation between the Republic of Abkhazia and the Republic of Nauru has consistently encountered resistance from Georgia and its Western partners. As joint initiatives turned into practice, a campaign of aggressive external pressure was unleashed against the Republic of Nauru.

For many years, states maintaining diplomatic relations with the Republic of Abkhazia have faced external pressure aimed at abandoning their independently determined foreign policy course. Small states, with limited resources to counter large-scale political, diplomatic, and economic instruments of influence, are particularly vulnerable to such pressure.

Such practice contradicts the fundamental principles of the UN Charter, including the principles of the sovereign equality of states and non-interference in their internal affairs.

The Republic of Abkhazia remains committed to strengthening its international subject status, protecting its national interests, and developing mutually beneficial cooperation with states that share the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, and international law,” the statement said.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and Georgia’s Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to support the move backed by Moscow.

Nauru is a small Pacific island state in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 sq km (8 sq miles), it is home to around 12,000-13,000 people.

World.title: Pashinyan: ‘Russia wants either exclusive ties or nothing’
World.content:
Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has once again addressed the current state of relations between Armenia and Russia. He commented in particular on Russia’s restrictions on imports of Armenian goods, an issue that has caused growing concern in Armenia. During a briefing, Pashinyan said the country should view the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify its economy.

Journalists asked him to address the political dimension of the issue, arguing that it clearly extends beyond economics. Pashinyan said the problem stems from Armenia’s search for alternatives that it previously did not have.

As an example, he pointed to the signing of strategic partnership agreements with China, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France and other countries.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia had never before had — and could not have had — strategic relations with so many partners.

“I cannot speak about Russia’s feelings. I can say that Russia sees this as a problem. There is also an element of exclusivity here. The issue is this: either the relationship is exclusive, or there should be no relationship at all. We do not share that view,” he said.

Pashinyan said Yerevan’s position is “legitimate.” Armenia’s ties with Russia are not exclusive, he said, but the relationship should continue.

“I ask that our position be treated with understanding and respect, especially since its legitimacy is not questioned in practice,” he said.

Pashinyan also stressed that Armenia would continue discussions with Russia over the economic restrictions that Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union have imposed on Armenian goods.

“That would be the worst possible course of action,” he added.

“What was wrong with Armenia? What did Armenia do?”

Journalists asked why Russia places such importance on Armenia’s political orientation and whether Pashinyan had given Moscow any reason to doubt that Armenia remains a reliable partner. In response, the prime minister posed a series of questions:

“What was wrong with Armenia in 2022 that the Collective Security Treaty Organization failed to fulfil its obligations? What did Armenia do wrong? Whom did Armenia harm? What did Armenia do that justified what happened?” he said, referring to Russia’s and the CSTO’s failure to respond after Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s internationally recognised territory in 2021–2022, despite the alliance’s obligation to act in the event of an attack on a member state’s territorial integrity.

What was wrong with Armenia that the Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh failed to fulfil their mission? Was the problem October 2022?” he continued, referring to the 6 October 2022 statement signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan in Prague, in which the two countries recognised each other’s territorial integrity. “But there were incidents even before that. What was wrong with Armenia? And why is it always assumed that we are the bad partner?”

“We are showing who needs Armenia”

Continuing on the issue, Pashinyan referred to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s remark, “Who needs Armenia?”

“Has Armenia harmed anyone? Has it harmed Belarus? How can anyone speak about a sovereign state like that?” he said.

Pashinyan argued that the Belarusian president had asked the question but failed to find an answer. Now, he said, Armenia is showing exactly who values relations with it.

“Armenia matters to China, the United States, the European Union and Iran. And Armenia needs all of those partners as well. Georgia needs Armenia, and Armenia needs Georgia. Armenia matters to France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. That’s the whole story.”

“The alternative is not yet in place” for a referendum

In recent months, Moscow has repeatedly urged Armenia to choose between the Eurasian Economic Union and the European Union. Russian officials have insisted that Armenia should hold a referendum on the issue as soon as possible. At the end of May, the leaders of four EAEU member states issued a joint statement calling for such a vote.

“I respect the fact that, on 29 May, the leaders of four EAEU countries issued a statement supporting the idea of a referendum on EU membership. But there is still nothing to vote on,” Pashinyan said.

He reiterated that it would make sense to hold a referendum only after Armenia obtains EU candidate status or once the issue formally appears on the agenda.

According to the prime minister, Moscow does not challenge Yerevan’s right to pursue alternatives. Instead, it is telling Armenia: “Decide today which alternative you choose.”

“But the alternative is not yet in place. The process of creating it has only just begun. It would be dishonest to ask people now whether they support an alternative that does not yet exist. They would ask many questions that we simply cannot answer today,” he said.

Pashinyan said the government would continue working to answer those questions before asking the public to make a choice.

Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

World.title: Nina Kennedy is often superhuman, but in Glasgow she was a super human
World.content:
That's not how this was meant to go.

When Nina Kennedy steps into an athletics arena, the expectation is gold, and she carries herself accordingly.

The definition of a smiling assassin, Kennedy's friendly and beaming demeanour disguises a competitor's heart that beats with propulsive force.

It launches her down the runway and, usually, to great heights.

In Glasgow, Kennedy fell short of her own lofty goals and the standards we've come to expect from her, but still came away with silver in the women's pole vault final, albeit in a final that won't go down as one of the greats.

Kennedy snags silver, teen grabs surprise gold Flag bearer Nina Kennedy settles for silver in the pole vault and Australia's sprint stars return to the track after a host of medals at the velodrome.

Tailwinds at Scotstoun Stadium have been helping the sprinters, hindering the throwers and terrifying the hurdlers, and on Friday night, local time, made life difficult for the vaulters.

The crosswind kept the final from being a true jump-off between the strong field, with Kennedy clearing the bar only three times from seven attempts and 2016 Olympic bronze medallist Eliza McCartney winning on countback.

The top clearance of 4.65 metres by the gold and silver medallists was 30 centimetres lower than both of their personal bests.

Nina Kennedy came to Glasgow for gold. (Reuters: Isabel Infantes)

Kennedy topped by 1-centimetre McCartney's eight-year-old Oceania record of 4.94 metres just a couple of weeks before the Commonwealth Games began.

So, despite sporting a pretty gnarly scar from last year's hamstring surgery, there's no question Kennedy was fit and in form.

She carried her typical energy into the final, sitting out the early heights and waiting in the tall grass for her chance to pounce once half her competitors had already X'd out.

Why no other runner embraced the 200m gold medallist A doping scandal dating back to 2024 was the backdrop of the women's 200m final in Glasgow, and the frosty post-race scenes.

By the time she got out of her thick coat and stood at the top of the runway, piercing blue eyes fixed on her first attempt at 4.45m, half the eight-woman field was already gone.

She got over on her first go, but not with the sort of convincing clearance over the bar we were used to seeing.

Conserving energy? Shaking off the cold? No, as it turned out. Just a tricky competition.

New Zealander Olivia McTaggart stumbled at that hurdle three times assuring Kennedy of a medal — and most likely silver at least after 2022 bronze medallist Imogen Ayris took three tries to clear 4.30m — but minor medals are not what Kennedy came here for.

Kennedy cleared 4.65m as her top vault. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The 29-year-old has been in Glasgow as long as any of Australia's 255-strong team, having arrived early to carry the flag in the opening ceremony.

She has been so ever-present around the team that it made her success feel even more inevitable than usual, especially for folks who may have only watched her jump at Commonwealth Games, worlds and Olympics.

In those competitions, she had gone gold, gold, gold since her breakthrough win in Birmingham.

But so many things have to go right for an athlete to consistently catapult themselves 5 metres into the air with the accuracy and control required, and sometimes the pieces just don't quite fit.

Pole vault is hard enough in perfect conditions. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

By the time she was preparing for her third attempt at 4.70m, the stare no longer looked so steely.

Having missed three of her last four jumps to that point, it didn't feel like a foregone conclusion that she'd pull it out in the clutch yet again, and so it proved.

"Of course I'm disappointed, I wanted to win and I didn't," she said, emphasising that she was "genuinely really happy" to see veteran McCartney win her first major international gold.

"I'm superhuman most of the time, but I'm also human a lot of the time and I make mistakes and that's OK.

"I'm a high achiever and I push myself to be that, but I think it's also important to remember I'm human and I make mistakes. I didn't want to make mistakes out there tonight, but I did and that's OK."

The epitome of a big-moment performer, Kennedy has now not been able to defend her 2023 world or 2022 Commonwealth Games titles.

She missed the 2025 athletics world championships because of her torn hamstring and missed the mark in Glasgow, but results aren't all that matters for a woman who has ticked off every career goal at this point.

Kennedy was thrilled for Eliza McCartney (centre) to get her first major international gold medal. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

She said before the opening ceremony that she would probably forget to soak in the moment as the team's flag-bearer, but after a long campaign and a surprisingly short time on centre stage, it seems she has figured it out.

"Sometimes sport is more than just the medals, it's about the memories made and the connections and the officials and the volunteers," she said.

"The crowd out there was so awesome. Everyone was just so happy to be here. I'm walking way with a lot of memories.

"I'm happy. Like, I'm sad, but I'm happy."

World.title: Breaking: FIFA scraps World Cup sell-off plans
World.content:
FIFA has scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup after the move caused a major backlash.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino said in a statement: "Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place".

World.title: Torquay netballers face decade wait for crucial facilities
World.content:
Before each home game, netballers from the Surf Coast Suns have to put up two large gazebos to be used as their change rooms.

Spectators are called to help wrestle with the structures at the Suns' notoriously windy home courts at the Banyul-Warri Fields in Torquay, and some players opt to get changed in their cars to avoid the hassle.

"In simple terms, it's horrible. The facilities for netballers are next to non-existent," player and under-19s coach Codi Emery said.

" The fact that we class a gazebo on game day as 'facilities' is outrageous. It's not good enough. "

Players who do not want to risk their privacy by using the gazebo have the option of using shared facilities 70 metres away.

Elisa Hall says it is hard to fully focus on playing netball when her belongings are not secure. (ABC Geelong: Jonathon Kendall)

A-grade co-captain Elisa Hall said not having a courtside change room and toilet was particularly tough for young players.

"They're still figuring out how long they can have a pad on or a tampon in without getting a leakage," she said.

"If they get one, they have to walk past a footy oval, in front of everyone and a bunch of strangers while bleeding."

Codi Emery says the Surf Coast Suns deserve better. (ABC Geelong: Jonathon Kendall)

Emery said girls tended to drop out of sport when they were about the age of 14 or 15.

"We can obviously associate that with body changes," she said.

"How are we expected to encourage girls to stay in sport when we can't even give them a bit of privacy?"

The netballers are being asked to share a change room 70 metres from their courts. (ABC Geelong: Jonathon Kendall)

Calls for council to step up

According to the Surf Coast Shire Council's social infrastructure plan, the club may have to wait up to 12 years for dedicated courtside change rooms, toilets, shelter, storage, drinking water, umpire and first aid facilities.

In the meantime, the council says the netballers can walk the 70 metres from the courts to nearby Grant Pavilion to access change rooms shared with football, hockey and soccer players.

Surf Coast Shire agrees its facilities need to be improved. (ABC Geelong: Jonathon Kendall)

Hall said that simply was not workable.

"There was one Saturday where we shared that change room with the junior footy, the soccer, us, and our opposing team," she said.

"It's not ideal."

She said 70 metres might not seem far, but it was a long way for a young netballer at night.

"I can't trust my girls will be safe to go to the toilet during training," Hall said.

"It's a very open, communally used space … so you don't know who's going to be there."

The club's football president, Jay Williams, agreed.

"We don't have any line of sight to toilets or things like that, so it's a real safety concern," he said.

"We have girls and women getting changed in their car, which is pretty unacceptable in this day and age."

Jay Williams says netballers need access to better facilities. (ABC Geelong: Jonathon Kendall)

Waiting a for decade or more

The Surf Coast Suns team was established 10 years ago as a junior club to absorb increasing demand in Torquay, one of the fastest-growing towns in Victoria.

This year the club fielded its first senior netball and football sides in the Bellarine league.

But as other sports in the town have grown, netball has seemingly been forgotten, Mr Williams said.

"The hockey club's just had a brand new pitch and they've got designs for brand new toilets, change rooms and admin rooms and netball's been left out," he said.

Surf Coast Shire is planning to extend a nearby basketball stadium in the next 10 or 12 years, which would include netball change rooms.

Chris Pike says several sporting clubs in the area want improved facilities. (Supplied: Surf Coast Shire Council)

The council agrees facilities need to be improved, but placemaking and environment general manager Chris Pike said there were "differing views on the best solution".

He said the council had been investigating whether the netballers could use the toilets at a nearby aquatic centre.

Playing catch-up

More than 1 million Australians play netball each year, making it the country's largest female team sport.

According to the Australian Sports Commission's AusPlay data, about a quarter of Australia's 14 million females participate in a sport-related activity at least once a week.

"All of a sudden female participation rates are booming and infrastructure decisions, which have been traditionally made around men, just haven't caught up," Deakin University associate professor Helen Brown said.

The Australian Sports Commission senior research fellow has surveyed 325 women about barriers to playing sport.

Helen Brown has surveyed hundreds of women about menstruation and sporting infrastructure. (Supplied: Deakin University)

"Most of them said they'd either missed a training session or a game because of inadequate facilities for their periods," Dr Brown said.

"They were really worried about 'what happens if I bleed and there's nowhere to go quickly' or if they're bleeding heavily, which is very prominent with a lot of young girls especially."

She said spaces for period care, breastfeeding and changing clothes were vital.

The Grant Pavilion at Banyul-Warri Fields opened 15 years ago. (ABC Geelong: Jonathon Kendall)

"Most community sporting facilities in Australia were built at a time when men's sport dominated everything from participation to membership and, as a result, all the change rooms and playing facilities are often just designed for men," Dr Brown said.

"Each state does have female-friendly guidelines for policymakers and councils to use.

"Whether or not they use them, I'm not sure."

A room with a door

On a dark and wet night water pools near the kit bags of the junior girls training for the Suns.

The netball courts the Surf Coast Suns train and play on. (ABC Geelong: Jonathon Kendall)

Emery says they're not asking for a lot.

"Just a simple change room — a room with a door that we can go into," she says.

"Just for privacy, so no-one can view us changing dresses.

"A tap to be able to fill up our water bottles would be fantastic, and the safety of walking to a toilet within 10 metres that's well lit and that isn't used predominantly by males."

World.title: Quick hits: Aussie walker's 'in your dreams champ' taunt before gold
World.content:
An Australian gold medallist refuses to be intimidated by his Kenyan rival, while an English weightlifter makes a stunning revelation ahead of her Celebrity MasterChef debut.

Here are the quick hits from day eight of the Commonwealth Games.

1. 'In your dreams champ'

Isaac Beacroft (left) exchanged words with Stephen Kihu during the men's 10,000m walk final. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

Isaac Beacroft was not going to be told what to do in the men's 10,000m walk final.

The 19-year-old Australian stuck to his guns while exchanging words with Kenyan Stephen Kihu, whom he beat home for the gold.

"I knew he'd be there waiting for me to kick because he was taunting me the entire race, telling me to go around and lead it," Beacroft said.

"I was just saying, 'In your dreams champ, this is not happening today.'

"I knew he'd come back around me and then as soon as he did I thought I'd really drop the hammer and see if I could break him, and I did."

Beacroft added: "We were moving pretty quick at some stage and he was just telling me, 'Go around, go around.'

"I wasn't going to go around. I wanted it to be slow.

"You saw the kick that I had at the end, so I guess he backed himself at the end and so did I.

"If someone's going to give it to you, I'm going to give it back."

Isaac Beacroft refused to be told what to do by his Kenyan rival. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Beacroft was a member of Greater Western Sydney's junior academy until he was 16.

"I probably wasn't going anywhere in AFL, but I like to claim it," he said.

"I like to think I've made the right choice, especially when I'm about four-foot tall.

"I was usually just a step-ladder playing AFL."

2. Weightlifter's MasterChef reveal

English weightlifter Emily Campbell is also accomplished in the kitchen. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

As an Olympic and World Championships medallist, English weightlifter Emily Campbell knows a thing or two about dealing with pressure.

So it was no surprise when she won gold as favourite in the women's +86kg classification in Glasgow, setting a Games record (278kg) in the process.

But there is one stage Campbell admits she finds daunting: the Celebrity MasterChef set.

Campbell shifted from the weights room to the kitchen as a contestant in an upcoming series of the program in the UK.

"MasterChef was definitely more nerve-racking than this [Commonwealth Games], absolutely," Campbell told reporters.

"MasterChef was very tough. It was a very tough competition, but I enjoyed it thoroughly."

And what can viewers expect Campbell to cook up on Celebrity MasterChef?

"My signature dish is Caribbean, and that's all I'm going to give you because I want you to watch it," Campbell said.

3. Aussie pursuit women disqualified

Sophie Edwards was disqualified for an illegal addition to her helmet. (Getty Images: Sam Mellish)

One moment, 21-year-old Tasmanian Felicity Wilson-Haffenden was celebrating breaking the Australian 4,000m individual pursuit record and preparing to race again in the bronze medal race.

The next, she was staring, heartbroken, at the three letters no athlete wants to see on the official results next to her name: DSQ.

Both she and teammate Sophie Edwards were sensationally disqualified from the women's individual pursuit.

The official report stated that Edwards used "a helmet that has been altered or had any element added or removed in terms of design or form", while Wilson-Haffenden fell foul of a rule that prohibits riders from wearing clothing or any other accessory that could modify her morphology.

AusCycling executive general manager of performance, Jesse Korf, said Edwards had additional safety padding in her helmet and that she's "not upset".

He was not impressed about Wilson-Haffenden's disqualification, though.

"She's been seen by the medical team early this morning because of genuine shoulder discomfort and mobility issues," Korf said.

"Her shoulder got taped up to the middle of her [upper] arm

"On inspection after the race, the UCI concluded that the taping of the shoulder constituted a morphological change, but they weren't able to articulate what that exactly was because it's a grey area; you cannot measure what a morphological change is.

"Unfortunately, that conclusion is final, which we're most certainly not happy with. Felicity is upset, who is now our main concern."

4. Aussie's bronze at teammate's expense

Eliza Ault-Connell's crash in the first running of the women's 1500m T54 final prompted the re-run. (Getty Images: PA Images/Martin Rickett)

Someone was always going to be unhappy with the re-run of the women's 1,500 T54 race.

And it seems that Australian Mikaela Dingley copped the worst of it.

In the original race on Wednesday, Australian Eliza Ault-Connell and Mauritian world champion Noemi Alphonse were both taken out by Canadian Nandini Sharma.

She had gone on to finish second across the line, but was disqualified for causing the crash, which had promoted Australia's Dingley into the bronze medal position.

But because Australia and Mauritius protested the decision, authorities decided to re-run the race on Friday morning.

That proved a fateful decision, with the hampered athletes Alphonse and Ault-Connell going on to claim silver and bronze medals respectively.

"It's been an absolutely massive few days," the 44-year-old veteran told AAP.

"To have the opportunity to have this race re-run and for everyone to be able to go out there and put on their best in great conditions is really the outcome that all the athletes want."

Eliza Ault-Connell finished third in the re-run 1,500m race. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Perhaps not all the athletes.

The re-run meant that Dingley, who finished sixth in the re-run, was only bronze medallist for around 36 hours.

The silver medallist in the original race, England's Ellis Kottas, finished fourth in the re-run having told media she was "low-key traumatised" when she heard the race would be re-run.

"It's rough, but it is racing," Ault-Connell said.

"If she loves what she does and she continues to show up, it will happen.

"It's almost like 'cruel to be kind ', but we all go through that, and those opportunities are going to help you grow as an athlete."

Easy for her to say.

Somewhat pleasingly, Scottish athlete Melanie Woods won gold again, proving her result on Wednesday was no fluke.

5. Lawn bowler's 'once-in-a-lifetime opportunity'

Botswana's Charles Diteko hopes he can see Celtic play while he is still in Glasgow. (X)

Does Botswana's lawn bowler Charles Diteko have an ulterior motive for competing in Glasgow?

"I used to be a soccer player, and I'm a big fan of Celtic," Diteko said.

"So if there is a match on and I have time, I will try to get to it. It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity."

Of course, we're kidding.

We know his sole focus in Glasgow is competing for his country.

But Diteko may be in luck if he sticks around a day or so after Sunday's closing ceremony.

Celtic play Dundee in the Scottish Premiership on Monday night.

In the meantime, Diteko and Kaizer Geche are representing Botswana in the men's pairs competition.

World.title: Family's plea after daughter unable to donate organs
World.content:
John and Anne Apter say their daughter Sheridan was unapologetically herself, but also very generous with her time.

"There is no doubt whatsoever that if she could have helped someone, she would have said yes, 100 per cent," Mr Apter said.

But in the 35-year-old's final moments she was unable to give one last gift, and Australia's definition of death may have got in the way.

The last time Sheridan's parents saw her conscious was a family lunch that, typically, she had organised, before she left to spend the evening at a friend's place.

Sheridan Apter's parents say she was unapologetically herself and very generous with her time. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

Later that night she was found unconscious and blue in the bathroom.

Sheridan was taken by ambulance to hospital and put on a ventilator in an intensive care unit at Sydney's St George Hospital.

Her family was told she had suffered severe brain damage from a lack of oxygen. Eight days later, they were informed her condition would not improve.

Mr and Mrs Apter knew Sheridan would like to donate her organs, so she was moved to a theatre in the hospital where surgeons waited as her life supports were removed.

Sheridan Apter's death is being investigated by the coroner. (Supplied: John and Anne Apter)

She continued to breathe and have a heartbeat for four hours. It meant her organs had deteriorated too much to be suitable to be used as transplants.

Her parents were devastated, having lost their daughter and knowing she wasn't able to donate her organs.

"I couldn't be more certain of anything in my life than what she would have wanted with her organs," Mr Apter said.

" She would have loved to go, 'Yep, yep. My heart's beating somewhere else.' "

The Apters want a discussion on how Australians could change the system so people like Sheridan could still donate their organs.

"If there is a way that those organs can be maintained … so that when that person finally passes away, the organs are still able to be donated, well, that would be magnificent," Mr Apter said.

John and Anne Apter want more of a discussion about increasing the possibility of organ donation. (Supplied: John and Anne Apter)

Laws on death

What may have prevented Sheridan from donating her organs is the way Australia defines death.

That definition under human tissue law says death is either the irreversible cessation of circulation of blood in the body or the irreversible cessation of all function of the brain.

Helen Opdam, national medical director with the Organ and Tissue Authority and an intensive care specialist, says no other country has that precise wording around blood circulation.

"Our wording in our legislation is very specific and fairly unique, and particularly the fact that we've got [the] wording irreversible cessation of circulation of blood in the body of the person," Dr Opdam said.

Helen Opdam says the way Australia defines death is relatively unique. (Supplied)

" For example, in the UK, they talk about permanent loss of consciousness and the capacity to breathe. That's their definition of death. "

Experts say Australia's definition prevents the use of modern technology that protects the organs from deterioration and increases their suitability for transplant.

Normothermic regional perfusion (NRP) is one method used in countries such as Spain, France and the UK. It restarts circulation to part of the body, as a form of organ support.

However, Dr Opdam said using NRP arguably invalidated the determination of death because of the restarting of circulation.

"It can be argued that if you restart blood flow to even just a part of the body of the person, the donor, the patient, then you're invalidating the criteria on which death was determined," she said.

Health ethics professor Dominique Martin, from Deakin University, said NRP could increase the number of organs donated.

A 2023 study in the United Kingdom found the number of organs able to be donated increased from 2.6 to 3.3 per donor when NRP was used.

"That might sound like sort of a small difference, but when you think about the number of DCD [donation after circulatory death] donors overall, it can make quite a big difference in terms of opportunities for transplant," Professor Martin said.

Dr Opdam said there were 2,000 people on the waitlist for an organ transplant, while just 557 people were able to donate organs last year, resulting in 1,438 people receiving donations.

She said there were also 14,000 people on dialysis, some of whom could benefit from a kidney transplant.

"The opportunity or the chance for donation is actually quite small," Dr Opdam said.

"In fact, any of us, we're all more likely to need a transplant in our lifetime than we are to die and be a donor."

Death definition under review

An Australian Law Reform Commission (ALRC) review of the death definitions is due to report to the federal Attorney-General on August 16.

A discussion paper released by the ALRC proposes a brain-based definition of death, which may open the door to NRP.

The paper explains that NRP is not used in Australia because it is considered inconsistent with the existing legal framework for determining death.

Dr Opdam says the definition of death was last done in Australia in 1977 and should be modernised.

"It's clear that our current human tissue acts need to be updated to reflect contemporary medical practices and understanding of death," Dr Opdam said.

Any change of laws would need to be done by the states and territories.

702 ABC Sydney approached the office of NSW Health Minister Ryan Park for comment, but our enquiry was redirected to the NSW health ministry.

"NSW has contributed to the Australian Law Reform Commission's review process and will carefully examine any findings or recommendations included in the final report," a spokesperson for NSW Health said.

More conversation about organ donation needed

While she wasn't able to give her organs, Sheridan's corneas were still able to be donated and restored sight in someone.

Her family has also continued her generous spirit in supporting the Confident Girls Foundation, which uses her beloved sport of netball to support girls from marginalised communities.

While the Apters were unaware of NRP at the time of Sheridan's death, they hope her story can spark discussion about increasing the possibility of organ donation.

That discussion during DonateLife week this week is timely as recent NSW figures show the number of registered donors has been falling.

Just 34,516 in NSW joined the Australian Organ Donor Register last year, a 19 per cent decrease from the year before.

"More lives could be saved if there was more of a discussion around exploring all the alternatives out there around organ donation and having more donors," Mr Apter said.

World.title: EPA recommends stricter pollution rules for Santos and Inpex
World.content:
The Northern Territory Environment Protection Authority (NTEPA) has recommended changes to the licences of Darwin's two major gas processing companies, Santos and Inpex, following a review triggered by substantial under-reporting of toxic emissions.

The report, released on Friday, calls for pollution limits, limits on hot venting, and continuous monitoring of emissions.

The review was launched after Inpex revealed it had drastically under-reported toxic emissions — including the carcinogen benzene — from its Ichthys LNG plant on Darwin Harbour, sparking concerns that residents and workers could be breathing in harmful emissions.

Santos's Darwin LNG tank is set to be filled again as part of the company's Barossa gas project. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

In March, independent consultants found widespread failures in how Inpex calculated and reported emissions dating back to the start of production in 2018.

Santos has also faced scrutiny over its Darwin LNG facility, where a leaking tank has released vast amounts of methane, and there has been frequent flaring.

The review follows months of criticism of the NTEPA's oversight and transparency from both members of the public and experts, including accusations the NTEPA has been "asleep at the wheel".

On Friday, NTEPA chairman Paul Vogel said the public should have confidence the regulator had their "health at heart" and insisted the recommendations would not be watered down by the companies.

Regulator in gas leak 'scandal' paid hourly rate by industry lobbyist The man in charge of the Northern Territory government's handling of a major methane leak at a Santos gas plant was working with a lobbyist for the project's co-owner.

Mr Vogel said while the review found the current environmental licences governing Santos and Inpex were among the strictest in the country, there was room for improvement.

He said the unusually close proximity of the facilities to Darwin city — around 6 kilometres away — and the likelihood of expansion "means that we really should have a world-class regulatory regime in place that goes further than we currently have".

"There's been independent health risk assessments conducted by the chief health officer to assure the community that their health is protected from [Inpex's] emissions," he said.

"But we need to make sure that continues in the future, and there's a lot more transparency around reporting and availability of information from the company to the community."

Regulation 'alarmingly slipshod'

Environment Centre NT climate campaigner Bree Ahrens welcomed action from the regulator, but said there were still "gaping holes in the recommendations" that would continue to put Darwin's air quality at risk.

"This review is an admission that the NT EPA's regulation of Inpex and Santos's toxic air pollution under the current licences has been alarmingly slipshod and needs to be fixed," she said.

NT EPA orders Santos, Inpex licence conditions review The Northern Territory environment regulator will re-examine the licence conditions of major gas facilities in Darwin, after one of its biggest operators admitted to under-reporting potentially toxic emissions at its Ichthys LNG plant.

Ms Ahrens said it was concerning the recommendations did not limit flaring or put a cap on how long acid gas incinerators — anti-pollution systems that burn harmful gasses at high temperatures before releasing them into the atmosphere — can be out of action.

Instead, the review recommends they are "operational" 99.5 per cent of the time.

"The effectiveness of this review will depend on its implementation," she said.

"The gas industry has shown again and again it can't be trusted when it comes to our air quality and health.

"The NTEPA needs to hold the line and impose the strongest possible licence conditions, with real consequences for non-compliance."

Other recommendations include expanding enforceable pollution limits, requirements to operate and maintain a "high level" of pollution control equipment, and regular audits.

Paul Vogel says the NT should have "a world-class regulatory regime in place that goes further than we currently have". (ABC News: Charlotte Hamlyn)

Documents submitted to a 2024 Senate inquiry revealed Inpex's incinerators had been out of service for extended periods since 2019.

Mr Vogel said it could take up to 12 months before licences were fully implemented, if both companies endorsed the 23 recommendations.

In a statement, Inpex senior vice-president Bill Townsend said the company was working with the Department of Lands, Planning and Environment to assess what the potential new requirements may mean for its operations.

Santos has also been contacted for comment.

World.title: Farmer posts reward after dog shot at family nursery
World.content:
A north-east Victorian farmer is offering a $20,000 reward after his family dog was shot in a suspected drive-by attack.

Tom Powell was driving an all-terrain vehicle at his plant nursery in Stanley, near Beechworth, when his German short-haired pointer, Daisy, was shot just metres from where he was driving.

The dog was running with eight other family dogs before the incident around 8:40am on May 15.

Two staff members were also on site nearby weeding garlic.

Mr Powell said Daisy survived the shooting; the bullet entered her rear leg and exited her abdomen.

Daisy was fortunate to recover from her bullet wounds. (Supplied: Tom Powell)

The beloved family pet is recovering well having received around $2,700 worth of veterinary care.

The family initially offered a $5,000 reward for information leading to conviction, and has since ramped up the offering due to concerns about community safety.

"$20,000 is not actually a lot when you're talking about people's lives; it's quite a small amount actually," Mr Powell said.

Daisy is at home recovering from her injuries. (Supplied: Tom Powell)

"Daisy was shot, but what if that was one of my boys — they're 25, 30 years old, working here all the time, our grandchildren, staff, customers.

" It's not a lot, but it may get people talking and might make a difference. "

Mr Powell said he has lodged a police report and that an investigation is underway, but that no leads had been uncovered.

He said he was convinced the shooting was deliberate after the family was subject to a string of complaints over the past decade in relation to the business.

"There's no consequences for people's actions anymore, and it's probably taking advantage of that … and just people trying to scare us and Daisy got shot."

Stanley is a popular town for families to visit orchards in north-east Victoria. (ABC News: Erin Somerville)

Mr Powell said he believed she was shot by a person driving by the nursery on Stanley Road.

The family previously successfully turned to social media around four years ago when $20,000 worth of bikes and tools were stolen from their property.

They offered a $10,000 reward, with the community call-out generating important information, Mr Powell said.

Victoria Police has been contacted for comment.

World.title: How Gen Z sees money — and how it drives their spending and saving
World.content:
Liam* was never taught how to manage money.

So, when he earned his first pay cheque at 16, keeping it was a challenge.

His purchases started small — treating himself to things he'd gone without growing up, like a steak at a restaurant.

Then the habits escalated — gaming consoles, online spending, takeaway.

His pay started to only last days.

"Tapping my card felt too easy because I never actually saw the money leaving my hand," he said.

Growing up in a financially unstable household where money was uncertain and rarely discussed, Liam entered adulthood without learning basic skills like budgeting or saving.

Watching his pay disappear reminded him of the instability he experienced as a child, when his financial security depended on someone else's decisions.

He realised he was repeating the pattern.

Liam spent the next six months consciously changing his habits, and by the end of it, he had almost $10,000 in the bank.

Gen Z savers, against the odds

Liam isn't alone.

Data from the NAB Wellbeing Survey Q1 2026 found young Australians aged 18-29 have the highest saving intention compared to older age groups.

In total, 94 per cent of Gen Z women were trying to save compared to 93 per cent for Gen Z men.

Both sat above the 81 per cent national average of all Australians putting money aside.

But Gen Z are also navigating a financial world that looks very different from previous generations — shaped by tap-and-go payments, buy now, pay later services, online ads and an endless stream of financial advice online.

So, how are young people managing their money?

To find out, we spoke to a few.

Hugo's parents gave him the freedom to manage his own money, but still encouraged him to save. (ABC News: Marc Eiden)

Hugo, 16. Supermarket worker.

Hugo works part-time at a supermarket and spends most of his pay on car modifications.

His understanding of money came from learning through trial and error.

"I sort of just started saving after realising I had no money left," he said.

His parents encouraged saving but left him to manage it. Hugo said he's better with money now but uncertain about the future.

" I don't feel 100 per cent confident I'll buy a house, but I'm hopeful. "

Bree says she feels confident managing her money because she has strong influences and support around her. (ABC News: Dimitria Panagiotaros)

Bree, 16. Fast food worker.

Bree spends most of her income on phone data and food, with the occasional splurge on music or gifts. She's saving for a car.

"I only spend what I know I can afford based on my shifts," she said.

Her parents taught her to budget using their own financial books.

"They really wanted us to learn from their mistakes."

Her mum can view her bank account but doesn't control it. She hopes to buy a house one day, though she worries about the current market.

Evelynn says whenever she has money, her mum reminds her not to blow it all. (ABC News: Amber Irving-Guthrie)

Evelynn, 16. Cello busker.

Evelynn earns money busking and spends most of it on social outings with friends.

She has her own bank account, but is still figuring out how to manage it.

"I feel like managing money is really stressful. I don't think most kids are very well educated on money," she said.

Evelynn has searched for advice online, like, 'How do I save money faster?' but felt she "never got a good answer on that".

When financial education falls short

Behind those different experiences is a common factor: not every young person starts with the same financial education or support.

Alyssia Kennedy, 29, runs the Life After School program, visiting Tasmanian high schools to teach students the practical money skills they're not getting in the classroom or at home, including tax, work rights and budgeting.

She said the demand told its own story.

"So many schools are reaching out saying, 'We need your help because we as teachers don't know these things either.'"

Ms Kennedy said the gap was generational.

Alyssia Kennedy founded the Life After School program to bridge educational gaps. (ABC News: Audrey Courty)

"People in their 50s and 60s were taught this, whether it was by mum and dad or through school," she said.

"But the curriculum has changed a lot since then. I'm seeing gaps with those whose parents are in their 40s or under."

"Some parents want to know how to have these conversations, while others don't have the knowledge themselves."

Ms Kennedy said what young people were spending on had not changed dramatically, but what had changed was their ability to access those things, making it easier than ever to spend without registering the cost.

Where Gen Z are getting their advice

When financial education is inconsistent, many young people are turning elsewhere for guidance.

The ASIC Moneysmart Gen Z Financial Behaviours Report 2026 found that 63 per cent of Gen Z use social media for financial guidance, while 52 per cent trust 'finfluencers' and 64 per cent trust AI platforms.

Nearly one in four own cryptocurrencies, with 29 per cent saying they trade based on social media or influencer recommendations.

Still, the data doesn't paint Gen Z as careless with money.

Sixty per cent also use professional sources for financial advice, while half turn to family and friends.

The findings suggest Gen Z is actively seeking financial information, but doing so through unregulated digital platforms, where algorithms can shape the content they see.

Nearly three in four Gen Z Australians saw ads encouraging cryptocurrency investment, while more than four in 10 were contacted directly by someone offering investment advice. (Adobe Stock)

Figuring it out anyway

For Liam, now 17, changing his financial habits meant rethinking his relationship with money.

He decided to put most of his pay aside in cash, limiting his access to digital spending. He cooked cheap meals and repaired things instead of replacing them.

"I realised that if I put a majority of it away in cash, it built up really quickly," he said.

For a generation raised on digital payments, tap and go has made spending faster and more convenient. (AAP: Dan Peled)

The almost $10,000 he saved bought a car, paid for a holiday, and helped him move out of home, things he said once felt out of reach.

Liam's story is one example of how Gen Z is learning how to manage money in a financial landscape unlike previous generations.

*Liam's name has been changed..

World.title: FIFA scraps World Cup sell off plans, Infantino says
World.content:
Breaking SportSoccerFIFA World Cup FIFA scraps World Cup sell off plans, Infantino says Updated August 1, 2026 — 9:51am ,first published 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

FIFA president Gianni Infantino said on Friday world soccer’s governing body has scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors after widespread backlash. “Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place,” Infantino said. Infantino’s confirmation came as one of his senior advisor’s quit in protest at plans to sell a stake in the World Cup as European football threatened a boycott and regional confederations united in opposition to the proposal. FIFA President Gianni Infantino Getty Images Carlos Cordeiro resigned with immediate effect, calling the plan “a bad deal for football”.



Cordeiro, who was appointed in 2021 by Infantino to help shape FIFA’s future, said the body was “mortgaging football’s future without any compelling justification. “It is a bad deal for FIFA’s Member Associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game,” Cordeiro said in a statement. A former banker and ex-US Soccer Federation vice president, Cordeiro added that he had no involvement in the proposal and opposed it “unequivocally”. Meanwhile, FIFA’s chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said staff were “deceived” by Infantino, describing the proposal as a “project of one person”. “Our mission ... is to serve football. Not to serve the personal interests of a person who, unfortunately, believes he embodies FIFA when he is supposed to be at its service,” he wrote in a statement shared with the Associated Press.



FIFA had planned to proceed Despite the mounting opposition, Switzerland-based FIFA had previously said “incorrect media reports” this week had disrupted its planned consultation process but that it would press on with putting the proposal in front of its 211 national football associations. “We will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA (Member Association) has the ability to express its vote based on facts,” it said in a statement issued in the middle of the European night. FIFA has proposed creating a $20-billion subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run the World Cup and its other events, with a stake of up to 20% to be offered to external investors. Thrive Eternal, a fund run by Thrive Capital, founded by Joshua Kushner, was expected to lead the proposed investor group, FIFA said. Joshua is the brother of Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.



Trump, however, said he did not speak with Infantino about FIFA offering stakes to external investors despite having a close relationship after the US co-hosted the World Cup. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was critical of FIFA’s plan when it was announced earlier this week, told reporters on Friday that Infantino was “the wrong man to lead the organisation”. Infantino, 56, is up for re-election next year and North American football chief Victor Montagliani is reportedly looking to challenge him for the FIFA presidency. UEFA led opposition to FIFA plan European soccer’s governing body, UEFA, has led the widespread opposition to the proposal, accusing FIFA of putting the sport’s “soul” up for sale.



On Thursday, UEFA’s 55 member nations voted unanimously to boycott all FIFA tournaments, less than two weeks after Spain were crowned world champions. FIFA’s next major event is the women’s Under-20 World Cup in September. Hosts Poland said on Friday they had not received any information about the potential withdrawal of any team from the

tournament. “Nobody is selling football. This is not something FIFA would ever entertain,” FIFA said in Friday’s statement. “Everyone has the right to express their opposition and to seek further clarification but no single entity can claim to represent all 211 MAs (member associations) around the world. “Each MA should be allowed to review the proposal and have a say in shaping their own future. These are the democratic principles of FIFA.”



South American soccer governing body CONMEBOL said on Friday it had requested more information from FIFA on the proposal and would continue to analyse it before taking a position. “We recognise that the development of football requires commercial and financial decisions. However, such decisions must always serve football and never take precedence over its very

essence,” CONMEBOL said in a statement. CONCACAF, the regional federation for North America, Central America and the Caribbean, rejected the proposal during a meeting on Thursday but the 41-member body did not follow UEFA with a boycott threat. The Asian Football Confederation, which has 47 members, issued a statement on Friday saying it “stands in solidarity” with UEFA and CONCACAF, but also stopped short of threatening a

boycott. Related Article Analysis

FIFA World Cup FIFA’s offering Australia $45m to back selling the World Cup. Saying no might not be easy



The AFC, which has not historically been as frequent or vehement a critic of FIFA as its European counterpart UEFA, questioned the viability of the proposal and raised doubts about FIFA’s decision-making processes in a thinly veiled attack on Infantino. Stuart Dykes, the director of European and Institutional Affairs at Football Supporters Europe, said such decisions could not be taken behind closed doors by a small group of people. “The national associations should be demanding proper governance, proper consultation, proper stakeholder involvement,” Dykes told Reuters. “Football is not for sale. It’s a social good. Its value is created by the fans and the players ... That value is not for FIFA to extract in the interest of private investors.”



FIFA says process is a democratic one Infantino said in a letter to all member associations that they would receive $40 million each if they agreed to FIFA’s proposal by September 19. On Friday, FIFA said it would not go ahead with the plan without the support of the majority of its member associations. “These principles underpin the FFE proposal: unprecedented development funding, truly global ownership of the commercial opportunities of our sport, and full self-determination through a democratic process for all MAs,” FIFA said. UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC combined have 143 associations, well over half of FIFA’s 211 members.



However, not all individual member nations are certain to follow their federation’s line. The Czech FA’s President David Trunda told Sky Sports he could see the “positive impact of FIFA’s intentions”, but it has since rejected the proposal while endorsing UEFA’s stance. The Mexican Football Federation said it would study the proposal before deciding its position, despite CONCACAF’s rejection. Reuters

World.title: Before they find a new coach, the Waratahs need to find an identity
World.content:
SportRugby UnionSuper Rugby Opinion Before they find a new coach, the Waratahs need to find an identity Paul Cully Rugby columnist August 1, 2026 — 9:33am

August 1, 2026 — 9:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The last time the Waratahs were a rugby team with a crystal-clear sense of who they were was May 2014, far from the bright lights of Sydney. In New Plymouth, New Zealand, the Waratahs turned up and physically dominated the Dave Rennie-coached Chiefs. Israel Folau Getty Images They were too big, too strong, and filled with too many power athletes for the Chiefs to handle. They won the match 33-17. There and then, the Waratahs knew what they were about, and the rest of the competition got the message as well – they weren’t soft touches coming out of the Eastern Suburbs.



Twelve years later, does anyone have a clue what the Waratahs stand for? Can you describe Waratahs rugby in a sentence? Everyone knows what Brumbies rugby is. The Reds have a much more identifiable style after the Les Kiss years, and the Force are developing their own thing in Perth under Simon Cron: fighters, technically well-drilled, with a bit of a chip on their shoulder. Loading The Waratahs should have a rugby brand, given that NSW is an absolute goldmine for collision-sport athletes. There should be a constant stream of big men and superior athletes feeding into the Waratahs system. Everyone should know before the season starts that the Waratahs have the best raw materials to work with.



That doesn’t guarantee success every year, but it should mean that if all the tactical and cultural bases are covered off by good coaching, the Waratahs will be a consistently competitive side. They should be the Australian team that everyone loves to hate because of the volume and quality of players coming through. Instead, they’ve become the Australian team everyone loves to play. The 2026 season was another forgettable campaign for the Waratahs. Getty Images The failed answer to this problem has been to sack the coach, with Dan McKellar the latest out the door. As a result, the Waratahs have developed a saviour complex. It’s always the new coach who is going to save them.



But every time a new coach comes in, he brings new ideas, new thoughts on which players they need, and what style of rugby they will play. They’ve got it upside down. Those things should already be embedded in the organisation’s walls. The new coach should know exactly what he is stepping into the moment he starts, and that he is just a relatively small part of a bigger picture that started long before he was hired and will continue long after he leaves. Dan McKellar’s time in charge of the Waratahs didn’t yield great success. Getty Images That has not been happening at the Waratahs. Where is the consistency of approach between, say, a Daryl Gibson and a McKellar? They are chalk and cheese. And to emphasise the failure of the Waratahs as an organisation, they punted Rob Penney, and he then went on to win a Super Rugby title with the Crusaders. He was the same coach in Christchurch that he was in Sydney.



Calls to reinstate Michael Cheika, therefore, are surely rooted in the idea that Cheika is synonymous with the last time the Waratahs had a playing style that was theirs alone – lots of size, lots of natural talent and some smart guys pulling the tactical strings. Related Article Wallabies Kiss era is under way, but can he spark Wallabies in time for World Cup? I have no idea if a Cheika return would work. It is hard for the same coach to make the magic happen twice. But if it is not him, there will be enough men with enough knowledge and passion within the NSW rugby community to understand the 2014-era Waratahs blueprint and have a clear idea of how to bring it back. That could include 2014 Waratahs alumni Stephen Hoiles, now a young coach himself, but in all likelihood there will be plenty of parties whose blood runs blue who have roles to play.



This masthead reported last week that Rugby Australia was considering Joe Schmidt as an option, but he is not the right fit. In fact, the coach hunt isn’t even the Waratahs’ main problem – it’s the lack of continuity over the past decade. When you look at the Waratahs, with all the natural playing resources they enjoy in NSW, the first thought is: “All the gear, and no idea.” The second is: “What a damn shame.” They really stood for something in that short Cheika era. The 2014 title and the crowds that followed were simply a consequence of understanding who they were.

World.title: How the ‘Miracle in Mudgee’ inspired an unlikely bond between two Origin stars
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 How the ‘Miracle in Mudgee’ inspired an unlikely bond between two Origin stars Christian Nicolussi August 1, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of the first things Ethan Strange did when he was named to start in the halves for NSW on the eve of Origin I was to ask Nathan Cleary about the Miracle in Mudgee. Not to gloat about that length-of-the-field try that won the game in extra time – Strange wanted to discuss the other play he ran against Penrith that night. In the 75th minute of the Raiders’ epic 20-16 golden point win in round 25 of last season, Canberra were attacking Penrith’s line when Strange drifted from the left side of the field to the right. Halfback Jamal Fogarty threw a short ball for Strange on the runaround, and he used his speed and power to get on the outside of Scott Sorensen and inside Blaize Talagi to score a try. Cleary, a student of the game, knew exactly what Strange was talking about when the subject was raisedbefore Origin I. The chat came not long after it had become clear Strange would be starting ahead of the injured Mitchell Moses.



Cleary and Strange rehearsed it at the captain’s run on the Tuesday, then attempted the play approaching the hour mark at Accor Stadium as the Blues started their comeback against a 12-man Queensland. Strange, 21, playing in his first Origin game and growing in confidence with every minute, did much the same as he did that night in Mudgee – drifted to the right, called for the ball and steamrolled Cameron Munster to score. The play worked to perfection, but a mistimed run from back-rower Haumole Olakau’atu, who collided with Harry Grant while serving as a decoy runner, resulted in the four-pointer being overturned by the video referee. Four points might not have been the result in Origin, but the manner in which the playmakers replicated the move was there for all to see. The connection had been quickly established.



In the countdown to Saturday’s Penrith-Canberra clash in the town in NSW’s central western, Cleary praised Strange for backing himself on the big stage. “It’s a credit to him – it’s a play he likes, and as soon as he found out he was playing [Origin I], he came up to me and said, ‘Let’s run it’,” Cleary said. Origin halves Nathan Cleary and Ethan Strange will go head-to-head on Saturday. Getty Images “I was like, yeah sweet, and we got it on. Unfortunately, it didn’t end up a try, but it was nice to have someone there with that confidence to say, let’s do it. “All I remember from that night last year [in Mudgee] was me missing the field goal, then ‘Strangey’ cracking me with the left foot, then they ran the length. It was a pretty bad feeling. Hopefully we can turn it around on Saturday.”



NSW coach Laurie Daley recalled the pair discussing the play. “The only time I can remember them trying that play was at the captain’s run,” Daley said. “I knew once they got into the position they did in game one, then Strangey started to move, I knew it was coming. “You just wait to see what happens off the back of it. I thought it was great. You have to play to your strengths. “You don’t always see that play because a lot of the five-eighths aren’t runners – some just hold an edge – and you also need the power to do it. It also shows you what Nath is about and how he’s happy to listen and try anything – he’s all about the team. Related Article Exclusive

NRL 2026 Parramatta Eels rising star sidelined over safety concerns amid Sydney gangland war



“Those two will come up against each other on Saturday on the same side of the field. Penrith will know how strong Ethan is. He’s such a wonderful player.” The Raiders are chasing a fifth straight win in the hope of keeping their finals hopes alive, while Penrith are without Dylan Edwards (shoulder) and Talagi, who was dropped to reserve grade for Jack Cogger, and will do well not to let their attention drift to the next fortnight when top-four opponents the Warriors and Sydney Roosters await.

World.title: ‘No real rules’: Meet the Australians driving the Dungeons & Dragons craze
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Not long ago, playing Dungeons & Dragons was considered akin to making deals with the devil. The role-playing game inspired immense panic in the 1980s, with some parents and fundamentalist religious groups worrying it would expose children to dark, demonic whims. This panic didn’t last forever, of course. Concerns subsided as psychologists and players pushed against the ludicrous claims. However, even as it became more socially acceptable, the game remained largely relegated to the periphery of society – something only “nerds” would play. Dungeons & Dragons used to be labelled “satanic”. Now, it’s just seen as a devilishly good time. Joe Armao Thankfully, being “nerdy” no longer means what it used to. Nowadays, D&D is everywhere – the teens of Hawkins play it in Stranger Things, Chris Pine lives through it in Dungeons & Dragons: Honour Among Thieves, and voice actors master it for millions of viewers in Critical Role. Even Vin Diesel has played it. Over its 50 years, the game has gone from a satanic ritual or nerdy pastime to an all-out pop-cultural juggernaut. While the game itself is everywhere, less is known about the people driving it. D&D wouldn’t be possible without its dungeon masters (DMs), those who build and lead the fantastical adventures. They’re so sought after there are Australian online marketplaces, helping players connect with experienced D&D masters across the country. From Stranger Things to Critical Role, Dungeons & Dragons has become a pop-cultural juggernaut. So, what exactly does it mean to be a DM, and what does it take to be at the forefront of an ever-growing cultural phenomenon?



Matt Hillman Fantasy always appealed to Matt Hillman, a 44-year-old game master at Melbourne’s HP Gamemasters. It eventually led him to D&D in high school, where he’d play with a group of friends during lunch. However, it wasn’t until the COVID-19 lockdowns, when he suddenly had ample spare time, that the game really took hold of his life. Dungeons & Dragons isn’t just a job for Matt Hillman, it’s father-daughter bonding time. Ruby Alexander Being a DM is now Hillman’s full-time job. Each week, he spends around 15 to 40 hours planning “home-brew” campaigns (adventures based entirely on his own imagination rather than pre-written journeys), some of which he releases for other groups to enjoy. So detailed are his campaigns that he sometimes fills out three entire notebooks with character traits, notes on narrative developments, setting descriptions and so forth. One of his favourite campaigns, “Tyranny of the Dragons”, ran for over a year, with its war finale lasting 16.5 hours. There is some debate over whether DMs should be paid for this kind of work, Hillman says. However, it’s becoming more common, particularly given the time people like himself invest. Even Chris Pine got on-board the D&D train, starring in Dungeons & Dragons: Honour Among Thieves in 2023. Aidan Monaghan/Paramount Pictures



“It’s meant to be a hobby, but the benefits of having a paid DM is you then have someone with experience,” he says. “They have materials, kit and supplies to make the experience more spectacular. They’re also not necessarily a friend, which is good because sometimes when you’re DMing for friends and something goes wrong, that can be friendship-breaking. People get very passionate about this, particularly if you have a problem player at the table.” Related Article Streaming Stranger Things is finally about to end. But does anybody even care? D&D isn’t just Hillman’s job, it’s also a way for him to bond with his 12-year-old daughter. She was in one of his first-ever campaigns, during which she just repeatedly set fire to everything with fireballs. She has since focused, Hillman says, and recently requested a D&D-themed birthday party. She’s even running some of her own games. “Anyone can be a DM,” he says. “There’s no prerequisite. You just have to be willing to sit behind the screen, plan out what’s going to happen for your players, and help drive the collective story you’re telling. There’s no real rules.” Alicia Warren Alicia Warren’s first D&D campaign ended in literal flames. The curtains were drawn while they played, and when they opened them hours later, a fiery red sky from the 2003 Canberra bushfires greeted them. “It was almost like the D&D universe had followed us back into our universe,” Warren says.



Sydney-based Dungeon Master Alicia Warren (right) says you can find campaign inspiration anywhere – from native birds to songs on the radio. Sitthixay Ditthavong This experience immediately hooked her, leading to the establishment of Geek on a Leash, a Sydney-based business that helps connect people with game masters for various role-playing games. Nowadays, Warren runs around four to five games a week, for which she’s paid on average $40 to $80 per hour. “You just need the drive to do it, and the capacity to either learn a pre-written module or understand the structure of the world enough to be able to create a story for your players,” Warren says. “It helps if you’ve got a passion for performing. If you bring enthusiasm to the game, it’s almost impossible for your players not to be drawn in.” Clear communication skills help too, whether you’re a meticulous planner or a looser improviser. You can hone these skills by watching other DMs in action, she says, either in-person or via webseries like Critical Role. A short improvisation course could even help, Warren says. It isn’t necessary, though – you can ultimately draw inspiration from anything. “I can be staring at a blank page for a long time before something will finally spark inspiration. It can be the strangest things. I could be walking my dogs, and a thought comes to mind after seeing a native bird,” Warren says. “Other times, it’s the lyrics of a song. I’m in the middle of completing a four-week campaign inspired by the lyrics to the Eagles’ Hotel California.”



Related Article Review How Dungeons & Dragons inspires, and feeds off, the rise of geek culture The only real challenge, she says, is co-ordinating times to play. The game also used to have a reputation for gatekeeping, being a pastime largely dominated by white men. However, Warren says this has changed significantly over the past decade. “When you look at the statistics of who plays D&D, many are of minorities and different neurodiversity. You get a lot of people coming together. It’s a co-operative game where there’s a lot of acceptance and love of people just as they are,” she says. “People share their experience of using D&D to help discover more aspects of their own self and personality that they weren’t otherwise aware of or didn’t feel comfortable expressing in the real world. It’s helped some people really discover themselves and feel more complete.” Lachlan Jones Lachlan Jones began playing D&D at the tail-end of the “satanic panic”. He was nine years old, and had just discovered a neighbour’s beginners’ box set. This didn’t sit well with his other neighbours, however, who advised his parents to stop him from playing such “devilish” games. Thankfully, his parents didn’t heed this advice, and Jones is still playing to this day. He also runs games around twice a month, taking players on all kinds of adventures, from Pirates of the Caribbean-themed escapades to battles against gargantuan sharks with laser-beam eyes.
