World.title: Funding for more local GPs to remove suspected skin cancer
World.content:
The government has announced funding for more local GP clinics to be able to remove suspected skin cancer.

Health Minister Simeon Brown said it's the first stage of a $23 million investment in community healthcare.

He said in some parts of the country, the only option to check and remove suspicious skin spots and moles is a long hospital wait or paying to go private.

"This first stage will build on the skin cancer services that already work well across the country, creating a nationally consistent approach to how this care is delivered."

The funding was set to go towards upskilling more GPs to offer skin cancer services, including training in dermoscopy, which uses a specialised magnifier to examine spots closely, and skin excision.

Brown said over time it would also include cataract follow-up with optometrists, symptomatic bowel cancer detection, and respiratory care.

"New Zealand has among the highest rates of melanoma in the world. Skin cancer is our most common cancer, and it is one of the most treatable, but only if it is caught early."

Brown highlighted this as a build on the $5 million the government invested last year to enhance general primary care services.

"This initiative means more New Zealanders will be able to have suspicious spots checked and removed sooner, without waiting for a hospital appointment or paying to go private.

World.title: Boxing bronze medals for Fiji and Tuvalu at Commonwealth Games
World.content:
There's been bronze medals in boxing for Fiji and Tuvalu at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Fiji's Jasmine Daunakamakama has been beaten in the women's 57kg semifinals by Northern Ireland's Michaela Walsh.

But in boxing, once a fighter is beaten they cannot fight again, so the losing semifinalists both get bronze medals.

She told FBC it was a privilege to share the ring with Walsh - the Birmingham 2022 champion - and she was grateful for the experience.

"When I get back to Fiji, I'm going to work even harder, push myself, so I can come back even stronger," she said.

Tuvalu's Tarona Khanum Badi Pasoni Taafaki also lost her semifinal, in the women's 75kg, to India's Lovlina Borgohain, but also gets a bronze medal.

Her father, Badi Ta'afaki, is her coach, while her brother Pasoni Ta'afaki has also carried Tuvalu's flag in the men's 70kg division in Glasgow.

Her sister, Francis Ta'afaki, won silver at the Youth Futures Cup in Thailand earlier this year.

Tarona Taafaki told World Boxing it means a lot to her to represent her small nation.

Tuvalu's Tarona Khanum Badi Pasoni Taafaki got a boxing bronze medal at the Glashow Commonwealth Games. World Boxing Facebook screenshot

"Everyone's that asking me my entire life where I'm from and I say I'm Tuvaluan, they don't even know where that is, if it's like Pacific country or African country," she said.

"For Tuvaluans specifically I just encourage them to go out, do whatever they want, go make it big.

"Me being able to get a bronze at the Commonwealth [Games] should inspire other Tuvaluans out there."

Meanwhile, two judokas from Kiribati and one from Nauru were beaten in the elimination rounds of 16.

Cook Islands' Max Teuruaa finished 11th of 12 starters in the men's decathlon - the combination of 10 track and field events. He threw a personal best in the decathlon shot put of 11.31 metres, which was 11th of 12 throws.

In the netball, the Tonga Tala have beaten Wales, 63-53, to finish 9th overall.

World.title: Kingmaker candidate elected new president of New Caledonia's government
World.content:
A member of New Caledonia's Eveil Océanien kingmaker's party, Milakulo Tukumuli, has been elected as the new president of the territory's 'collegial' government.

He was elected by New Caledonia's 54-member Congress during a special sitting on Friday where the 11 members of the French Pacific territory's "collegial" government were elected.

The Congress sitting directly stems from the recent provincial elections held on 28 June.

Based on the principle of proportional representation, the new executive is a reflection of the recent provincial elections, as well as the "governance pact" sealed between the pro-France bloc and the small Eveil Océanien party, often dubbed the "kingmaker's party".

Under the pact, which already propelled pro-France candidate Virginie Ruffenach (pro-France Rassemblement party) to the Chair of the Congress earlier this month, the head of Eveil Océanien (a Wallisian-based party he founded in 2019), Milakulo Tukumuli, 41, takes the helm of New Caledonia's government as its President.

Tukumuli is the first New Caledonian government President of Wallisian heritage.

Who is in the mix?

Another prominent figure from the previous government, Christopher Gygès (Les Loyalistes party), is now the local government's Vice-President.

Gygès previously held key economy-related portfolios and is also likely to follow-up on the implementation of a massive economic and social recovery plan mostly financed by France by way of a mix of loans and grants.

Another key figure in the new government is Alcide Ponga (Rassemblement party), who was Government President under the previous government.

Ponga's tenure as former President was marked by a difficult period especially after the serious unrest which started in May 2024 and caused 14 dead and over €2.2 billion in material damage, as well as the economic and social repercussions from massive destructions and job losses in the economic and business sector.

Ponga is also a former executive in the nickel mining sector and is highly likely to be given New Caledonia's mining portfolio to address the sector's worst crisis in decades.

Pro-France Philippe Blaise (Les Loyalistes party), a former Vice-President of the Southern Province, is also part of the new team with an experience mostly related to the economic and finance sector.

Another newcomer, pro-France Laurent Bonnefond, (Les Loyalistes party) also specialises in matters related to business and civil society initiatives.

Front view of New Caledonia's Congress building in Noumea Supplied

Meanwhile, Nina Julié (pro-France Les Loyalistes party), whose pre-politics career includes experience in teaching, is one of the newcomers to government, and is widely tipped to take charge of the education sector.

On the pro-independence (UC) side, Johanito Wamytan, with an artistic and cultural background, is also part of the new government, one of a new generation of leaders brought forward by pro-independence grouping, UC-FLNKS.

Also from the UC-FLNKS, Ernest Déméné specialises in youth and social-related issues.

Meryl Marlier, another pro-independence new member of the government, has a background marked by agricultural, rural and farming matters.

Billy Forest is the only minister from New Caledonia's other pro-independence party, the UNI (Union for Independence). He has a finance and budget-oriented background.

Sensitive allocation of portfolios

After the vote in Congress, on Friday morning, the local Parliament held a separate vote, at New Caledonia's government house, for the 11 new government members to elect, in restricted committee, their President and Vice-President.

Even though the position of President was reserved for Milakulo Tukumuli, under the "governance pact" struck between the pro-France bloc and Tukumuli's Eveil Océanien, the most difficult part of the ministerial "conclave" seems related to a formal announcement regarding the allocation of ministerial portfolios.

The announcement has not yet been made, but New Caledonia's government has ten days to do so.

Tukumuli is expected to deliver his general policy address before the Congress in the coming days.

The finalisation of New Caledonia's government, under previous tenures, has sometimes proved lengthy, painful and marked by eleventh-hour intense negotiations between opposing camps.

On occasions, the position of President was left vacant for as long as five months (from February to July 2021) after the election of the government.

This was due to differences within the pro-independence camp before UNI's Louis Mapou effectively took office on 8 July 2021.

On other occasions, in 2019, for similar reasons, the delay (one month) was caused by divergence within the pro-independence camp regarding the appointment to the position of Vice-President.

World.title: 'Should never be taken lightly': Police call for caution after two alpine rescues in a week
World.content:
Police are urging alpine trekkers to be more cautious after two snowboarders got lost near a Wānaka ski area on Thursday afternoon - the second incident of its kind this week.

Sergeant Darren Cranfield said just before 2pm, Wānaka Police were informed that two people who ventured beyond the boundaries of the Treble Cone ski field to explore the backcountry could not find their way back.

He said at the time there was heavy snowfall, strong winds, and near-zero visibility.

The snowboarders were found just before sunset after a roughly six-hour ground and aerial search.

"The search was complex and required the expertise of the Wānaka Alpine Cliff Rescue Team, multiple ski patrol units, and an aerial search team. Aspiring Helicopters operated in very difficult flying conditions, and it was only through the pilot's extensive local knowledge, experience, and exceptional flying skills that search teams could be safely deployed into the alpine environment.

"The snowboarders were located approximately one hour before nightfall. Had they not been found before darkness, the outcome could have been significantly more serious.

"This incident serves as another timely reminder that venturing beyond ski area boundaries into the backcountry should never be taken lightly.

World.title: Property market's 'longest and deepest downturn' in 30 or 40 years
World.content:
New Zealand's housing market is going through the longest and deepest downturn in 30 or 40 years, property data firm Cotality says.

It has released its latest property market data, which shows a 0.3 percent fall in July, after a similar drop in June.

It reported a national median value of $804,303 in July, down 1 percent from three months ago and 0.7 percent lower than the same time last year.

Dunedin was up 0.2 percent in July, Christchurch was up 0.2 percent but Hamilton dropped 0.2 percent, Wellington fell 0.5 percent, Auckland was down 0.6 percent and Tauranga 0.7 percent.

Cotality's data has shown that first-home buyers have been a record share of the market but investor activity has been more subdued.

Property economist Kelvin Davidson said they were a "really interesting" group because lower prices and a large number of properties for sale should create good buying conditions for them.

What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

"But they're also just getting a bit warier of things. They're seeing flat rents, rising costs in terms of rates and insurance… I think they've also got a pretty clear eye now on the election around what might happen and in terms of the result.

"If we see a switch of government, what that would mean for tax policy around property. It looks pretty certain we'll get a capital gains tax if we shift government. And then just waiting on any announcements around interest deductibility - would that be phased out again, if so, does it go all the way to 100 percent phasing out or does it stop halfway? That is really on investors' minds at the moment."

He said investors were worried about cashflow because even the prospect of future capital gains was "all a bit academic" if they could not afford to hold the property in the meantime.

He said it was now probably close enough to the election that many investors would decide to wait and see what happened.

"We've already seen the figures that our investors are pulling back a little bit."

He said it would be something that he would keep an eye on over the coming months.

Overall, he said the data was a continuation of the trend of the first six months of the year.

"Property sales volumes have inched lower so far this year, although they're still at a relatively normal level. But the stock of listings remains elevated and this is giving buyers the balance of power when it comes to pricing.

"It's therefore no surprise that values generally remain sluggish. The major downturn actually happened back in 2022 and 2023. But it's been a soggy picture ever since and there's certainly little sign of any meaningful upturn on the horizon yet."

Davidson said the economic outlook was more uncertain than usual, given the conflict in the Middle East and problematic inflation.

"Mortgage rates haven't moved much in recent weeks, but the likelihood is that some rises are on the cards again in the short term."

Davidson said North Shore and Waitakere were the softest parts of Auckland.

"The super-city seems to be lacking a bit of economic confidence right now, which will be weighing on housing activity and prices. But the pipeline of new housing supply is still relatively large, especially for townhouses, and this is also generally dampening property values. While this won't be welcomed by existing property owners or vendors, it's good news for first home buyers, who remain active across Auckland."

In Wellington, prices had dropped 3.1 percent in the past three months, and Davidson said buyers had the pricing power.

"Economic confidence generally remains subdued, and election uncertainty may just keep a lid on sentiment for at least the next few months as well."

Invercargill had the strongest gains in property value over the past year of any district in or city in the country. It is up 8.2 percent over 12 months.

"It's also one of only four areas to have median values at a record high ($565,397), alongside Gore, Mackenzie, and Hurunui," Davidson said.

"Each of those areas tends to be strong in either farming or tourism, or both, and with these sectors of the economy faring well, it's no surprise that there's been some degree of spillover into the property market. They're not seeing a spike in prices. But there is more resilience than many other areas."

Davidson the broader national "downphase" in the property market was the longest and deepest recorded in at least 30 or 40 years.

"Values will almost certainly start to rise again at some stage, reflecting long-term factors such as population and wage growth. But this may be a story for next year, and in the meantime, there seems to be a mindset shift underway."

He said house sales and listings were tracking sideways, and buyers having the pricing power were keeping prices flat.

But he said there were relatively few forced sales, which meant vendors did not have to capitulate.

"Yes, buyers have the power, but it's not all the power. Vendors don't have to sell at any price."

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Sami Donnelly gets second silver medal, Devon Briggs wins gold
World.content:
Kiwi cyclist Sami Donnelly has claimed a second Commonwealth Games silver medal in as many days.

Donnelly initially was deemed to have won bronze in the Women's 10km Scratch Race Final, but a disqualification bumped her into the silver medal position.

Competing at her first games, the 24-year-old won her first medal as part of the 4000m Team Pursuit on Friday.

A total of three New Zealanders lined up in the Women's Scratch Race final, with Prudence Fowler and Olympic double-medalist Ally Wollaston finishing 16th and 18th respectively.

Para-cyclist Devon Briggs had also won a gold medal for New Zealand, and set a new Commonwealth Games record in the process.

Para-cyclist Devon Briggs has won gold in the 1km C1-3 time trial final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. supplied

Briggs has taken first place in the 1km C1-3 time trial final in Glasgow.

Earlier cyclist Ellese Andrews' was taken out of the medal race in the individual sprint.

The Olympic champion was beaten in consecutive races in a best-of-three quarter final against Welsh rider Emma Finucane.

Ellesse Andrews during the Women's Sprint Qualifying at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games. Olly Hassell / SWPix / Photosport

Andrews was also part of the New Zealand sprint team that was bundled out during qualifying on Friday.

Rebecca Petch and Olivia King both were unable to get past the round-of-16 stage in their respective sprints.

On the endurance side, Bryony Botha was given a second life in the 4000m individual pursuit following the disqualification of two Australian riders but was beaten by Scotland's Erin Boothman.

AusCycling executive general manager of performance Jesse Korf addresses media after two of his team were disqualified. RNZ / Adam Burns

Botha initially failed to qualify, placing fifth, as did team-mate Emily Shearman, who finished eighth.

However, officials said Australian Felicity Wilson-Haffenden, who originally finished fourth, broke protocols due to strapping on her shoulder that "altered her morphology".

Fellow Australian rider Sophie Edwards was also disqualified due to a non-compliant helmet.

World.title: Samoa captain and coach urge resolution for their country's 'best interests'
World.content:
Samoa's national rugby team captain and coach have written to the prime minister, appealing to him to resolve the current crisis affecting Lakapi Samoa, the governing body for Samoan Rugby.

The government announced on Wednesday that it was pulling its support of Lakapi Samoa due to "unresolved internal issues and division" at the national rugby union.

World Rugby has denied reports that it gave Samoa an ultimatum to sort out problems over which body governs the sport in the country, or face a ban from international competition.

Manu Samoa rugby appeals to govt to resolve issues Pacific Waves Download MP3 5m

In a letter seen by RNZ Pacific, Manu Samoa captain Theo McFarland and head coach Lemalu Tusiata Pisi addressed prime minister Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt.

"Our greatest concern is the possibility that the current situation could result in sanctions from World Rugby," the letter said.

"Such an outcome could deny Samoa the opportunity to compete at the 2027 Rugby World Cup, despite the years of sacrifice, commitment and hard work that have earned our qualification."

McFarland and Pisi said they are not taking sides.

Instead, they appealed for a pathway that would address the government's concerns while protecting Samoa's place in international rugby.

"For us, the Rugby World Cup is about far more than rugby," they wrote.

"It is an opportunity to represent our flag, our families and our people on the world stage, while inspiring the next generation of Samoan players."

The letter said the appeal is made "not for any individual or organisation, but for the players, the future of Samoan rugby, and the best interests of Samoa".

The captain and coach said they remained proud to represent Samoa and hoped a solution could be found.

Tensions developed earlier this year following concerns raised by La'auli about the administration and governance of Lakapi Samoa, going so far as to state that he would establish a rival rugby union.

Lakapi Samoa board chairman Namulauulu Sami Leota told local media at the time the launch of a rival rugby union could spell disaster for the sport in Samoa.

He said Lakapi Samoa remained the constitutionally established governing body for rugby in the country and was recognised internationally by World Rugby.

The Samoa Observer reported World Rugby representatives met with the prime minister on Friday morning, before holding separate talks with representatives of the rival Samoa Football Rugby Union.

World.title: Eliza McCartney finally claims elusive Commonwealth crown
World.content:
After years of injuries that at times left her wondering if she would ever compete again, New Zealand pole vaulter Eliza McCartney has finally added Commonwealth Games gold to her decorated career.

In challenging conditions at Glasgow's Scotstoun Stadium, the 2016 Olympic bronze medallist edged Australia's Nina Kennedy on countback in a tense final. Fellow Kiwi Imogen Ayris clinched bronze, matching her effort in Birmingham four years ago.

McCartney and defending champion Kennedy both cleared 4.65m, but the New Zealander took the title after clearing the height at the first time of asking. Kennedy needed two attempts at 4.65m before both athletes were unable to clear 4.70m.

It is the first Commonwealth Games title for the 29-year-old, who won silver on the Gold Coast in 2018 and has spent much of the past decade battling chronic injuries.

In a competition made difficult by cold conditions and a troublesome crosswind, consistency proved decisive.

While neither McCartney nor Kennedy could find a clearance at 4.70m, McCartney's cleaner card through the earlier heights ultimately made the difference.

Fellow Kiwi Imogen Ayris completed a memorable night for the team, claiming bronze with a clearance of 4.55m to bookend the medal placings for New Zealand.

Olivia McTaggart finished fourth after bowing out at 4.30m.

The 25-year-old was visibly devastated after her third and final miss, remaining on the landing mat for several moments as she composed herself before eventually rising to acknowledge the crowd.

World.title: FIFA executive lashes Infantino over sell-off plan
World.content:
FIFA's chief operating officer said its staff were deceived by president Gianni Infantino's World Cup sell-off plan, and suggested the project must not go ahead.

Zurich-based executive Kevin Lamour all but invited Infantino to fire him in a statement to the Associated Press that defended his colleagues amid intense fallout from the FIFA boss's plan to sell stakes in future World Cup profits to private equity funds.

Mr Lamour wrote that staff were "deceived" by Mr Infantino's lack of openness in planning the sale over recent months and "deserve better than contempt and intimidation".

"It is the project of one person," wrote Lamour, a long-time colleague of Infantino at both FIFA and European soccer body UEFA.

Gianni Infantino (left) and Donald Trump were often seen together during and in the lead-up to the 2026 World Cup. (Getty Images: Chris Brunskill)

"Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions."

Mr Lamour's statement came hours after Mr Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker who represented the soccer body on the White House Task Force for the World Cup, resigned and urged other senior FIFA staff to speak out.

"I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup," Mr Cordeiro wrote in a statement. The former US Soccer Federation president said he was not included in talks about the plan backed by a New York investment fund created by Joshua Kushner.

"Let me be clear. I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally," Mr Cordeiro said. He called the $US20 billion ($28.5 billion) commercial subsidiary "a bad deal for football".

Mr Lamour did not resign the post he has held since 2024 but said he had a duty to his colleagues.

Joshua Kushner (right) with brother Jared, is leading the charge to make a private investment in FIFA. (Getty Images: Patrick McMullan)

"And if that means I lose my job then so be it," the French official said.

"I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

Mr Lamour came to soccer from politics two decades ago as an aide to then-UEFA president Michel Platini. He often had an international role in soccer politics, liaising with FIFA member federations in Africa and Asia, who are weighing their own decisions on Mr Infantino's offers of $US20 million each by a deadline of September 19.

Mr Cordeiro often joined Mr Infantino on working visits to meet US President Donald Trump at the White House in recent years.

"Football has been central to my life, and after more than 35 years in banking I understand both the value of this asset and the consequences of giving part of it away," he said.

"That is why this proposal should be rejected."

Mr Infantino has proposed spinning off FIFA's commercial businesses — including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women — into a $20 billion subsidiary with 20 per cent owned by private investors.

The "anchor investor," described by FIFA, is Kushner, the younger brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

"FIFA already has access to extraordinary financial resources. The organisation sits on billions of dollars in reserves and no debt," Mr Cordeiro said. He noted FIFA's revenue of $15 billion in the past four years tied to the men's World Cup just ended.

A breakdown of FIFA's bid to sell the World Cup Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in FIFA's events and competitions arm to investors would grant them control over the World Cup.

"Against that backdrop, selling a permanent stake in football's most valuable asset to raise $4.2 billion makes little sense. It is mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification," he said.

Mr Cordeiro said he shared five years of working for FIFA alongside Infantino with "dedicated, principled people who care deeply about the game".

"I hope they, too, will speak up," he wrote, "because decisions of this magnitude should be made in the interests of football, not those who stand to profit from it."

Mr Infantino has been president of FIFA for more than 10 years and seemed sure to be re-elected unopposed next March. FIFA has set a November 18 deadline for challengers to come forward.

Mr Lamour was part of Mr Infantino's inner circle that campaigned for him to become the surprise winner of that FIFA presidential election in February 2016.

World.title: Why no other runner embraced Adaejah Hodge after her 200m win
World.content:
Australian sprint star Torrie Lewis says she is not surprised no-one embraced gold medallist Adaejah Hodge after the women's 200m final.

Lewis finished sixth in her pet event after something of a surprise bronze in the 100m final a few nights prior.

The 21-year-old won her semifinal and was one of the fastest qualifiers into Friday's final, local time, where she was drawn alongside Hodge, who broke the Commonwealth Games record in the semis.

Hodge stormed to gold in 22.07 seconds, but the customary hugs and embraces between competitors were absent.

"Let's just say I'm not surprised no-one shook her hand and I'm not supposed to say any more than that," Lewis said.

Torrie Lewis was told not to talk about Adaejah Hodge. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

She added: "I've been told not to say anything. I would love to say some words, but I'm not allowed to.

"I think everyone knows what I would like to say, but just fill in the blank yourself."

If you are slightly confused, the context goes back to 2024.

Hodge, from the British Virgin Islands, tested positive for a banned substance from a sample given at the under-20 world championships in 2024, where she won the 200m ahead of Lewis on August 30 in Lima.

Hodge tested positive for banned metabolic modulator GW1516, also known as Cardarine or Endurobol, which increases fat metabolism and improves exercise adaptation, according to Sport Integrity Australia.

Lewis was elevated to the gold-medal position when Hodge was banned in March 2025, with the Australian celebrating being "the 1st clean runner across the line" on Instagram.

Loading Instagram content

The findings from an Athletics Integrity Unit investigation at the time revealed that Hodge was told about the positive test in November and she gave "an explanation" and "additional information" that convinced investigators she accidentally (on the balance of probabilities) ingested the substance.

Hodge's explanation and "substantial assistance" in the case meant what would have been a two-year ban, taking her through to August 27 this year, was reduced by seven months, allowing her to resume competing in January and make it to Glasgow.

Both runners received automatic places in the semifinals of the 200m, with Lewis winning the first race in 22.64 and Hodge running a Games record of 22.01 to win hers, setting up their first rematch since that infamous race in Peru two years ago.

Hodge said she came out with a point to prove.

Adaejah Hodge's doping ban was reduced by seven months for her cooperation with the investigation, allowing her to comepte in Glasgow. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"I've put all that behind me. I just wanted [to] move forward and work extra hard to show I didn't need it. I never will need it," she said.

"I just knew I had to put in extra work to prove to the people, the haters, that I'm Adaejah Hodge."

And she was unfazed by the lack of connection with her rivals.

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

"It's competition. Everybody's goal out here is to win. I don't really know what to say about that," she said.

"It's about competing, and if you want to shake my hand, you want to shake my hand. If you don't, you don't. I'm going to be a good sport, I'm going to tell everybody good job because we all put in the hard work to be out here and compete to the highest level."

As for Lewis's embraces with the rest of the field.

"This is my first time meeting some of the girls, but they all seem really nice," the Australian said.

World.title: Chaos vs calm: What to expect when Australia and Ireland go head-to-head
World.content:
Last year, when the AFL reached out to the Irish players in the AFLW to gauge their interest in a representative game, it was a resounding yes please.

"Everyone was screaming yes, being like, 'Let's do it,' we wanted this for so long," GWS star EIlish O'Dowd told ABC Sport.

"We're so delighted that it's been put in place … It's hard to tell how it's going to be."

The inaugural clash between Australia and Ireland was officially announced in May, with plans for it organised quickly.

The players were offered a Gaelic ball or Sherrin to play with, with the Irish contingent opting for the latter and playing under Australian Rules.

Irish fans of AFLW These Irish families get up at all hours of the night to watch AFLW and host viewing parties with 30-plus people for big games.

Irish captain Orla O'Dwyer joked that if they had chosen the sphere ball used in Ireland, the Australian girls would just get "hammered".

"(But) having the top Irish and Aussie players come together and play, I suppose that's why we're here, we're here to play AFLW, that's why we got drafted, that's why we came," O'Dwyer said.

"You might have Irish fans go to this game to support Ireland, and they might leave being AFLW fans for the season, and that's huge as well for the growth of our game."

Irish players are known to be fast, and at times, chaotic. There is more running with constant play in Gaelic football.

Vikki Wall of Ireland is tackled by Ash Riddell of Australia during yesterday's captain's run. (Getty: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

Given the short turnaround time to get the marquee game going, including players going into camp just days ago with not even a main training afforded, the styles of play expected are the chaos of the Irish versus the composure of AFLW under North Melbourne's Darren Crocker.

The Irish coach, also Sydney's new head coach, Colin O'Riordan, joked at the pre-match press conference he did not want to "give away all the secrets that we don't have".

"You just have to adapt and overcome. That's the mentality probably. (And) speaking from an Irish person, that's a lot of our mentality as Irish people is adapt and overcome," O'Riordan said.

"We haven't had a main training session; we'll do a captain's run today, but at the same time, does that really matter? Probably not. It just forces us to come together quicker."

Crocker said his Australian side had the chance to come together and speak about their identity for the clash.

He gestured to Australian captain Jasmine Garner, also the captain under him at the Kangaroos. "If you look at the person sitting next to me, just so skilful, great decision maker, really composed, really calm," he said.

"I think we've got a really well-balanced team in regards to that. Colin's mentioned the word chaos … I feel like it could be a little bit of composure and control against chaos.

"You know, that sounded quite like a Get Smart episode!"

Fans turned out to opening training for pictures and signatures from the AFLW players. (Getty: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

He added that it would be a mistake to underestimate what this game means for both sides.

"It is a great honour to be the first to play a historic AFLW international game against Ireland. It's fantastic and a real privilege for us. I hope the Irish aren't underestimating how patriotic the Australians are as well," he said.

Fans are keen to see particular match-ups, especially between players from the same team, such as O'Dwyer and her Brisbane teammate and Australian representative Sophie Conway on the wing.

They'll see a lot of players rotating through the game.

The game being on the eve of the upcoming season, just one week before the season opener at Docklands Stadium between Carlton and St Kilda, means there are some concerns about workload and conditioning.

To manage these physical demands, both teams will use an extended nine-player interchange bench (four more than in standard AFLW matches).

"There are (some players on managed minutes), but that's the beauty of having nine players on the interchange. We can give this experience to all 25 players, knowing that a few of them are being load managed. … It allows those players to experience this," Crocker said.

There are 46 current Irish players across the AFLW competition. (Getty: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

There are 46 Irish players across the competition. A lot of big-name stars will feature in today's clash against Australia, such as Sarah Rowe, Vikki Wall, Áine McDonagh, Niamh McLaughlin, Erika O'Shea, Dayna Finn and Aishling Moloney, while some lesser-known names also got the call-up to fill out the squad.

Meanwhile, Australia had almost 500 players to pick from, meaning Crocker's side could pull from a much larger pool of All Australians, premiership players and best and fairests, with each selection known across the competition as a star player.

For this reason, and playing under Australian Rules, O'Dwyer said she is fine with the Irish not going in as favourites.

"Us Irish, we love being an underdog, it's something we thrive off of," she said.

World.title: Infantino's advisor quits as FIFA's World Cup plan triggers backlash
World.content:
A senior advisor to FIFA President Gianni Infantino resigned in protest at plans to sell a stake in the World Cup on Friday, as European football threatened a boycott and regional confederations united in opposition to the controversial proposal.

Carlos Cordeiro resigned with immediate effect, calling the plan "a bad deal for football".

Mr Cordeiro, who was appointed in 2021 by Mr Infantino to help shape FIFA's future, said the soccer body was "mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification".

"It is a bad deal for FIFA's Member Associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game," Mr Cordeiro said in a statement.

A former banker and ex-US Soccer Federation vice president, Mr Cordeiro added that he had no involvement in the proposal and opposed it "unequivocally".

Senior adviser to FIFA president Carlos Cordeiro resigned with immediate effect. (Reuters: Kent Nishimura)

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also called for Mr Infantino to resign over the plans, labelling them an "outrageous".

"The idea that it could even be brought forward, in my view, shows that the FIFA [president] is the wrong man to lead the organisation," Mr Burnham said.

Despite the mounting opposition, Switzerland-based FIFA said "incorrect media reports" this week had disrupted its planned consultation process but that it would press on with putting the proposal in front of its 211 national football associations.

"We will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA (Member Association) has the ability to express its vote based on facts," it said in a statement issued in the middle of the European night.

FIFA has proposed creating a $US 20-billion subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run the World Cup and its other events, with a stake of up to 20 per cent to be offered to external investors.

Thrive Eternal, a fund run by Thrive Capital, founded by Joshua Kushner, was expected to lead the proposed investor group, FIFA said. Joshua is the brother of Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

UEFA leads opposition to FIFA World Cup plan

The European football association, UEFA, has led the widespread opposition to the proposal, accusing FIFA of putting the sport's "soul" up for sale.

FIFA equity plan hits strong opposition FIFA boss Gianni Infantino's controversial plan to sell 20 per cent of the organisation's commercial operations to private investors hits trouble, with European nations threatening a World Cup boycott if it goes ahead.

On Thursday, UEFA's 55 member nations voted unanimously to boycott all FIFA tournaments, less than two weeks after Spain were crowned World Cup champions.

"Nobody is selling football. This is not something FIFA would ever entertain," FIFA responded in Friday's statement.

"Everyone has the right to express their opposition and to seek further clarification but no single entity can claim to represent all 211 MAs around the world.

"Each MA should be allowed to review the proposal and have a say in shaping their own future. These are the democratic principles of FIFA."

CONCACAF, the regional federation for North America, Central America and the Caribbean, rejected the proposal during a meeting on Thursday but the 41-member body did not follow UEFA with a boycott threat.

The Asian Football Confederation, comprised of 47 members, issued a statement on Friday saying it "stands in solidarity" with UEFA and CONCACAF, but also stopped short of threatening a boycott.

The AFC, which has not historically been as frequent or vehement a critic of FIFA as its European counterpart UEFA, questioned the viability of the proposal following an overwhelmingly negative response.

It also raised doubts over FIFA's decision-making processes in a thinly-veiled attack on Mr Infantino.

FIFA says process is a democratic one

This week, Mr Infantino said in a letter to all member associations that they would receive $40 million each if they agreed to FIFA's proposal by September 19.

On Friday, FIFA said that it would not go ahead with the plan without the support of the majority of its member associations.

"These principles underpin the FFE proposal: unprecedented development funding, truly global ownership of the commercial opportunities of our sport, and full self-determination through a democratic process for all MAs," FIFA said.

UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC combined have 143 associations, well over half of FIFA's 211 members.

FIFA boss reveals $US20b plan to sell World Cup FIFA president Gianni Infantino earns more criticism after unveiling a brazen plan to "unleash the commercial potential" of the World Cup.

However, not all individual member nations would be certain to follow their federations' line.

Czech Football Association President David Trunda told Sky Sports that he could see the "positive impact of FIFA's intentions", while the Mexican Football Federation said it would study the proposal before deciding its position, despite CONCACAF's rejection.

Xabi Alonso, a World Cup winner with Spain in 2010, said on Friday that football had to prioritise the people who watch the game, not private interests.

"We have to defend the interests of all the people," the Chelsea coach told reporters in Sydney.

"I think that it's the common feeling of football people that we want something that we keep in the hands of everyone, that it's for all the people. So, hopefully it won't happen."

Reuters

World.title: Freo all but seal minor premiership with hard-fought win over Bulldogs
World.content:
Josh Treacy has broken through the Western Bulldogs' flood in his 100-game milestone as Fremantle all but sealed the minor premiership with a 37-point win at Perth Stadium.

Fremantle's perfect record in Perth this season was under threat in Friday night's blockbuster after the Bulldogs' flooding tactics ensured scores were level at half-time.

(Getty Images)

But spurred on by 53,524 fans, Fremantle kicked seven goals to one in the second half to secure the 11.12 (78) to 5.11 (41) win.

While key forwards Jye Amiss (0.1 from six disposals) and Pat Voss (1.0 from eight disposals) struggled in the flooded forward line, Treacy used his big frame to take some important contested grabs on the way to 3.2 and eight marks to go with 13 disposals.

Treacy's contested mark above three opponents and subsequent goal early in the final quarter gave Fremantle a 19-point buffer, and more importantly finally broke the spirit of the flood.

It sparked a four-goal burst from the Dockers as they extended their record at Perth Stadium to 11-0 this season.

The win guaranteed a top-two berth and two home finals for Fremantle (18-2).

And if Sydney (14-5) lose to St Kilda on Saturday, the Dockers will be crowned minor premiers with three rounds still remaining.

The Bulldogs (12-8) face North Melbourne, Carlton and Melbourne in their final three rounds, and they may need to win all three in order to snare a top-six berth and avoid the wildcard round.

Ed Richards (26 disposals, nine clearances, 752m gained) and Tom Liberatore (28 disposals, six clearances) racked up big numbers for the Bulldogs, while Cooper Hynes kicked two goals from 22 disposals in the absence of Aaron Naughton and Cody Weightman.

Fremantle star Luke Jackson (26 hitouts, five clearances, 16 disposals, two goals) edged Bulldogs big man Tim English (27 hitouts, one clearance, 15 disposals) in an intriguing ruck battle.

AAP

World.title: It's easy to see why Australia brought a psychiatrist to Glasgow
World.content:
When Kiana Elliott finished fourth for the second straight Commonwealth Games, to say the Australian weightlifter was crestfallen would be an understatement.

Over the Birmingham and Glasgow Games, a combined 11 kilograms of weight on the bar kept the gymnast from back-to-back bronze medals.

After faltering on the 118-kilogram clean and jerk that could have secured her third place on the podium, Elliott sat on the Armadillo stage and dropped her head to a depth only permitted by her background as an elite gymnast.

Australian weightlifter Kiana Rose Elliott after missing her last lift at the 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The 29-year-old was distraught to have missed the medals just as she did four years ago in Birmingham, graciously speaking to the media in barely a whisper as she tried to maintain her composure.

For a woman who embodies strength and power, her vulnerability was incredibly affecting.

"It's just a moment in time, and you're just hoping that everything will be there," she said.

"Sometimes it is, and sometimes it isn't."

Competition weightlifting is a tricky beast, with athletes having to walk a fine line between lifting the most they can, while also ensuring they can fall into the optimum weight class.

Kiana started weightlifting after an injury. Now, she's a Comm Games athlete Kiana Elliott thought gymnastics would be her pathway to the podium, but turned to weightlifting after an injury forced her to retire.

Elliott was in the 71kg weight class in Birmingham four years ago. At last year's Commonwealth Championships, she won as a 58kg competitor. In Glasgow, she lifted as a 63kg athlete.

She said it was a "really tough decision" to go up to the higher weights where the lifts need to be bigger, but she did it for her mental health.

"In Australia we do sport and we do life, and I needed my brain and my mind for the rest of my life," she said.

"Pushing my body fat down that low was not a sustainable thing for me, so I chose the competitive option.

"Weightlifting is about lifting weights, it's about lifting more weights, it's not about being a smaller person, and I'm proud that I chose the difficult option and fought my hardest.

"This isn't the end of my story. I'm not done yet."

Kiana Elliott is a study in determination while lifting. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

But for this one moment it was. As painful as the result was, she could drop her shoulders and unclench her jaw in an enormous release of emotion.

"So much has gone into this and while I was hoping for a podium result, I think it's just all a culmination of all that's gone into this starting to come out," she said of her reaction after the competition.

"There's so much to process as part of this; there's more stuff to do when I get home. I think I just need to breathe a sigh of relief and move on."

It was five minutes of wholly self-aware introspection, spoken like a woman who has done and will continue to do a lot of work on her brain.

That reflects an emphasis for the entire Australian team, so much so that, for the first time, they have an in-house psychiatrist travelling with the team.

Australian team psychiatrist Adam Deacon. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Adam Deacon is part of a varied team of experts embedded within the team, with one of the floors of the Team Aus HQ effectively transformed into a mini hospital ward.

"We'd be very surprised if any other country has matched the standards that have been established here in the headquarters," Dr Deacon told ABC Sport.

"There's an extraordinary range of talented, experienced people who are able to cater to the broad needs of the athletes.

"It's really just a pop-up sports medicine clinic where all aspects are covered as it would be in a regular clinic."

The margins are fine and tension is high at meets like the Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

And while massage therapists, physios, nutritionists and dietitians have been working to keep Australia's 255 Commonwealth Games athletes physically fit over 10 days of intense competition, Dr Deacon is focusing on their minds.

"I think most athletes would argue when they're in a good mental space they're more likely to perform at a high level," he said.

"And you could argue they can't compete at a high level unless their mental health is well. So I think that's a necessary focus."

The team has travelled with sports psychologists before but, after consultation with the athletes, feedback was received that many of them, with their own dedicated psychologists, would like to stick with those programs.

Dr Deacon provides a different, more clinical than therapeutic, service.

"The athletes are people before they're athletes and they can experience everyday issues and concerns and mental health challenges as we all do," he said.

"There are particular things that arise in this environment, in terms of performance or lack of performance or perceived failure, and that can be really, really challenging for the athletes and also the staff.

Failure is a part of sport, but it's still hard to swallow. (Supplied)

"Injuries, illness, these sort of interruptions are not necessarily expected or anticipated, and that can be enormously stressful, and that's where an acute level of crisis response is sometimes necessary."

Unlike footy players who get to take it "one week at a time", for many the Commonwealth Games is the culmination of four or more years of tireless, single-minded work.

Elliott's teammates Chloe Perkins, who missed her 48kg weight, did not even get a chance to compete, and Brenna Kean and Ridge Barredo, both suffered nasty injuries while on stage at the Armadillo.

Dr Deacon, of course, did not reveal any of the people he had spoken to in the team, but the weightlifters like Elliott, Perkins, Kean and Barredo perhaps best exemplify the risky prospect of this high-stakes quadrennial cycle.

Some athletes seek him out, some are referred to him, and for some he attends their competition for a little extra care.

Whatever form it takes, the Australian team is lucky to have him here.

World.title: 'Disappointed' but 'OK' Kennedy snags silver, teen grabs surprise gold
World.content:
Olympic pole vault champion Nina Kennedy could not defend her Commonwealth Games title against New Zealand's Eliza McCartney in a huge upset on day eighth of the Glasgow Games.

Kennedy missed gold on a countback and had to settle for silver in Glasgow.

The Australian flag bearer had one miss at 4.65 metres before clearing on the second attempt.

The difference was New Zealand's McCartney, who also cleared 4.65m, did not miss a height before missing three times at 4.70m.

"I'm disappointed. I wanted to win, and I didn't, and that's OK, you know," Kennedy said.

" I'm superhuman most of the time, but I'm also human a lot of the time. I make mistakes, and that's OK. "

McCartney held the Oceania record with 4.94m until Kennedy broke it by clearing 4.95m in Monaco last month.

It was the fifth-best height on the all-time list and best in the world for the past five years, and had Kennedy eyeing the five-metre mark.

It was a full trans-Tasman podium in the women's pole vault. (Getty: Michael Steele)

But the 29-year-old conceded she didn't handle the cold conditions well at Scotstoun Stadium.

"I don't think I've jumped that low in like four years, and I think that just demonstrates how tough it was," Kennedy said.

"I know I'm in better shape than that, and I'm excited for the rest of the season.

"But … the Comm Games, it's just so much fun.

" I know this sounds silly, but sometimes sport is more than just the medals. It's about the memories made and the connections. "

Elsewhere on the track, Lachie Kennedy and Torrie Lewis were unable to repeat their 100m medal magic in their respective 200m finals, both finishing sixth.

Earlier, Isaac Beacroft won gold in the men's 10,000m race walk before Sarah Billings dug in to take bronze in the women's 800m, sharing the podium with a pair of world champions.

Billings was the first Australian woman to win a medal in the 800m since Sharon Stewart claimed bronze in 1990.

Baker enters elite cycling company

Georgia Baker after winning the women's 10km scratch race. (Getty Images: Sam Mellish)

Georgia Baker has won her fifth Commonwealth Games gold medal, joining a select group as Australia enjoyed another prolific day at the velodrome.

Outstanding team work set the Tasmanian up for the win on Saturday morning in the women's scratch race — her fifth Games gold.

After three gold in Birmingham and another in the team pursuit on day one of track cycling in Glasgow, Baker has joined esteemed company.

Anna Meares, Matt Glaetzer and Brad McGee are the fellow members of Australia's five cycling gold club.

And with the points race and elimination to come over the next two days, the 32-year-old could be out on her own.

"You never know — could be," Baker said with a grin.

Baker did not know about the pending milestone until fellow Australian cyclist and good friend Alex Manly messaged her before the scratch race.

"I was like, wow, I didn't realise that statistic. It's very good company and it's an honour to be in that list," she said.

"Just to be alongside [them] is great."

Fellow team pursuit gold medallists Sophie Edwards and Alyssa Polites were faultless, and when Polites gave the leadout with two laps left, Baker held on for the win.

Georgia Baker's (centre) name will be on the medal, but her teammates gave her a "dream run" in the women's scratch race. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

"That was our dream run," Baker said.

"I was definitely wanting the finish line to come, that's for sure. I'm so happy."

After three gold on day one, Australia racked up three more wins to dominate the track cycling program.

The faultless execution in the scratch race was also a morale boost for the track endurance women after the frustrating and confusing start to day two.

Teammate Felicity Wilson-Haffenden was disqualified from her individual pursuit bronze medal ride because of her shoulder strapping.

While Edwards was also disqualified because of too much padding in her helmet, it was the Wilson-Haffenden ruling that concerned the Australians.

Not only did it deny their rider a shot at another medal after the team pursuit gold, but team management said there was no explanation from the race judges.

Australia swept the podium in the men's 4000m individual pursuit. (Getty Images: Rob Casey)

Also setting aside their loss to England in the men's team pursuit Ashes final the day before, Oliver Bleddyn led an Australian sweep of the individual pursuit.

He beat Conor Leahy in the final and James Moriarty won the bronze ride-off.

The fourth rider from the team pursuit, Blake Agnoletto, then stormed past brave Scottish rider Mark Stewart to win the elimination race.

While Australia had half the six-rider field in the men's keirin final, Malaysian great Azizul Awang has forgotten more about the event than Leigh Hoffman, Danny Barber and Tayte Ryan know.

Awang, who has strong Australian connections, rode brilliantly to win gold ahead of Hoffman.

In a mark of respect to the rider known as Pocket Rocketman, Hoffman and English bronze medallist Harry Ledingham-Horn put Awang on their shoulders after the medal ceremony.

It was an emotional win for veteran Mohd Azizulhasni Awang of Malaysia in the men's keirin. (Getty Images: Owen Humphreys)

"Azizul is just an inspiration. To lose to him, he's a great of the sport," Hoffman said.

" He knows how to ride a keirin better than anyone in the world. "

Gordon Allan also claimed silver in the C2-C3 1km time trial amid another big day for Australia at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.

"Australia has so much depth in every event. It's gold fever out here," Hoffman said.

See how the day unfolded in our blog below.

AAP

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

World.title: 'We're not going to the finals': Storm set for 16-year first after loss
World.content:
Melbourne Storm coach Craig Bellamy has conceded his side will not be playing finals in 2026, with the club set to miss out for just the fourth time in its history.

The Storm entered the round 22 clash needing to win all five of their remaining games to finish the season on 32 points, which has been needed to make two of the past three finals series.

Missing captain Harry Grant, five-eighth Cameron Munster, and halfback Jahrome Hughes ruled out 90 minutes before kick-off, the Storm threatened a famous upset win when they led 22-16 early in the second half.

But the Bulldogs rallied with the final four tries of the match to record a sixth win in their last seven matches, and leapfrog North Queensland into the NRL top-eight.

The loss ends Melbourne's realistic chance of making the top eight, but Bellamy said he will not be accepting a drop in standards during the final month of the home and away season.

Melbourne Storm coach Craig Bellamy (left) says his side will not be playing finals in 2026. (NRL)

"If anyone wants to go through the motions, if I see that at training and feel that at training, they won't be playing first grade," he said on Friday.

"At the end of the day, every game is important. It's not quite as important as it has been the last few years because we're not going to the finals now.

"But we're out there to play for each other and play for our fans."

The Storm have only missed finals three times since their inaugural season in 1998. The Victorian club missed finals in 2001 and 2002, the two seasons prior to Craig Bellamy becoming head coach.

Roosters put up 82 points for highest NRL score in 91 years The Roosters have scored the third-most points ever seen in Australian rugby league first grade match and beaten the clock against a hapless North Queensland side.

The only time the Storm have not made finals under Bellamy was in 2010, when the club was not allowed to earn premiership points as punishment for salary cap breaches which led to the stripping of the 2007 and 2009 premierships.

The Storm, who have lost the previous two grand finals, have been one of the league's most injury-affected teams in 2026.

Several players have made their NRL debuts this year for the Storm, including playmakers Hayden Watson and Jai Bowden on Friday night.

Bellamy, who is contracted until the end of the 2028 season, said the tough results the club is going through now will hopefully be worth it in coming seasons.

"We haven't got a lot of that experience playing at the moment, with these guys making their debuts or it's their third or fourth game," Bellamy said.

"But next year and the year after, that experience will be really handy for us.

"It's just hard to see past the results at the moment of our games."

Earlier, the Dolphins consolidated fifth place on the NRL ladder with a nervous 28-22 win over the last-placed St George Illawarra Dragons.

Tech.title: With Switch 2, iPhone, and laptop tricks, the Sharge Disk Pro 2 is finally a worthy EDC
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sharge, the company that makes delightful retro Mac-shaped chargers and see-inside batteries, is finally impressing me with a portable SSD. I couldn’t recommend the Sharge Disk, Disk Plus, or even the Disk Pro, but I’d be happy to own the new Disk Pro 2 Ultra.

This isn’t just a drive. It’s a 4K HDMI dock and a USB-C hub too. It’s a veritable USB-C Swiss Army Knife for all your main gadgets: laptop, tablet, phone, Steam Deck, even the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2.

And this USB multitool has built-in MagSafe pattern magnets to stick it to your iPhone, Pixel, or anything where you’re willing to stick a magnetic ring. (One stick-on ring is included.)

In total, this pack-of-playing-cards-sized gadget adds one 4K 144Hz HDMI 2.1 video output, a 5Gbps USB-A port, SD and microSD card readers, plus USB-C passthrough charging — plus a slot to add up to 8TB of solid-state storage with a full-sized M.2 2280 (or smaller M.2 2242 and 2230) stick SSDs.

By plugging in a single cord, I gave my MacBook Pro a second external monitor, four simultaneous sources of storage (SSD, USB flash drive, SD, microSD), and 80W of USB-C PD juice.

And when I plugged in my Android phone and a USB-C iPhone, both of them saw the SSD and showed up on my HDMI screen. It also unlocked 4K60 ProRes video recording on the iPhone… more on that in a minute.

Some of these features exist together in other gadgets, and this 10Gbps external SSD enclosure certainly isn’t the fastest in town now that 40Gbps and 80Gbps enclosures exist. With big 100GB and 195GB transfers, my write speeds with a budget 1TB Lexar NM710 in the Disk Pro 2 averaged around 700MB/s.

I stuck a magnetic ring to my MacBook so I could hang the Disk Pro 2 on the back of its lid. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

But that’s still nothing to sneeze at, and how many enclosures double as USB-C HDMI docks, let alone ones that speak Nintendo’s language and magnetically attach to your phone? How many have a built-in fan to keep them cool? And how many are low-power enough that you can power the HDMI and USB ports from your phone or laptop, no need for a power cord?

Things get a little tricky with the low wattage, though.

First, Sharge is selling two models of the Disk Pro 2, the “Ultra” that requires at least 1.5W of USB-C bus power, and and the “Lite” which needs 5W for its more power-hungry chips (and only does 4K60 over HDMI 2.0, instead of 4K144 over HDMI 2.1).

Second, to achieve such low power draw on the Ultra, it can only route 3W of power from your laptop or phone to a connected SSD, Sharge marketing manager Leo H. tells me. Reviews show my borrowed Lexar NM710 draws more than that during writes — and sure enough, the Disk Pro 2 shut down right after I started ProRes video recording on an iPhone 15 Pro or a big transfer on my Galaxy S25.

(There’s a simple solution: just plug an external USB-C battery or charger into the Disk Pro 2. When I did that, I recorded over five minutes of 4K60 ProRes video, no problem. You could instead try to find a lower-power SSD.)

The main HDMI, USB-A, and USB-C charger port are all on one edge. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

Third, while the HDMI dock does work with both my Switch 2 and my original Switch, Nintendo’s handhelds explicitly check for a relatively specific external power source before docking. Sharge is still tweaking the firmware, but says I currently need a 85W or higher USB-C PD charger plugged in for Switch 2 in particular.

You should also know there’s a long pause before the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 appear on a connected TV, like some other third-party docks, and you won’t get variable refresh rate (VRR) with a Steam Deck or other PC handhelds. It does 4K144 and 4K120 with HDR, but the Steam Deck claims my VRR TV is not VRR-capable with the Disk Pro 2 as a go-between.

And while I successfully worked with a mouse, keyboard, headset, monitor, webcam, and more plugged into the Disk Pro 2 for several days — by daisy-chaining an extra USB hub — I did occasionally see the monitor go dark for a minute, roughly once a day.

There’s still work for Sharge to do. But it’s the first drive from the company that I’d happily add to my go bag.

Sharge Disk (yellow), Disk Plus (silver), Disk Pro (fixed cable), and Disk Pro 2 (detachable cable). Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

The original Sharge Disk was a bulky dongle with a ridiculously noisy tiny fan. The Disk Plus marketed itself as barely-there stylishly thin SSD enclosure that magnetically attaches to your phone, but the magnets were actually a stick-on accessory that made the drive much thicker. The first Sharge Disk Pro had a power port so tiny and recessed that most charging cables wouldn’t fit, and buttons that could actually cut power to the drive mid-transfer.

IMO, Sharge should’ve done more user testing before releasing these predecessors. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

The Disk Pro 2 fixes all that. The included cable is now detachable, the magnets are built-in, the ports are no longer weirdly recessed, the fan isn’t noisy by default, you can turn off that fan entirely, the switch doesn’t cut power to the drive, and the drive has a larger airflow path. Plus, you can bring your own SSD — though I’d prefer toolless swaps to the current screws.

No more heavily recessed USB ports. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

You won’t always see much higher transfer speeds turning that fan on full blast. My 195GB transfer took 4 minutes and 55 seconds with the fan on full power, and 5 minutes 5 seconds with it off — a difference of just 10 seconds, even though I let it cool between tests. The real difference is the one I felt when trying to pick up the Disk Pro 2 afterwards. Without fan, the metal sides were burning hot to the touch.

The Disk Pro 2 Ultra is $75 on Kickstarter for early bird and will be $89 full retail. While the typical caveats apply with Kickstarter projects, Sharge has a very solid track record for shipping (even if it’s hit and miss on design).

Tech.title: Apple’s new AirTags are back down to their best price
Tech.content:
We spotted a great deal on Tile trackers earlier this week that’s still live, but if you’re an iPhone owner, we ultimately recommend Apple’s latest AirTag. Right now, you can pick up a four-pack for $89 ($10 off) at Amazon and Target, matching the bundle’s all-time low price. If you’re a member, Costco also has a deal that throws in a fifth AirTag for free.

A growing number of Bluetooth trackers can tap into Apple’s Find My network these days, but none combine that with Apple’s latest ultra wideband (UWB) chip, which powers even better Precision Finding than before. Precision Finding uses on-screen arrows and distance indicators in the Find My app to guide you directly to a misplaced item, while the second-generation AirTag’s upgraded chip and extended Bluetooth range make it faster and more reliable to locate tags, even in multistory homes. You can also use Precision Finding to find lost items on an Apple Watch, provided you have a Series 9 or later. And if all else fails, the built-in speaker is noticeably louder than before, making it easier to track down an AirTag by sound.

Plus, like its predecessor, the second-generation AirTag comes with a handful of features that are especially useful if you’re traveling this summer. AirTag sharing lets up to five people keep track of the same item, while Apple’s Share Item Location feature allows you to temporarily share an AirTag’s location with participating airlines, including United, Delta, and American Airlines. It’s still a shame Apple doesn’t include a built-in lanyard hole, meaning you’ll need to buy a separate loop or holder, but the tracker continues to use a replaceable CR2032 battery, so you won’t have to replace the entire device when it eventually runs out of power. And at $89 for a four-pack, it’s also a little easier on your wallet today.

Tech.title: Google Earth’s AI deepfake tool only lasted one day
Tech.content:
Google has shut down Google Earth feature it launched Thursday that allowed users to edit satellite images with text prompts using AI. The tool essentially let users create AI deepfakes of the real world using text prompts; Digital Digging’s Henk van Ess, for example, intentionally generated images adding things like refugees near the Mexican border and a bomb crater by a hospital in Gaza. On Thursday, Google’s initial response to van Ess noted that images generated with Nano Banana 2 in Google Earth included a digital watermark and that the company prevented “image creation on harmful topics.”

One day later, Google’s new statement says that “We know that people uniquely trust Google Earth for a reliable view of the world. We’ve seen geospatial professionals using this feature for a range of useful purposes, however we’ve also seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies. So we’re rolling back this feature in Google Earth while we work on implementing stronger guardrails. It’s important to note that generated images didn’t appear in the main Google Earth experience for others to see and were watermarked as AI generated.”

van Ess pointed out that he was able to fool Hive’s AI detection tool with a video generated in Google Earth, showing how the generated media could spread despite the watermarks, and said in his testing, “Nothing was refused, nothing was softened, and nothing suggested I try a different prompt.”

Tech.title: The NHTSA is investigating 1.2 million Tesla vehicles over suspension failure reports
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is probing nearly 1.2 million Tesla vehicles after receiving complaints about a suspension failure that could cause “a loss of vehicle directional control,” as reported earlier by Reuters. The preliminary investigation includes the 2018-2020 Model 3 and 2021-2023 Model Y, according to a filing from the NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation.

The NHTSA says it received 156 complaints about the issue, which “involves the detachment of the front lower lateral link.” In most cases reviewed by the NHTSA, failure occurred with “no advance warning,” but some “cite noises occurring prior to failure.” The NHTSA hasn’t recorded any crashes, injuries, or fatalities related to the potential issue.

This isn’t the first time Tesla dealt with suspension issues. In 2021, Tesla recalled 2,791 Model Y and Model 3 vehicles over a potential suspension defect. It later recalled another round of Model 3 vehicles after the NHTSA found that a “loose fastener could cause the lateral link to separate from the sub-frame.” The NHTSA says the complaints linked to its current investigation don’t appear to be related to these issues.

Tech.title: The ban on robot vacuums won’t make them safer, only worse
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

All the smart home news, reviews, and gadgets you need to know about

No other gadget knows as much about your home as a robot vacuum. They map your space, learn your routines, and many now carry a camera and microphone into every room in your house. As AI gives them a better understanding of what they see, the privacy and security risks these autonomous robots pose are only growing.

That’s why greater scrutiny makes sense, but the ban on foreign-made mobile robots issued by the Federal Communications Commission earlier this week — implemented to address “unacceptable risks to the national security of the United States or the safety and security of United States persons” — doesn’t actually judge products by how secure they are, just where they’re built. It effectively means no new robot vacuums from major companies can enter the US market unless they are built here. And spoiler alert: none are.

This ban means Americans will see fewer new models, slower innovation, and more expensive robot vacuums.

Cybersecurity and manufacturing are not the same thing. If the goal is safer robot vacuums (and robot lawnmowers, companion bots, humanoids, and all the other robots this ban sweeps up), this policy misses the mark. A meaningful security standard for robots would require encrypted map storage, security audits, vulnerability disclosures, and clear data retention policies.

Instead, this ban means Americans will see fewer new models, slower innovation, and more expensive robot vacuums. In short, we’ll get worse vacuums than those we have today.

The Matic robot vacuum is the only model currently assembled in the US, but it doesn’t use enough US-made parts to be considered American made. Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Those failures don’t point toward regulating manufacturing, but toward the need for stronger cybersecurity requirements, like those defined by the government’s Cyber Trust Mark program. But that program doesn’t exist yet, and if it ever does, it will be entirely voluntary.

This manufacturing ban applies to any foreign-made robot, but footnotes in the FCC’s public notice indicate that China is a particular concern, warning that foreign governments could use vulnerabilities found in advanced robotics to access sensitive data. China’s commerce ministry has already called the policy “discriminatory and suppressive against Chinese companies and products.”

A robot vacuum made in Massachusetts isn’t automatically more secure than one made in Shenzhen.

There are real security advantages to domestic robot production. Mehul Nariyawala, president and co-founder of Matic, the only robot vacuum currently assembled in the US (although with too many foreign parts to be considered US-made), points out that domestic manufacturing makes it easier to ensure there are no hardware backdoors and to hold companies accountable for any failures.

But a robot vacuum made in Massachusetts isn’t automatically more secure than one made in Shenzhen. And the FCC’s ban doesn’t actually take steps to ensure they will be.

The robot ban is a carbon copy of those the FCC has issued to Wi-Fi routers and drones over the last few months. So far, it has already granted several waivers to router companies that don’t appear to be moving their manufacturing to the US, which the waivers require. This raises questions about how consistently and fairly the new rules will be enforced and whether they can actually achieve their intended effect.

Today, the practical consequences won’t be better security — the millions of robot vacuums already in American homes remain unaffected, as do any currently sold models. If these really are a risk, and we’ve seen plenty of evidence they can be, why leave the largest source of that risk exactly where it is?

In an optimistic future, the ban could spur American manufacturing. Nariyawala believes it “creates the conditions for American startups to design, engineer, and build all manner of trustworthy robots at scale.” He adds that consumer robots are where robotics manufacturing reaches scale, and the supply chains they require are the same ones defense, industrial, and healthcare robots will depend on. “Get it right, educate customers to demand it, and that domestic supply chain stops being an aspiration and becomes an industry,” he says.

But even if he’s right, and he has more incentive than most to hope he is, that transition will take years. Today’s Matic relies heavily on imported parts, and its price is going up to $1,495 in September, showing how far building these products in the US is from replacing the $300 robot vacuum you can buy at Walmart. Meanwhile, restricting the import of new products means US households will miss out on the next wave of innovations in a fast-moving category.

This was iRobot’s first combination mopping robot, which arrived in 2022. iRobot’s reluctance to adopt lidar and to offer mopping on its robot vacuums hurt it, leading to the company being swallowed up by its Chinese competition. Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Chinese manufacturers may have started out as fast followers, but they have transformed the robot vacuum industry over the past decade. Fierce competition brought better navigation, improved obstacle avoidance, self-emptying docks, and much better mopping systems. That competition also squeezed American manufacturers out of business; iRobot, the American pioneer in this space, filed for bankruptcy last year and is now owned by its Chinese manufacturing partner.

“We see this as part of a broader moment for US robotics, one where the opportunity lies in building domestic leadership.” — Colin Angle

Without that competitive pressure, progress in the US market will slow, and prices will rise. But the competition I would most like to see isn’t who can build the wildest appendages or produce the highest suction power — it’s competing on privacy; I want a robot vacuum that doesn’t require an internet connection to clean my house, maps that stay on the device instead of the cloud; object recognition that runs locally instead of on remote servers; and clear explanations of what data leaves my house and why.

Matic does much of this today, which is one reason it’s my top pick of the many robot vacuums I’ve tested, but it’s a high price to pay for what should be easy features to deliver.

It feels too late to save the American robot vacuum industry. But iRobot co-founder and former CEO Colin Angle, whose startup Familiar Machines & Magic is developing a robotic companion that could fall under this ban, supports the ban’s stated goals. “We see this as part of a broader moment for US robotics, one where the opportunity lies in building domestic leadership,” he told me. “That means continued investment in domestic manufacturing, R&D, and talent, and we’re committed to being part of that effort as the category grows.”

If that is the goal, it may well succeed, but only because it shuts out the competition — which is the same thing Angle argues the Chinese government did to help its burgeoning robot vacuum market a decade ago. But if the goal is making robots more secure, we’re still floundering.

Dreame’s latest X60 robot vacuum could be one of the last the Chinese manufacturer releases in the US. So much for its dream of a huge US expansion. Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Meanwhile, Chinese robot vacuum makers and their US-based users are in limbo. Current products will continue to work and be sold, but the path forward is murky at best. One bright spot is that current products can continue to get security updates; the FCC doesn’t regulate software patches unless they change the radio characteristics of a device.

Kristen Marion, global PR brand lead at Eufy, owned by Anker, told me that they plan to continue to sell, support, and update existing products, adding that “Like others across the industry, we are seeking further clarity on how the rule will be applied to future products, and we will keep our customers informed.” Narwal was more bullish. Yunlin Kong, president of Narwal Overseas Business, told me, “We’re not going anywhere. The US is one of our most important markets, and our commitment here is unchanged.” I reached out to several other Chinese manufacturers who either said much the same thing as Eufy or politely declined to comment.

The concerns driving the ban are legitimate. Robot vacuums deserve more scrutiny than they’ve received, especially as AI expands their capabilities far beyond the original purpose of cleaning our floors. But a broad manufacturing ban that ignores what’s already in your house and can’t tell a secure product from an insecure one isn’t solving that problem. It’s just slowing down the only thing that’s actually worked in our favor: competition. If the government wants safer robot vacuums, don’t regulate where they’re made; regulate how securely they work.

Tech.title: Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream is a quirky life sim that’s worth buying at this discount
Tech.content:
Brad Bourque is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Looking to start your own island paradise full of Miis based on family, friends, and celebrities, but don’t feel like paying full fare? Woot has Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream for Switch on sale for $52.99 (usually $59.95). Sort of like Animal Crossing, but more off-kilter, this unique game sees you building and managing relationships on an island of custom Mii characters. You’ll set up and decorate housing, discover what the inhabitants like and dislike, and watch as they interact with each other and form their own community. This discount is for the region-free international version (so it’ll work in all Switch consoles), and includes improved loading times for Switch 2 owners.

The second game in the series, Living the Dream adds a variety of new tools for you to build your island paradise, which folks have used to recreate simulacrums of celebrities, fictional characters, and real people in their lives. Once they’ve settled in, these characters will mingle in unpredictable ways. They may date, become platonic besties, argue, or possibly get married, frequently leading to situations that are as touching as they are funny.
